{{header:Introduction}}

The beginning of the Karaite Jewish settlement in the Crimean Peninsula, on the northern coast of the Black Sea, is shrouded in mystery. Based on the existing documentary evidence, the Jewish presence (both Karaite and Rabbanite) can be traced to the thirteenth century. What can we learn from these documents about the beginnings of the Crimean Karaite communities? What was the nature of their everyday life; what books did they study, copy, and compose; what were their relations with Rabbanite Jews; how did their communities survive during the difficult periods of their history, such as wars, natural disasters, famine, and despotism? Through this work, we answer these questions with the help of numerous sources (i.e., ancient manuscripts, correspondence between community members, Karaite oral traditions, and other scattered evidence), thus enabling a partial reconstruction of the nature of Karaite life and culture in the Crimea.
{{h3:Karaite Theories on Their Origins in the Crimean Peninsula}}

The Karaites themselves developed many unlikely tales and ahistorical theories regarding their arrival in the Crimean Peninsula. These theories first appeared during the nineteenth century after the annexation of the Crimea by the Russian empress Catherine II in 1783. Some of these stories and tales originated with the famed Karaite Abraham ben Samuel Firkovich (1787–1874), a voracious collector of manuscripts and a leader of the Eastern European and Crimean Karaite communities. According to Firkovich, the Karaites were descendants of the tribe of Judah and the ten lost tribes of Israel, and were brought to the Crimea in the sixth century BCE by the Persian king Cambyses, son of Cyrus, who gave them the Crimean Peninsula as a reward for their services to his throne. Firko- vich also claimed that in the ninth century, the Karaites converted the king of the Khazar Empire{{fn:1}} to Karaite Judaism.
content.comments: [1] The Khazars were a semi-nomadic Turkic people whose empire lasted from the seventh to the tenth centuries. This empire included the territories between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea—the Crimea, Dagestan, the South Caucasus, and the Lower Volga region. In the late eighth century, the Khazar elites may have converted to Judaism. See, for instance, Peter Golden, Haggai Ben-Shammai, and András Roná-Tas (eds.). {{em:The World of the Khazars: New Perspectives—Selected Papers from the Jerusalem 1999 International Khazar Colloquium}}. Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2007.

content.english: 70 Based on these theories, which were unsupported by any documentary evidence, some of Firkovich’s followers tried to prove that the Crimean Karaites had descended from the Khazars and other Turkic peoples and were never part of the Jewish people. One argument was that the Crimean Karaites spoke a Turkic language that was common among the local Tatar population. However, this fact cannot serve as evidence of their Turkic origin because other Jewish communities of the Diaspora (both Karaite and Rabbanite) who spoke local languages—Arabic, Aramaic, Persian, Greek, and many others—were not descended from the native speakers of these languages.

Another Karaite leader of Crimean origin who further developed this Khazar narrative was Seraya Szapszał/Shapshal (1873–1961). He claimed that Karaites were the descendants of Khazars and other Turkic peoples who maintained pagan elements in their religion and culture. Szapszał turned this novel origin story into the narrative officially accepted by Soviet authorities, who tended to favor theories that detached and alienated the peoples of the Soviet Union from their historical roots and cultural heritage. These ahistorical theories are still common today in the territories of Poland and the former USSR.
{{h3:A Brief Overview of the Development of Karaism}}

Karaism began not in the Crimean Peninsula but in other lands, where it gradually took shape as an organized movement with its own beliefs, conceptions, practices, and institutions. This overview traces Karaite intellectual thought from outside the Crimea and explains how these ideas made their way into the Crimean Karaite communities.

The emergence of Karaism as a distinct movement prior to the thirteenth century underwent several stages, starting with the movement of ʿAnan ben David in eighth-century Abbasid Baghdad. ʿAnan rejected the authority of the Oral Law and introduced his own halakhic regulations. The first known use of the appellation {{em:Bnei Miqraʾ}} (or “the Children of Scripture,” a synonym for Karaites) appears in the writings of the first Karaite scholar, Benjamin ben Moses Nahavendi, the author of a {{em:Sefer Miṣvot}} (Book of Commandments), his {{em:Sefer Dinim}} (Book of Laws), and several biblical commentaries. Nahavendi was active in Persia in the first half of the ninth century. A century later, Jacob al-Qirqisani, in his work {{em:Kitab al-Anwar wa-ʾl-Maraqib}} (The Book of the Lights and Watchtowers), written in 937, provides unique information on the history of various Jewish currents, sixteen of which he surveys. He writes extensively on the Karaite movement and on various beliefs, customs, and {{em:halakhah}} in the contemporary Karaite communities of Babylonia. Al-Qirqisani describes the different halakhic practices of the Karaites of Basra, Baghdad, and Tustar regarding the laws of Shabbat and {{em:kashrut}}. He also reports on some aspects of the relations between Karaites and Rabbanites as well as between Karaites and non-Jews. Like many other medieval authors, al-Qirqisani surveys numerous beliefs within Judaism to serve the apologetic goal of identifying the one true religion. He lived in a formative period when Karaism was developing its own worldview, laws, and literature. This process occurred amid the emergence of numerous currents and sects within Judaism and Islam, along with the beginning of religious polemics between Saʿadya Gaʾon (and other Rabbanite sages) and Karaite scholars. These polemics were a decisive factor in developing a multifarious apologetic literature on both sides and in shaping a separate Karaite identity.

The Golden Age of Karaism extended from the early tenth century to the end of the eleventh century, spreading to Egypt, Byzantium, and North Africa, among other places. Its most important center was in Jerusalem, where Karaite immigrants from Islamic lands established a separate quarter with their own stores, synagogues, and study halls. Karaite scholars in Jerusalem polemicized with Rabbanites and composed a rich exegetical, philosophical, and legal literature in Arabic. Designating themselves the “Mourners of Zion,”{{fn:2}} they believed that they were living in the messianic epoch and called on their coreligionists in the Diaspora to gather in Jerusalem to accelerate the redemption. Daniel al-Qumisi, a Karaite from Persia, settled in Jerusalem and urged others to do the same: “Rise and come to Jerusalem and let us return unto the Lord.” However, if every individual could not do so, he insisted that each Diaspora community send at least five people: “But if you will not come because you are running about in tumult and haste after your merchandise, then [at least] send out five men of every city, together with their sustenance.”{{fn:3}} The leaders of the Karaite Mourners of Zion linked the return to the Written Torah with the return to the Land of Israel. Viewing the Talmud as an impediment to the redemption of the Jewish people, they blamed Rabbanites—the majority of whom believed that the return to Jerusalem must be postponed until the coming of the Messiah—for preventing the redemption.
content.comments: [2] Yoram Erder. “The Mourners of Zion: The Karaites in Jerusalem of the Tenth and Eleventh Centuries.” In Meira Polliack (ed.). {{em:Karaite Judaism: A Guide to Its History and Literary Sources.}} Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2003, pp. 213–237. | [3] Leon Nemoy. “Pseudo-Qumisian Sermon to the Karaites.” {{em:Proceedings of the American Academy for Jewish Research}} 43 (1976): 78.

content.english: Young Karaite intellectuals from Byzantium and other communities studied in Jerusalem under the guidance of Karaite sages, such as Salmon ben Yeruḥam, Yussuf al-Basir, and Jeshuah ben Judah. The books of Jerusalem-based Karaite sages were translated from Arabic into Hebrew by Byzantine Karaites, especially Tobias ben Moses, who studied for a number of years in Jerusalem. Tobias and some other Byzantine-educated individuals wanted to make these books accessible to Greek-speaking Karaites who had mastered the Hebrew language but not Arabic.{{fn:4}} Tobias returned toConstantinople in 1048 and became the main authority for the Byzan- tine Karaite communities, issuing halakhic decisions for all these communities.
content.comments: [4] Zvi Ankori. “The Correspondence of Tobias ben Moses of Constantinople.” In J.L. Blau, A. Hertzberg, P. Friedman, and I. Mendelsohn (eds.). {{em:Essays on Jewish Life and Thought: Presented in Honor of Salo Wittmayer Baron}}. New York: Columbia University Press, 1959, pp. 1–38; Zvi Ankori. {{em:Karaites in Byzantium: The Formative Years, 970–1100}}. New York: Columbia University Press, 1959, pp. 49–50.

content.english: The flourishing Karaite center in Jerusalem (as well as the Rabbanite one) came to an end in 1099, when Jerusalem was conquered by the Crusaders, who massacred its population. Following this tragic event, the spiritual center of Karaism shifted to Byzantium, where important Greek-speaking scholars worked, such as Judah Hadassi, Jacob ben Reuven, Aaron ben Joseph, and Aaron ben Elijah.{{fn:5}} Egypt was another large and important Karaite center, which served as a haven for refugees who had escaped the Crusaders’ massacres.
content.comments: [5] Golda Akhiezer. “Byzantine Karaism in the Eleventh to Fifteenth Centuries.” In Robert Bonfil, Oded Irshai, Guy G. Stroumsa, and Rina Talgam (eds.). {{em:Jews in Byzantium: Dialectics of Minority and Majority Cultures.}} Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2012, pp. 723–761.

content.english: The early Ottoman period saw the emergence of scholars of a new kind. Elijah Bashyachi, Caleb Afendopolo, Abraham Bali, and others lived in a period of social and cultural change and a great political shift, specifically the Christian Byzantine Empire falling under the Muslim rule of the Ottoman Empire following the conquest of Constantinople in 1453. In 1455, by the order of Sultan Mehmed II the Conqueror, Jewish communities and other ethnic and religious groups in the new empire underwent {{em:sürgün}}—mass deportation to Constantinople aimed at restoring the devastated capital. The largest Byzantine Karaite community, which was in Adrianople (the former Ottoman capital) before the conquest of Constantinople, was also forced to move to the new capital.

At the end of the fifteenth century, thousands of Rabbanite Jews started arriving in the Ottoman Empire as refugees who had been expelled from Spain and Portugal. They brought with them their knowledge of mathematics, medicine, astronomy, Kabbalah, history, and more, and they had a great cultural impact on the local communities—both Karaite and Greek-speaking Romaniote Jews. Despite the tension between the groups, the Karaites studied the Torah, as well as secular sciences, under the guidance of Rabbanite sages. This period, from the fifteenth to the sixteenth centuries, was a time of cultural encounters between various Jewish communities and of rapprochement between Karaites and Rabbanites.

This atmosphere led to some changes in Karaite {{em:halakhah}}. Elijah ben Moses Bashyachi (1420–1490), the most prominent scholar in the fifteenth century, set forth a number of rulings and systematically expounded on them in his book ʾ{{em:Adderet Eliyahu}}, which serves Karaite believers to this day. Some of these rulings had already been suggested by Elijah’s grandfather or great-grandfather. For instance, his grandfather, one of the leaders of the Adrianople Karaites, permitted leaving candles lit during Shabbat, provided that they were kindled before sunset, as was the Rabbanite practice.{{fn:6}} Elijah Bashyachi, an expert in astronomy, introduced a combination of calendrical calculations and lunar observations and suggested calendrical tables. He established the beginning of the Karaite annual cycle of Torah readings in Tishrei. These and some other legal decisions that he introduced were supported by some members of the Ottoman, Crimean, and Polish–Lithuanian communities, while others rejected his rulings.{{fn:7}}
content.comments: [6] Golda Akhiezer. “Byzantine Karaism in the Eleventh to Fifteenth Centuries.” In Robert Bonfil, Oded Irshai, Guy G. Stroumsa, and Rina Talgam (eds.). {{em:Jews in Byzantium: Dialectics of Minority and Majority Cultures.}} Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2012, pp. 723–761. | [7] In his book, Bashyachi emphasizes that all of his innovations stem from the written text of the Scripture, logical inference, and “the yoke of inheritance.”

content.english: Elijah Bashyachi dealt with exegetical and theological issues. He viewed the Torah as both a divine and a philosophical book, which, nevertheless, was intelligible by common people. According to Bashy- achi, to understand the Torah, one must comprehend logic, mathematics, geometry, astronomy, and Aristotle’s writings. Bashyachi also recommended that his students read {{em:Intentions of Philosophers}} by Al-Ghazali and {{em:ʿEṣ Ḥayyim}} by Bashyachi’s Karaite predecessor Aaron ben Elijah. Bashyachi set forth his own version of the ten principles of faith, which included his belief in the coming of the Messiah. This principle of faith is found among Maimonides’ thirteen principles of faith but is absent from ʾ{{em:Eshkol ha-Kofer}}, the twelfth-century compendium of Judah Hadassi, who was the first Karaite scholar to compose principles of faith. Bashyachi, in fact, adopted many Maimonidean concepts; for instance, Bashyachi’s proof of God’s existence is not based on the Creation but on Maimonides’ Aristotelian arguments. His model of the Messiah also resembles that of Maimonides: the Messiah would be a king from the dynasty of David, bringing an end to the exile and enabling political independence and the reconstruction of the Temple.{{fn:8}}
content.comments: [8] Daniel J. Lasker. “Byzantine Karaite Thought.” In Meira Polliack (ed.). {{em:Karaite Judaism: A Guide to Its History and Literary Sources}}. Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2003, pp. 522–523.

content.english: 100Elijah Bashyachi was considered an expert in astronomy, both in his community and among Rabbanite intellectuals. Bashyachi’s letters to the Karaite community in Lutsk (Volhynia, presently in Ukraine) testify that one of his prominent students, whom he taught astronomy, was R. Moses ben Jacob ha-Goleh of Kiev, the earliest Rabbanite Kabbalist from Eastern Europe and the author of numerous books on Kabbalah and astronomy. R. Moses, who conducted polemics with Eastern European Karaites on halakhic issues and tried to convince them to accept the principles of rabbinic law, studied under Bashyachi during R. Moses’ stay in Adrianople and apparently had extensive contacts in Byzantine–Ottoman Karaite intellectual circles.{{fn:9}}
content.comments: [9] Jacob Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies in Jewish History and Literature}}. Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society of America, 1935, vol. 2, pp. 700–711.

content.english: Another prominent figure was Bashyachi’s younger contemporary, Caleb Afendopolo (c. 1465–1525), a scholar well educated in various spheres of knowledge. He was married to Bashyachi’s sister and supported all of Bashyachi’s legal decisions. Afendopolo also studied under the Rabbanite scholar Mordecai Comtino and corresponded with Moses Kapuṣato, another Rabbanite sage who was a follower of Maimonides’ teachings.{{fn:10}} Afendopolo was a prolific author who penned a number of works on various topics, including {{em:halakhah}} in general and the laws of incest in particular. He also authored {{em:Patshegen Ketav ha-Dat}}, a book on different aspects of reading the weekly Torah portion, and wrote several epistles on ritual slaughter and libation wine. He wrote the astronomical treatises {{em:Mikhlol Yofi}} and {{em:Gal ʿEinai}}, as well as commentaries on the book {{em:Arithmetic of Nicomachus}} and on Ptolemy’s {{em:Almagesta}}. Afendopolo planned to write commentaries on Euclid’s {{em:Book of Roots}} and other works, but he did not carry out these plans. His treatise {{em:Gan Melekh}} is an eclectic work that contains riddles, issues of ethics and customs, and more; {{em:ʾAvi Ner ben Ner}} is a poetical treatise. He also wrote about fifty liturgical poems. In his philosophical book {{em:ʿAsarah Maʾamarot}}, Afendopolo summarized some concepts from Aaron ben Elijah’s {{em:ʿEṣ Ḥayyim}} concerning God’s existence, divine providence, the Creation, and so on. He also completed Bashyachi’s book {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}} after the author’s demise.
content.comments: [10] Jean-Christophe Attias. {{em:Le commentaire biblique: Mordekhai Komtino ou l’herméneutique du dialogue}}. Paris: Cerf, 1991.

content.english: Elijah Bashyachi and Caleb Afendopolo, the last representatives of Byzantine Karaite scholarship, grew up amid traditional concepts but found themselves in a new cultural reality. They strengthened the tendencies of Karaite spiritual life that were especially important in their period: the liberalization of {{em:halakhah}}, the development of thought in accordance with the new ideas of the Jewish intellectual world, and an acceptance of a wider spectrum of knowledge, including philosophy and the sciences. They felt a responsibility to transmit the traditional Karaite legacy and endeavored to do so not only in the Ottoman Empire but also in Eastern Europe and the Crimea.

These developments bring us back to the focus of the present work: the Karaites of the Crimean Peninsula. In the fourteenth century, Karaites, who may have arrived from the Crimea, settled in Eastern Europe. Their major settlements were Troki in Lithuania, Lutsk and Derazhne in Volhynia, and Halich and Lwów in Galicia.{{fn:11}} These communities maintained connections with the Byzantine and Ottoman communities and with the Crimea. Elijah Bashyachi and Caleb Afendopolo played a major role in the formation of Karaite education and {{em:halakhah}} in the Crimea and in Poland–Lithuania. Young Karaites came to Constantinople from Troki, Kiev, and Lutsk to study under these scholars. Bashyachi and Afendopolo corresponded with the community leaders of these cities, instructing them in {{em:halakhah}} and other issues. In a letter in 1483, Karaites from Troki asked Bashyachi to send them {{em:Sefer ha-Miṣvot}} by Tobias ben Moses.{{fn:12}} In his reply in 1484, he wrote:
content.comments: [11] Mikhail Kizilov. {{em:The Karaites of Galicia: An Ethnoreligious Minority among the Ashkenazim, the Turks, and the Slavs, 1772–1945}}. Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2008. | [12] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 1143.

content.english: Concerning the book of Tobias that you asked about and also the commentaries of our sages on twenty-four [books of the Tanakh], we have not yet found a scribe to copy them rapidly because the honorable persons who delivered us your letter could not stay here until these books were to be copied… But now we have given them to the scribes to copy, so let us know who could deliver them to you.{{fn:13}}
To a request by the Troki community to send teachers from Istanbul, Bashyachi responded:

Know that such a man would not leave his family and his home to go to a distant land. Yet for the sake of the covenant of your forefathers, send from amongst yourselves two educated young men with some ability to read the books, and we shall teach them words of Torah and words of wisdom… and afterward they will come to you and propagate Torah in Israel.{{fn:14}}

These scholars’ works, as well as the Byzantine–Ottoman Karaite tradition as a whole, had a great impact on the educational system and religious thought of Crimean Karaites. During the sixteenth century, after the decline of Istanbul as the Karaite spiritual center, the communities of Poland–Lithuania (primarily the city of Troki) became the center of legal authority for all the Eastern European Karaites and, to some extent, for the Crimean communities. During the seventeenth century, the Crimea—primarily Chufut-Kale and Mangup—became an important cultural center with institutions, scholars, study halls ({{em:batei midrash}}), and libraries. The treatises of Byzantine and Ottoman Karaite authors became an important part of the curriculum of study halls from the fourteenth to the twentieth centuries in both Poland–Lithuania and the Crimea.
{{header:Chapter 1. Karaite Communities: From the Golden Horde to the Crimean Khanate}}
{{h2:1.1 At the Crossroads of Civilizations: Between Byzantium and the Golden Horde (From the Thirteenth to the Early Sixteenth Centuries)}}

From the thirteenth to the fifteenth centuries, the Crimean cities of Kaffa and Solkhat were important cultural and economic centers of the Jewish world—Karaite as well as Rabbanite—due to their location at a cultural crossroads between the Byzantine, Persian, Middle Eastern, Caucasian, Italian, and Eastern European Jewish communities. Members of these communities visited or settled in the Crimea, which was, during this period, a stable and safe place to live and engage in economic activity. The immigrants from these communities found Crimea to be a secure haven from persecution and from forcible conversion to Islam or Christianity. Some were brought to the Crimea by the Tatars{{fn:15}} as slaves and were usually redeemed there through the joint efforts of Karaite and Rabbanite communities.
content.comments: [15] The local Turkic-speaking Muslim population of the Crimea.

content.caption: A map of Karaite settlements in the Crimean Peninsula

content.english: The earliest Jewish settlement in the Peninsula appears to have been in the city of Solkhat—now called Staryi Krym (in Russian)—in the Old Crimea, formerly known as Solcati (Italian) and Eski Kırım (Tatar). The city was founded in the 1260s. Staryi Krym, today a small town with a population of 7,000, was established by the Mongols, who invaded the Crimea in the 1230s and built Solkhat to be the capital of the Golden Horde{{fn:16}} within the Peninsula. The Jews settled in Solkhat before the adoption of Islam by the Mongol elites under Khan Uzbek (1312–1342) in the 1320s. Subsequently, Islam gradually became the prevalent religion of the Golden Horde. From the 1260s until the mid-fourteenth century, this regional capital, located on the Silk Road, received merchants from near and distant lands who visited its market, stayed in its caravansaries, and sometimes continued their journey to Middle Asia, Iran, and China. Possibly among them were Jewish immigrants from other parts of the Mongol Empire—Persia or Middle Asia. Solkhat had Muslim, Christian, and Jewish quarters, along with their corresponding public structures.
content.comments: [16] The Golden Horde—one of the largest countries in Europe and Asia during the Middle Ages—was part of the Mongol Empire from 1224 to 1266. Following the fragmentation of that empire, it became a separate khanate, known as the Qıpçaq Khanate or the Ulus of Juchi. The territories under its rule extended from the Danube River to Siberia and included the Pontic steppe, the Crimea, the North Caucasus, Khorezm, Tabriz, northern Afghanistan, Rus principalities, and Itil Bulgars settlements. In the fifteenth century, it disintegrated into several smaller khanates, with the Crimea being one of them. See more on Karaites in Solkhat in Golda Akhiezer. “Hebrew Manuscripts and Scribes in the Crimean Golden Horde (Solkhat).” {{em:Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae}} 72.3 (2019): 333–354.

content.english: The origins of the Karaite community (as well as the Rabbanite community) in Solkhat are unclear. Its members may have immigrated from Byzantium and from different parts of the Mongol Empire, namely Persia or Middle Asia. Among the inscriptions in manuscripts owned by local Karaites, we find both Greek names, especially women’s names (e.g., Euphrosyne, Archontopola, and Khursi), and Persian names (e.g., Suleiman ha-Parsi, Hoja Ibrahim Shah, and Bahadur). These names represented the owners of these manuscripts, those who donated them to a synagogue or study hall, participants in their sale or purchase, or witnesses to these deals. This information was recorded in a manuscript, where it could be used as testimony of its status.

The earliest evidence of a Karaite presence in Solkhat comes from the Byzantine Karaite scholar Aaron ben Joseph the Physician (c. 1250–1320). In his {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}, he mentions that in 1278, a Karaite–Rabbanite calendrical dispute took place in Solkhat. However, he does not provide any details about these communities. The opinion that Aaron ben Joseph was born in Solkhat, although widespread among scholars, is unjustified. Neither {{em:Sefer ha-Miv}}-{{em:ḥar}}’s reference to the dispute in Solkhat nor other sources support this view, and the Karaite author Mordecai ben Nisan claims that Aaron ben Joseph originated in Constantinople.{{fn:17}} Mordecai ben Nisan’s claim is supported by the fact that Aaron ben Joseph was born before the establishment of Solkhat and that his mother tongue was Greek (he used Greek words in his writings).
content.comments: [17] See Mordecai ben Nisan. {{em:Dod Mordekhay}}. Vienna, 1830, p. 71; repr. Ramle: Ḥevrat Haṣlaḥah Li-Vnei Miqraʾ, 1966 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Another early substantiation of the Karaite presence in Solkhat was published by Ephraim Deinard, a collector of Jewish manuscripts from the Russian Empire.{{fn:18}} Deinard published a Karaite sale contract for the Pentateuch, with a colophon (a note by a scribe or author) dated 1322 on one of its pages (see its text at the end of Section 1.2).
content.comments: [18] Ephraim Deinard. {{em:Massaʾ Qrim}} [The Burden of the Crimea]. Warsaw, 1878, pp. 129–130 (in Hebrew).

content.english: The antiquity of the Karaite community of Solkhat is also reflected in a number of Karaite oral traditions, some of which were recorded and elaborated on by Karaite leaders in Eastern Europe during the nineteenth century. According to these traditions, Solkhat was the most ancient Karaite settlement in the Crimea during the Middle Ages, where the Karaites arrived during the Tatar conquest of the Crimea. The Russian historian Piotr I. Köppen testifies that in 1833, a tradition prevalent among the Crimean Karaites was that their forefathers had come to the Crimea along with the Tatars, Bukharans, and Circassians.{{fn:19}} Concerning the early presence of Karaites in Solkhat, Benjamin Duvan, the Karaite leader from Evpatoria in the eighteenth century, testifies to the existence of a Karaite settlement there about 500 years earlier (see Section 2.6).{{fn:20}}
content.comments: [19] Piotr Köppen. {{em:Krymskii Sbornik}} [The Crimean Collection]. Saint Petersburg: The Imperial Academy of Sciences, 1837, p. 290 (in Russian). | [20] Benjamin Duvan. “Travels of Benjamin Duvan ha-Karai from the Crimea.” In Abraham Yaari (ed.). {{em:Masaʿot Ereṣ Yisrael}}. Tel Aviv: Modan, 1996, p. 463 (in Hebrew).

content.english: In recent years, one of the most important developments to have shed light on the life of the Jewish communities of Solkhat was the discovery of a thirteenth-century synagogue in Staryi Krym (medieval Solkhat). Beginning in 2015, this synagogue has been excavated by Dr. Mark Kramarovsky, a historian and archaeologist from the State Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg. Preliminary conclusions suggest that the synagogue was located in the most ancient part of the city—the Jewish (Karaite and Rabbanite) quarter. This synagogue could accommodate more than 200 people, an indication that the congregation numbered about a thousand. We cannot definitively conclude whether this synagogue was built by a Rabbanite or Karaite community, but all existing documents testify that it was in the Karaite community’s possession. A “Great Synagogue”—apparently this one—is mentioned in a Karaite colo­phon dated 1390 in a manuscript of the book of Deuteronomy. The colophon says that this book was consecrated to the Solkhat Great Synagogue by Eliyahu ben Ṣadoq ha-Koen in the name of his mother, Malkah bat Moses.

The Rabbanite scholar from Solkhat, R. Abraham Qirimi, author of {{em:Sefat ha-ʾEmet}} (The Language of Truth), testifies in the fourteenth century that he had a Karaite student, Ḥizkiyah ben Elḥanan, a descendant of Gedalyah ha-Nasi. {{em:Sefat ha-ʾEmet}} is a rationalistic commentary on the Pentateuch written in 1358, and according to the work’s foreword and introductory poem, Qirimi composed it at the request of Ḥizkiyah. Qirimi called Ḥizkiyah “a friend in thoughts,” “full of knowledge,” “a Karaite prince,” and “head of officials and aristocrats.” These last two characterizations indicate that Ḥizkiyah was apparently a Karaite community leader in Solkhat. That a learned Karaite leader was a student of the greatest Crimean Rabbanite scholar is testimony to the intellectual collaboration between local Karaites and Rabbanites.{{fn:21}}
content.comments: [21] {{em:Sefat ha-ʾEmet}} reflects a rationalistic tendency common in Byzantine Jewish scholarship of this period, which had a strong focus on linguistic and philosophical textual commentary.

content.english: In the mid-fifteenth century, Haji Devlet Giray Khan established a new state that was independent of the Golden Horde—the Crimean Khanate, with its capital in Bakhchesaray—marking the beginning of a period of gradual decline for Solkhat. The Rabbanite population, as well as part of the Karaite community, migrated from Solkhat to the neighboring cities of Kaffa, Chufut-Kale, and Mangup. However, we still find a number of Karaite manuscripts from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries mentioning the “Great Synagogue” of Solkhat. The local Karaites made every possible effort to maintain their depleted community and keep the synagogue open. From two letters (1755) sent by the Karaite community of Chufut-Kale to the communities of Kaffa and Gözleve (Evpatoria), we learn that these Crimean communities tried to support Elijah Pasha, who planned to relocate from Chufut-Kale to Solkhat, apparently to function as the head of this community. Furthermore, at least two Karaite marriage contracts from Solkhat have survived, dated 1610 and 1650, which are now preserved in the National Library of Russia in Saint Petersburg. The latter contains a detailed list of the bride’s dowry.

The language spoken in Solkhat from the thirteenth to the early fifteenth century was Turkic-Qıpçaq, which was common in the Golden Horde and Mamluk Egypt. This language was gradually replaced in the Crimea by other Turkic-Tatar languages, possibly from the first half of the fifteenth century, after the collapse of the Golden Horde. As a result of Karaite immigration from Solkhat to Eastern Europe—Lithuania, Podolia, Volhynia, and Galicia— Turkic-Qıpçaq not only survived among their descendants as a spoken language but also became their literary language, in which Karaite sages created a rich literature, including liturgical poems, numerous translations of the Torah, and philosophical texts. The earliest liturgical Karaite poems in Qıpçaq are from the pen of the greatest Karaite sage of Lithuania, R. Isaac ben Abraham of Troki (1533–1594),{{fn:22}} well known for his anti-Christian polemical work {{em:Ḥizzuk ʾEmunah}}, which was translated from Hebrew into most European languages, including Latin and Yiddish. In the twentieth century, poetry, prose, and even newspapers were published in Poland in Karaite Qıpçaq. However, the spoken language of the Crimea has undergone considerable changes over time; with the Crimean Karaites shifting to the Tatar language, the Eastern European and Crimean Karaites can no longer understand each other.
content.comments: [22] Mikhail Kizilov. “Two Piyyutim and a Rhetorical Essay in the Northern (Troki) Dialect of the Karaim Language by Isaac ben Abraham Troki.” {{em:Judaica}} 1.2 (2007): 64–75.

content.english: The city of Kaffa (today called Feodosia), which neighbored Solkhat, was established by the Genoese in the 1270s. By the end of the thirteenth century, it had become a flourishing seaport and one of the foremost trade and transit centers for the ports of Asia Minor, such as Trebizond, Sinope, and, most significantly, Constantinople. Kaffa was an important enclave of Christian Europe in the Muslim world. The second half of the thirteenth century seems to have been a period of Jewish settlement in Kaffa. As previously mentioned, Kaffa was a crossroads between the Christian and Muslim lands from which Jewish immigrants came. As in the case of Solkhat, we have no evidence of whether Karaites and Rabbanites arrived in Kaffa from the same land(s) and at the same time.

Some details of the life of the Kaffian Karaite Solomon ben Abra- demonstrate the connections of this community with other com- munities during the fifteenth century.{{fn:23}} In 1450, Solomon studied in Adrianople, and in the 1480s, he resided in Constantinople. He corresponded with the Karaite community of Kiev on halakhic issues and eventually relocated to Lutsk with his large library. Solomon apparently intended to serve in Lutsk as a teacher or even as a spiritual leader, a position he could not attain in Constantinople; he died in Lutsk in 1488.{{fn:24}} In a letter to their coreligionists in Lutsk, the Constantinople community leaders wrote that Solomon had left behind a penniless wife, having spent more than 30,000 aspers of her dowry, and that she urgently needed support to raise her three orphaned grandchildren. In light of these circumstances, they asked the leaders of the Lutsk community to sell Solomon’s library and send them the proceeds. This sad story reveals the extent of the connections between the Karaite communities and of the book-transmission pathways between the Crimea, Constantinople, and Eastern Europe, as well as the spread of education from Byzantium (and later from the Ottoman Empire) to other Karaite centers in the late fifteenth century.
content.comments: [23] We learn about him from correspondence published by Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 711–714. | [24] Ibid., doc. 119, pp. 1175–1177.

content.english: The German soldier and traveler Johann Schiltberger reported in the first decade of the fifteenth century that two synagogues were located in the quarter of Kaffa where Karaites and Rabbanites lived together.{{fn:25}} Additional early Karaite centers were located in the fortress cities of Qirq-Yer (Chufut-Kale){{fn:26}} and Mangup, both of which were situated in the mountainous areas of the Crimea. According to epigraphical sources, the Karaites had settled in Qirq-Yer following the Tatar conquest; the earliest tomb inscriptions in the Karaite cemetery of this city are dated 1364 and 1387. In 1443, Haji Devlet Giray Khan relocated the capital of the Crimean Khanate to Bakhchesaray. The Tatar population of Qirq-Yer relocated to Bakhchesaray (following the order of the khan); nevertheless, the Armenian and Karaite populations remained in Qirq-Yer, and some Karaites relocated from Solkhat to Qirq-Yer.
content.comments: [25] Johann H. Schiltberger. {{em:Reisebuch}}. Tübingen, 1885, p. 63. | [26] The name Chufut-Kale (or Chufut-Qaleh) means “The Jews’ Fortress,” and Karaites often referred to it simply as Kale.

content.english: Mangup (Theodoro) was a Christian principality that emerged in the second half of the fourteenth century and existed until the Ottoman conquest in 1475. Its princes were in kinship with the ruling Byzantine dynasties. Mangup’s population included Goths, Alans, Armenians, Greeks, and Jews. The oldest inscriptions surviving in the Mangup Karaite cemetery date back to the fifteenth century. The earliest, dated 1457, is dedicated to Euphrosyne bat Joseph, who may have been part of a group of refugees fleeing Constantinople following its conquest by the Ottomans in 1453. However, one cannot exclude the possibility that prior to this dramatic event, there were already Greek-speaking Jews—both Karaites and Rabbanites—in the principality of Theodoro.

In 1475, the Ottomans conquered Kaffa and massacred and expelled the Genoese from Kaffa and other coastal cities. Starting in that year, the coastal Kaffa (and Mangup) came under the direct rule of the Ottoman Empire, while the rest of the territory of the Crimean Peninsula became a vassal state of the empire—the Khanate of Crimea. Jewish communities survived in Kaffa but went into a gradual decline, and from the late fifteenth to the early sixteenth centuries, new Rabbanite and Karaite centers in Mangup, Chufut-Kale, Gözleve, and Karasubazar emerged or increased in population due to immigration from Kaffa and Solkhat.
{{h2:1.2 Books, Libraries, and Scribes}}

Most of our knowledge about the life and culture of the Crimean Karaites in this early period comes from various inscriptions found on the pages of manuscripts, among them colophons, sale contracts, and ownership notes, which provide data about their authors, copyists, and buyers. Among the other information contained in these inscriptions, the authors or scribes of these books would sometimes write their names, their locations, the reason for copying, and the date of the work’s completion. In addition to the date and place, the sale contracts as a rule included the names of the participants to the transaction, the names of witnesses, and the amount paid for the book. These and other notes and inscriptions were usually written at the end of a book, in its margins, or in any free space on its pages, and they are a valuable source of information about community members, their libraries, their education, and contemporary events.

Manuscripts, mostly codices,{{fn:27}} were quite expensive before the emergence of the printing press (in the Jewish world, in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries); therefore, in addition to their educational purposes, manuscripts served as a means of investing money. We have even found books listed in brides’ dowry documents attached to marriage contracts. Due to the lack of Karaite printing houses, the Karaites in most of their communities continued to copy texts by hand until the twentieth century; small communities could not conduct such an expensive business and printed only limited quantities of books. Although the Rabbanite printers did not always agree to publish Karaite books, the Rabbanite printing house in Istanbul, which opened in 1506, printed a considerable number of Karaite works. In the Crimea, Karaite printing houses existed only during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The first one was active in 1734, another operated from 1804 to 1806 (both were in Chufut-Kale), and the last one functioned in Evpatoria (Gözleve) from 1834 to 1868.{{fn:28}}
content.comments: [27] A Hebrew codex was a handwritten book, usually constructed from sheets of paper, vellum, or a combination of both. In the early Middle Ages, codices supplanted scrolls (except in the case of Torah scrolls), which were less convenient to use and much more materially expensive because the text on a scroll was written on only one side. | [28] Barry D. Walfish. “Karaite Press and Printing.” In Meira Polliack (ed.). {{em:Karaite Judaism: A Guide to Its History and Literary Sources}}. Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2003, pp. 925–959.

content.english: Due to the huge demand for books, the profession of scribe was crucial in Karaite (as well as Rabbanite) society, although the scribe might have additional occupations. Manuscripts were usually copied by educated community members in response to a request by other members; the scribes sometimes also made copies for their own use. Manuscripts, colophons, and ownership notes often indicate the contents of the copyists’ libraries. Whether a particular title was copied—and how many copies were made—was primarily dictated by the needs of the market and much less by the decisions of the community leaders.{{fn:29}} Thus, Crimean Karaite private and communal libraries contained classical Byzantine Karaite books and works by Rabbanite authors on astronomy, philosophy, medicine, grammar, and other subjects. Many treatises, such as medieval Hebrew translations of the texts of Aristotle, Ibn Rushd’s commentaries on Aristotle, and the works of Avicenna (Ibn Sina), were also in demand among educated Crimean Karaites.
content.comments: [29] Malachi Beit-Arié. “The Individualistic Nature of Hebrew Medieval Book Production and Consumption.” {{em:Zion}} 65.4 (2000), pp. 441–451 (in Hebrew).

content.english: The earliest Karaite scribes in the Crimea are known, again, only from various notes on manuscripts. There is evidence for at least two Karaite scribes, both active in Solkhat, and both later migrating to Kaffa. One of them, Ḥizkiyah ben Elijah, copied a considerable number of manuscripts from 1359 to 1376. In some, he gives his full name and genealogy for seven generations: “Ḥizkiyah ha-Levi, the scribe, son of R. Elijah son of R. Ḥizkiyah son of the honorable R. Elijah, the teacher, son of Abraham son of Rav Shemuel son of R. Eliezer.” In addition to the books of the Pentateuch, in 1376, Ḥizkiyah copied the grammatical treatise {{em:Sefer ha-Shorashim}} by David ben Joseph Kimḥi and added his own poem after the colophon.{{fn:30}} In 1393, this copy was sold in Kaffa by his son, Moses ben Ḥizkiyah, the teacher, as evidenced by the sale contract at the end of that copy.
content.comments: [30] David ben Joseph Kimḥi. {{em:Sefer ha-Shorashim}}. RNL EVR 1 78, 246v (colophon by Hizkiya), 247v (sale contract).

content.english: Ḥizkiyah copied Jacob ben Reuven’s {{em:Sefer ha-ʿOsher}} twice, as well as Aaron ben Joseph’s {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}. The latter book, as reflected in its subsequent sale contract (1484), was sold in Istanbul by one Isaac ha-Ṣarṣurto the aforementioned Karaite scholar from Adrianople, Caleb Afendopolo, and the contract was signed by a witness named Shabbetai ben Mordecai Bashyachi.{{fn:31}} It is unclear under what circumstances Ḥizkiyah’s copy of {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}} arrived in Istanbul, but the historical context may shed some light. A Karaite community from Adrianople lived in Istanbul at this time, having been forced to move there following a {{em:sürgün}} and probably having lost part of their literary patrimony during the relocation. Writing in the years after the {{em:sürgün}}, Elijah Bashyachi (c. 1420–1490) laments that he failed to find any Karaite books on the schism between Karaites and Rabbanites. Shabbetai Provato (Provadia, Bulgary), a contemporary of Bashyachi, also mentions a shortage of Karaite books during this period.{{fn:32}} The conflagration in Adrianople in March 1446 during the soldiers’ (janissaries’) rebellion, in which the market and the central part of the city were consumed by flames, could also have been the reason for the book shortage in this Karaite community. In any case, they valued books highly and looked for adequate sources in more stable Jewish population centers, such as the Crimea.
content.comments: [31] Aaron ben Joseph. {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}. Oxford: Bodl. MS Opp. Add. Qu. 46. The name “Hizkiya ha-Levi” is marked on fol. 71v. | [32] See Elijah Bashyachi. ʾ{{em:Adderet Eliyahu}}, with a foreword by Zvi Ankori. Ramle: National Council of Karaite Jews in Israel, 1965–66, the beginning of the unpaginated introduction; Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, n. 11, p. 299.

content.english: Ḥizkiyah’s name is also found in the inscriptions on the ancient surviving Rabbanite manuscript of the Latter Prophets with Babylonian punctuation; it was copied in 916. This unique manuscript, which arrived in Kaffa under unknown circumstances, was sold in 1378, possibly in Kaffa, and Ḥizkiyah signed the sale contract as one of the witnesses to this deal.
In another manuscript (a codex of the Pentateuch), we find the signature of Ḥizkiyah’s father, Elijah ben Ḥizkiyah, as a witness of the deed of sale of this same book in 1322:

[This is] the testimony we, undersigned, bear, [today] first weekday, the eighteenth of the month of Iyar, 5082 [1322] of the Creation, according to our counting here in the city of Solkhat, in the land of the Crimea. On this day, Elijah ben R. Joseph sold this book to Elijah ben R. Caleb for 280 Crimean coins from the kingdom of King Uzbek. He, Elijah ben R. Joseph, received the money from the hand of Elijah ben R. Caleb… and thus was completed the transaction—no refund, no ruling, and nothing else—and anyone who will object [to this deal]—his words will be null and void as broken pottery—be it from a son, a daughter, brother, sister, or any close or distant relative. Everything we have heard from both parties, we have written down as evidence for the day of tomorrow and the days after, to attest for the record that [this] testimony is valid and in effect. R. Joseph ben Mar Abraham the departed, Abraham ha-Ger [the proselyte] and I…, Elijah ben Ḥizkiyah the teacher, may the Spirit of the God rest on him.{{fn:33}}
content.comments: [33] It was published by Ephraim Deinard (1846–1930), a self-educated historian from the Russian Empire. See Deinard, {{em:Massaʾ Qrim}}, pp. 129–130.

content.english: Two other inscriptions provide important evidence of the existence of a communal Karaite library and educational institutions in Solkhat; these inscriptions appear in another copy of the Pentateuch. The first inscription states that this Pentateuch codex was consecrated by a certain Shefi ben Abraham to the community of Solkhat so that “the orphans can use it for studying.” One of the witnesses to the consecration was “Abraham ha-Levi, the legislator” ({{em:ha-meḥokek}}), who later adds another inscription to this Pentateuch: “It was consecrated by myself, Abraham ben R. Ḥizkiyah, in its study hall [{{em:be-midrasho…}}] in the month of Tammuz, in 5096 [1336] from the Creation.”{{fn:34}} These words indicate that there was a Karaite study hall in Solkhat, one chosen by Abraham ben Ḥizkiyah to be a suitable place for this book (consecrated to the community; it seems to have been previously housed in the synagogue). This person, according to his name and the date of the contract, was possibly an uncle of the scribe Ḥizkiyah, son of Elijah Halevi.
content.comments: [34] Pentateuch. RNL EVR I B 5, 124v.

content.english: Another scribe from Solkhat was Joshua ben Naḥamu Qirimi, who lived in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries and, like Ḥizkiyah, migrated to Kaffa. In Kaffa, he copied some fragments from Karaite books composed by Elijah Bashyachiand Caleb Afendopolo. Joshua fiercely criticizes his coreligionists in his colophon (1502), where he explains the purpose of copying these fragments. He expresses his worry about the Jews of Kaffa and states that they

leave our Torah… and are exerting themselves only with money, silver and gold, and pursue the fulfillment of their desires—food and drink… thus I decided to disseminate the Torah among them and among all communities of Israel, the communities of Yeshurun. I lift up my eyes to You, to You who sit enthroned in heaven [Psalms 123].{{fn:35}}
content.comments: [35] Joshua ben Naḥamu Qirimi (scribe). Miscellaneous Karaite Texts. RNL EVR I 635, 8r.

content.english: He is probably referring here to all Jewish communities, including the Rabbanite ones. None of the available sources indicates to what extent his critique reflected the real state of affairs. However, given that the Crimean communities possessed a great number of books in different genres, that were either brought from other lands or copied in the Crimea, it may be assumed that his rhetoric contains some exaggeration, which is typical of sermonic reproaches, and that the reality was somewhat different.

Some of the other manuscripts in Joshua ben Naḥamu’s library were his own works, the earliest known original books to have been composed in the Crimea. This collection of texts was apparently completed by a certain Moses ben Ṣadoq, who inserted his own liturgical poem into Joshua’s texts. Joshua’s writing indicates that he had a son-in-law named R. Moses, which means his son-in-law may have been Moses ben Sadoq.

Among the texts of Joshua’s personal library{{fn:36}} were a treatise on Karaite ritual slaughter and a text dealing with biblical chronology (the intervals between various events, such as the Creation, the Deluge, and the Exodus from Egypt). The author of this treatise further mentions the Hasmonean and Roman periods and concludes with Muhammad’s flight from Mecca to Medina. In addition to the works he authored, Joshua ben Naḥamu’s manuscript collection contained sermons by David ben Elazar ibn Pakuda and the tractate {{em:Milot ha-Higayon}} by Maimonides. In 1504, Joshua ben Naḥamu also copied the treatise {{em:ʾEshkol ha-Kofer}} by the twelfth-centuryByzantine Karaite scholar Judah Hadassi. The last mention of Joshua ben Naḥamu is found in a sale contract (1548) in one of the texts of a miscellaneous collection of Rabbanite manuscripts owned by a Karaite:
content.comments: [36] Joshua ben Naḥamu Qirimi (author). Miscellaneous Texts. IOS B 58.

content.english: This precious book is {{em:The Guide for the Perplexed}} by our teacher the Gaon, the honorable R. Moses the son of honorable R. Maimonides… in the holy community of Qirq-Yer [Chufut-Kale], may its Rock keep and safeguard it, that we bought it from Baba the son of honorable Rav Raphael of blessed memory, the son of honorable R. Joshua ben Naḥamu of blessed memory… and a buyer was Moses the son of R. Elijah of blessed memory… 1548…{{fn:37}}
content.comments: [37] Joshua ben Naḥamu Qirimi’s library. Miscellaneous Texts. RNL EVR I 479, 1v.

content.english: Apparently, Baba, the seller of this book, was Joshua’s grandson, who (or whose father) moved from Kaffa to Chufut-Kale and brought Joshua’s library with him. The collection contains the end of {{em:The Guide for the Perplexed}}, a philosophical lexicon by Samuel ibn Tibbon, and Al-Tabrizi’s commentary on Maimonides in its Hebrew translation.{{fn:38}} These texts may have been acquired by Joshua ben Naḥamu from the Rabbanites of Solkhat or Kaffa, for he signed his name in an acrostic on one of their pages.
content.comments: [38] Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Abu Bakr al-Tabrizi was a Persian Muslim scholar of the second half of the thirteenth century who commented (in Arabic) on the twenty-five propositions appearing at the beginning of the second part of Moses Maimonides’s {{em:Guide for the Perplexed}}. Tabrizi’s commentary was translated twice into Hebrew.

content.english: In sixteenth-century Crimea, we find among the original Crimean80 compositions the first historical chronicle written by Karaite authors. Such chronicles, which were composed until the nineteenth century, recorded historical events: wars, plagues, ethnic conflicts, prices, taxation, court intrigues, government policy, exemplary stories, and dreams. The authors focused on the history of nations but also wrote about the affairs of the Rabbanite and Karaite communities.

The overwhelming majority of the surviving Hebrew chronicles from the Crimea were composed by Karaite authors. The earliest known chronicle (1524) was written by a Karaite author, Samuel ben Naḥamu of Kaffa,{{fn:39}} who visited Egypt. Samuel describes the rebellion led by Ahmad Pasha against Suleiman I and the persecutions of the Karaite and Rabbanite communities during the uprising.{{fn:40}}
content.comments: [39] Samuel ben Naḥamu. Various Notes from 1523–1534. RNL EVR I 745. | [40] This text was published in Adolf Neubauer. {{em:Aus der Petersburger Bibliothek: Beiträge und Documente zur Geschichte des Karäerthums und der karäischen Literatur}}. Leipzig: Oskar Leiner, 1866, 118 n. xxia.

content.english: A number of early Kabbalistic texts circulated in Kaffa, reflecting, to some extent, the kind of intellectual exchange and mystical genres common in the Crimea. The earliest original Kabbalistic text from Kaffa was written by the aforementioned Karaite author Samuel ben Naḥamu.{{fn:41}} He recounts his own dream, in which he experienced a revelation of being transported to the Temple of Jerusalem and even saw God. The recording of dreams was a widespread phenomenon among Karaite authors in the Crimea and Eastern Europe, but all surviving texts date from the seventeenth century. The Kabbalistic texts that survived in private Karaite libraries are numerous and include many classical texts that may have been copied by Rabbanite individuals (see below).
content.comments: [41] Samuel ben Naḥamu. A Dream. RNL EVR I 745.

content.english: {{h3:1.2.1 {{em:Folklore, Exemplary Stories, and Historical Chronicles of the Crimean Karaites}}}}

The Crimean Karaites have a rich folklore that includes oral traditions, legends, anecdotes, proverbs, parables, riddles, and songs. These were all created in the Karaite ethnolect of the Crimean Tatar language. As early as the nineteenth century, the Crimean Karaites recorded these materials in special anthologies of different texts called {{em:mejuma}} s (collections), which were usually written in Hebrew characters and compiled and preserved by many Karaite families. These anthologies were typical of other Turkic-speaking groups of the Crimean Peninsula: namely, Rabbanite Jews (Krymchaks) and Crimean Tatars. Both the Crimean Rabbanites and the Tatars had similar text collections called {{em:jonka}} s (collections). Some themes of Karaite {{em:mejuma}} s’ are akin to those appearing in Tatar {{em:jonka}} s and contain topoi typical of Tatar and Ottoman oral and literary traditions. Dozens of {{em:mejuma}} s are preserved in manuscripts in different libraries and private collections.

Karaite proverbs and sayings from the Crimea (as well as from Eastern Europe) usually concerned the spheres of everyday life: family relations, good and evil, and attitudes toward other nations and their own community. These materials reflect, to some extent, the Karaites’ way of life, mentality, and self-perception, as well as stereotypes regarding other ethnic and religious groups, such as a proverb that signifies a Karaite view of the differences between and Christians: “The ringing bells call people to the church, while to the {{em:kenasa}} [Karaite synagogue] the community members hurry by themselves.” {{em:Mejuma}} s also contain various poems and songs. Some are holiday songs, such as Shabbat hymns or Purim songs; others are dedicated to Jerusalem or composed in honor of some event—a wedding, circumcision, or funeral.

One of the specific genres of Karaite folksongs is the {{em:chin}} or {{em:mane}} (from Arabic {{em:maʾna}}), a “ringing sound.” These improvised songs were sung by young men to young women. The songs included words of love, praise for the beauty of a beloved, and various kinds of jokes and jests.

Sometimes, {{em:mejuma}} s contained historical chronicles depicting events such as wars and community affairs. This literary genre was widespread in Hebrew among the Crimean Karaites. In addition to historical events, one can find accounts of miracles and stories from the biographies of nineteenth-century community leaders. All these genres occur not only as part of {{em:mejuma}} s but also as separate texts that were prevalent in Karaite communities.

The biographical genre of Crimean Karaite writings consisted of exemplary stories intended to extol the protagonist to the readers (or listeners). One such example is a story about Samuel ben Abraham Aga (1717–1770), known as “the Exilarch,” the head of the Karaite community of Chufut-Kale and the “court Jew,” who served as counselor for the Crimean khan Qirim Giray in the mid-eighteenth century. This story relates how the khan called upon Samuel Aga to convert to Islam, but Samuel refused. Samuel told him that a betrayal of the faith of his ancestors would make him faithless, even to the khan. The khan then dismissed and humiliated Samuel. Subsequently, the khan became convinced of Samuel’s loyalty and honesty. The khan brought Samuel back to the court three months later and raised Samuel above all his ministers.

Whether such an event involving these two real persons actually occurred or was fabricated sometime later in praise of the Aga family is unknown.{{fn:42}} In any event, although conversion to Islam was uncommon among the Crimean Karaites, there was the occasional individual who left the fold, and the objective of the story may well have been to offer encouragement to those who were vacillating. Another story (recorded in the eighteenth century) that demonstrates the obligation to observe the Torah’s commandments and perform good deeds concerns an unnamed “pious man” who “saved one soul of Israel” (i.e., redeemed a captive) when his own life was in danger. This deed enabled him to refute false charges that this “pious man” had murdered the father of his denouncer; the hero was saved from a death sentence by his charity and compassion, while the villain was put to death. These and similar texts were never published and are preserved in manuscripts. Most of these stories spread among Karaite communities as oral tales and were written down only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
content.comments: [42] Regarding the Aga family, see Section 2.2.

content.english: As previously mentioned, starting in the sixteenth century, we find historical chronicles by Karaite authors. This genre was apparently influenced by the sixteenth-century Rabbanite (Sephardic) historical writings in the Ottoman Empire, which constituted an effort to reconceptualize Jewish and general history following the various expulsions of Jews from Europe, especially the Spanish expulsion. Many such books were printed and circulated in Istanbul, and some were acquired by the Rabbanite and Karaite Jews who brought them to the Crimea. Furthermore, these books may have been influenced by the Tatar chronicles written in the same period by the chroniclers of the courts of the Crimean khans. This genre of Tatar writing appears to have been familiar to Karaite scholars, some of whom were courtiers or had ties with appointees of the khans. However, there was a fundamental difference between Tatar and Jewish chroniclers; whereas the Tatar chronicles were typically written by decree of the ruler and lauded the deeds of the Crimean khans, hence expressing specific political and ideological views, the Jewish chroniclers composed documents on their own initiative, selected their own topics, and, in some cases, offered their personal opinions and interpretations of events. In addition, the lifestyle of the Crimean Karaites, whose economic condition was relatively stable, enabled them to engage in writing that lacked a defined objective and to compose works or notes on matters unrelated to {{em:halakhah}} or exegesis. Karaites sometimes spent time in the company of Christians and Tatars in bathhouses and cafés, where they heard news and stories that they occasionally committed to writing.

Events and news of everyday life—wars, natural disasters, ethnic strife, price fluctuations, government policy, court intrigues, dreams, and miracle stories—were of interest to the general public. Hence, individuals with sufficient command of Hebrew enjoyed reading such texts, which served them in the same capacity as {{em:belles lettres}} or newspapers. One of the most significant chronicles was authored by the Karaite Azariah ben Elijah, a community leader of Chufut-Kale, whose life story is almost entirely unknown. Azariah’s name appears in a document dated 1784 that lists Crimean sages, where he is designated “the sage and master, our master, may his Rock keep and safeguard him, son of the sage and master, our master Elijah, the scribe and {{em:ḥazzan}}, of blessed righteous memory.”{{fn:43}}
content.comments: [43] See the List of Karaites in Chufut-Kale and Gözleve, RNL EVR II A, no. 1556. For details on Azariah ben Elijah and for the full text of his work, see Golda Akhiezer. “The Events which Occurred during the Reign of Shahin Giray Khan: The Historical Chronicle of the 18th Century by Rabbi Azaryah ben Eliya the Karaite from the Crimea.” {{em:Koveṣ ʿal-Yad}} 20.30 (2010): 281–385 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Azariah records what transpired in the Crimea from 1776 to 1783 during the conquest of that region by the Russian empress Catherine II, some of which he witnessed firsthand. He describes the events during the reign of the last Crimean khan, Shahin Giray the Reformer, the first Muslim ruler in the world who tried to liberalize Islamic law and modernize his state according to the European model, prompting a Tatar revolt against him. Azariah provides details of the khan’s reforms; the Tatar revolt against Shahin Giray, who was backed by the Russians; and the looting and killing suffered by the local population at the hands of the rebels and Russian soldiers during the revolt and its suppression. He discusses interethnic relations in the Crimea as well as the upheavals that local Karaite communities endured during the war. Several passages in Azariah’s chronicle relate specifically to the Karaites, describing their suffering during the war, the way in which they were saved from danger, libels against them (primarily by the Armenians), and their collaboration with the Rabbanites.

Like many traditional Jewish authors, Azariah maintains that the sons of Israel must keep a distance from the affairs of non-Jewish society because the Jews’ destiny differs from those of other nations. He opines that during trying times,

It is not good to speak things of the king and of the nations, and a son of Israel must be of short tongue and short arm, for thus are we commanded by King Solomon, and it is not fitting to speak of this people that achieves victory and that people that is defeated, for [all] are in the hand of [the Lord]. He judges. This one He brings low, and that one He raises [Psalms 75:8]. (17–20, 3a){{fn:44}}
content.comments: [44] Akhiezer. “The Events,” pp. 341–342.

content.english: Azariah also expresses his loyalty to and support for the authorities, and he views Shahin Giray as khan and the forces of the Russian Empire that backed the khan as the only ones capable of imposing order over the chaos found in the Crimea. He portrays the khan as protecting his people from the tyranny of the Tatars:

The king was a wise and understanding man and one who understood mysteries, none similar to whom has arisen in recent times… May He extend his days, for he has saved the oppressed from the oppressor, and if he had not emerged victorious in the war, we would have been set upon by all the Tatars… (138–139, 2b){{fn:45}}

Like other Jewish chroniclers, Azariah voices an opinion about the ruler based on his treatment of the Jews. The rebels, conversely, are depicted as cruel and traitorous riffraff erupting in irrational behavior: “And so too did the people of the Qara Tatar [that is, the Black Tatars, commoners] also form a single band and proceed to loot and kill each other” (92–93, 1b).{{fn:46}} In this unique chronicle, Azariah discerns the functions and positions of different ethnic groups. With intriguing additional material, some of which is discussed below, he also sheds light on such groups’ relations with the Karaites.

One of the texts can be regarded as the personal memories of an educated community member of Chufut-Kale: Joseph ben Ariye Kusdini. It contains evidence of a ship that sank while its passengers—Hasidim from Poland, who followed their rebbe, R. Menaḥem Mendl of Vitebsk—were on their way to the Land of Israel.{{fn:47}} This is a unique case in which the author expresses his political views and criticism of the Rabbanite messianic outlook, which, in his view, eventually took its toll in the form of human victims.
content.comments: [47] On this event, see Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 692–694. Both the text excerpted here and a similar one written by the same author were published by David Assaf. “She-yaṣʾah shmuʿah she-Mashiaḥ ben David baʾ: ʾOr ḥadash ʿal ʿaliyat ha-Ḥasidim bi-shnat 5537.” {{em:Zion}} 61.3 (1996): 328–329 (in Hebrew). There are also other Karaite documents (letters by Joshua ben David, a Polish Hasid who survived the shipwreck) that recount this event; Jacob Barnai. {{em:ʾIggrot Ḥasidim me-Ereṣ Yisraʾel min ha-maḥaṣit ha-shniyah shel ha-meʾa ha-shmone ʿesre u-me-reshit ha-meʾah ha-tshaʿ ʿesre}}. Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute, 1980, pp. 56–59 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Joseph identifies two reasons for the tragedy. The first concerns the militaristic pretensions of the Russian Empire, which he describes as having conquered the world. He alludes to the Rabbanite view of the wars waged by Russia as harbingers of the end of days. The second reason given for the tragedy is the Rabbanite interpretation of the end of days and the beginning of {{em:geʾulah}} (redemption), which Joseph sees as incorrect and as a sign of their folly. He argues that the messianic age has not yet arrived; when it does, God himself will gather the people of Israel, and there will be no need for a project similar to that of the Hasidim, which only endangers the people. For Joseph, this is an obvious fact that does not require further explanation:

As a memorial to the last generation of what happened at the time of the year 5537 from Creation [1777 CE], that word emerged that the Messiah son of David had come, and then the Rabbanites living outside the Land began going to Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, and as they were traveling in the sea on ships, one ship was wrecked in the midst of the sea, and some of them—i.e., of the Rabbanites—55 people, men and women, lads and maidens, infants and babes and sucklings at the breast, drowned. All of the people to be found on the ship numbered eighty people. May the Lord in His abundant mercy safeguard us from disease and destruction. Amen! The cause of their belief that the Messiah son of David had come was that at that time the wicked nation of Moscov [Russia]—the bitter, impetuous nation, a nation whose language we do not know—stretched forth its arm throughout the world; there remained no place that it had not seized by war, and they thought that it was the time of the End promised by the prophets, and in their great folly they did not know that there had not yet appeared the Light at whose appearance miracles and wonders will first be wrought in the world and after which the truth will be revealed, and He will gather the scattered of Israel from the edges of the earth, and in His hand shall they be gathered, and no Israelite shall be able to go to the chosen place except at his appearance, and this is known and clear, and there is no need for further detail [120b].{{fn:48}}
content.comments: [48] D. Assaf. “She yaṣʾah shmuʿah she-Mashiaḥ ben David baʾ”: 328–329.

content.english: This passage also indicates that in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the Karaite perception of messianism (at least in the Crimea) was quite different from the one prevalent among the “Mourners of Zion” in the Middle Ages, who called on all the sons of Israel to come to the Land of Israel immediately.
{{h2:1.3 Relations with Rabbanite Jews}}

The Karaites and the Rabbanites collaborated in various spheres of life, such as the shared use of books, economic support, the ransoming of captives, and the common education of children. In addition to the exchange and copying of books for each other, we find a phenomenon of Karaite and Rabbanite communities using the same Torah codices. Some of these were copied and owned by Karaites and later found their way into Rabbanite communities. This phenomenon has earlier precedents in Islamic countries. The most striking example is the case of the Aleppo Codex ({{em:Keter ʿAram Ṣovaʾ}}), which was copied circa 930 in Tiberias, purportedly by the {{em:Masorete}} Aaron ben Asher, who was a Karaite. In the mid-eleventh century, it was bought from his family and entrusted for safekeeping to the Karaite Nasi in Jerusalem. Both Karaites and Rabbanites who copied any book of the Pentateuch were permitted to check for correct spelling in keeping with the rules of the {{em:masorah}}, according to this codex. This precious book was part of the plunder of the Crusaders’ conquest of Jerusalem in 1099. It was redeemed by the unified efforts of Egyptian Jews, both Karaites and Rabbanites, and brought to the Rabbanite Jerusalemite community of Fustat.{{fn:49}} In this period, there is also evidence of collaboration between Karaites and Rabbanites in both Jerusalem and Egypt regarding the use of this codex, often referred to as the “Crown.” The shared use of Torah codices seems typical of this period, during which cooperation between the two communities (as well as marriages between Karaites and Rabbanites) still existed. The main reason for the use of the same Torah codices was that there was no controversy concerning the {{em:masorah}} between Karaites and Rabbanites. The aforementioned tenth-century Karaite author Jacob al-Qirqisani, who was a contemporary of Ben Asher, claims in his book {{em:Kitab al-Anwar}} {{em:wa-ʾl-Maraqib}} that his contemporaries recognized the exclusive authority of the Palestinian, not the Babylonian, {{em:masorah}}.
content.comments: [49] Shlomo D. Goitein. {{em:Ha-yishuv be-Eretṣ Israʾel be-rʾeshit ha-ʾIslʾam u-ve-tkufat ha-ṣalbanim le-ʾor kitvei ha-Genizah}} [Palestinian Jewry in Early Islamic and Crusader Times: In the Light of the Geniza Documents]. Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute, 1980, pp. 231–235 (in Hebrew).

content.english: The precedent of the shared use of the Aleppo Codex helps explain why so many Karaite Torah codices were owned by Rabbanites in the Crimea, as well as the presence of numerous Rabbanite Torah codices and scrolls in the Karaite libraries there. In addition, although the two communities used the same codices, they did so in different ways; Karaites allowed both the study and public reading of the Torah from codices, whereas Rabbanites only permitted public readings from Torah scrolls. Indeed, Caleb Afendopolo writes in his book {{em:Patshegen Ketav ha-Dat}} that the Karaites in the Byzantine and Ottoman empires used both codices and scrolls for public readings of the Torah, and we can surmise that the Crimean Karaite communities practiced the same customs.{{fn:50}}
content.comments: [50] Caleb Afendopolo. {{em:Patshegen Ketav ha-Dat}}. Ramle: National Council of Karaite Jews in Israel, 1977, pp. 20–21, 24–25, 27 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Another kind of collaboration between Karaites and Rabbanites is found in the colophons, which attest to the copying of books for Karaites by Rabbanite scribes. One such book, the astronomical text {{em:Sefer ha-Tekhunah}},{{fn:51}} was written in 1487 in Istanbul by the scribe Isaac ben Moses, who copied it for a Karaite from Kaffa:
content.comments: [51] This was a Hebrew translation of the treatise {{em:On the Configuration of the World}} ({{em:Fi hayʾat al-ʿalam}}) by the Muslim scholar Ibn al-Haytham (964–1040), who composed about 200 works on optics, mathematics, philosophy, astronomy, and more.

content.english: I, Isaac ben Moses, the orphan from the city of Ca[n]dia, completed [copying] this [book] here, in the Great Kustandina, for R. Judah, a Karaite from Kaffa, in 1487, 28 of Tammuz… God will award him, his descendants, and descendants of his descendants to understand it [this book] and to meditate therein.{{fn:52}}
content.comments: [52] Ibn al-Haytham. {{em:Sefer ha-Tkhunah}} [On the Configuration of the World]{{em:.}} RNL EVR I 354.

content.caption: On the Configuration of the World (RNL EVR I 354)

content.english: The Karaite and Rabbanite communities also collaborated in the redeeming of Jewish captives. The Crimean Tatars frequently invaded Eastern European lands and returned with captives, whom they usually sold in Kaffa, which had the largest slave market in the region. One striking example of such collaboration is the case of the capture of a Rabbanite sage from Lithuania who lived in Kiev: R. Moses ben Jacob ha-Goleh (the Exile, 1449–1520). One of the earliest Jewish Kabbalists of Eastern Europe, R. Moses died as the leader of the Rabbanite community in the Crimea. R. Moses spent time in Adrianople and Istanbul, where he studied the Torah, Kabbalah, and astronomy. One of his instructors in the field of astronomy was the scholar Elijah Bashyachi.{{fn:53}} On his return from Istanbul, R. Moses conducted legal debates in the Karaite communities of Kiev, Troki, and Lutsk. R. Moses tried to convince the Karaites of Troki to follow Rabbanite {{em:halakhah}} regarding the calendar, forbidden marriages, and the heating of homes on the Sabbath. In addition, in response to {{em:Gan ʿEden}} by Aaron ben Elijah of Nicomedia, he wrote 240 objections ({{em:hassagot}}) refuting a number of Karaite arguments concerning matters of {{em:halakhah}}. R. Moses composed his objections in the form of remarks in the margins of the book. This particular copy containing his objections disappeared for a time.{{fn:54}} Surprisingly, however, it reappeared in 1487 in the Crimea. The book had been part of the Tatars’ plunder and was later sold to a Karaite resident of Kaffa who presented or sold it to the Lithuanian Karaite sage Joseph ben Mordecai, who was passing through the region on his way to Istanbul. Upon reaching his destination, Joseph ben Mordecai handed this copy of the book to Elijah Bashyachi, who (along with Caleb Afendopolo) gave well-founded responses to the objections of R. Moses. Bashyachi, who was concerned about his former student’s activity among Eastern European Karaites, may have felt a personal dislike for R. Moses. In one of his letters, he writes:
content.comments: [53] Bashyachi mentions R. Moses in his letter of 1486–1487 to the Karaites of Lutsk: “Perhaps this man has forgotten the time when he humbled himself before me while learning astronomy”; Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, doc. 114, pp. 1165–1166. | [54] Ibid., doc. 117a, pp. 1170–1171.

content.english: So much more so inasmuch as that man [R. Moses] is an evil thing of creation—one bruise under another, his eyes white, the appearance of his hairs tending toward blondness—and such a man, the sages said that he is a horror of creation… and so there is no cause to be surprised by your disgrace, for you are recognized by your face.{{fn:55}}
content.comments: [55] Ibid., p. 1168. Regarding Afendopolo’s position on the conflict, see ibid., doc. 117–117a, pp. 1168–1173.

content.english: Despite the conflicts and controversies between R. Moses and various Karaite sages (including Eastern European Karaites as well as Elijah Bashyachi and Caleb Afendopolo), there was much mutual assistance and collaboration between the Karaites and Rabbanites. R. Moses’s children, who had been taken captive along with all of his property, were deported to the Crimea during the Tatar conquest of Kiev. R. Moses received contributions from the Rabbanite and Karaite communities to ransom his sons and daughters. Later, following the 1485 Tatar invasion of Kiev, R. Moses was himself taken captive by Tatars and brought to Solkhat, where he was ransomed by both Karaites and Rabbanites. He lived there for about ten years before relocating to Kaffa, where he was appointed head of the Rabbanite community and united the various Rabbanite Jewish denominations living in the Crimea (Ashkenazic, Romaniote, Babylonian, and others) into a single community by producing for them a uniform liturgy known as the Kaffa Rite. It is important to note that some of his treatises on Kabbalah, astronomy, and biblical exegesis—and even his prayer book—survived in private Karaite libraries.

An additional form of cooperation between Karaites and Rabbanites in the Crimean communities was the mutual study by scholars and pupils under teachers from both communities. This practice in the Crimea may have been influenced by processes that occurred in the Byzantine Empire in its late period and in the Ottoman Empire during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Rabbanite sages, such as Mordecai Comtino, Ḥanoch Ṣipporta, Moses Kapuṣato, and Solomon Sharvit ha-Zahav, taught Karaite students the Torah and secular sciences. Among their disciples were Elijah Bashyachi, Caleb Afendopolo, Abraham Bali, and Joseph Raviṣi. At the same time, as discussed above, the Eastern European sage R. Moses from Kiev studied astronomy in Adrianople under the guidance of Bashyachi. Despite the scarcity of sources on this issue, we can infer that the situation in the Crimean communities was quite similar. This inference is based on the abovementioned studies of Ḥizkiyah ben Elḥanan, the head of the Karaite community of Solkhat, under the Rabbanite scholar of this city, Abraham Qirimi. The author of the present work also uncovered that Rabbanite children attended the Karaite study hall in Chufut-Kale up to the late eighteenth century, as evidenced in at least two communal documents preserved in archival materials. In a report listing the books studied by every student of this study hall, we find the names of at least four disciples “from the Rabbanite community,” along with Karaite disciples’ names. We can surmise that this situation in the eighteenth century was a continuation of an earlier practice.

The aforementioned chronicler Azariah ben Elijah tells of the false accusation against the Karaite community by Armenians before Khan Shahin Giray. According to his evidence, Armenian soldiers traduced the Karaites to the khan as planning to rebel against him, offering as proof an ostensible flag that the Armenians them- selves had fashioned by stitching together several prayer shawls (“{{em:tal-}} {{em:lit}} s”). In this instance, the Karaites were saved from death by their “brethren [the Rabbanites],” who attested to the khan that the object in question was not a rebel flag but a prayer shawl:

Amalekite and Arnaut{{fn:56}} soldiers charged against us a great libel, saying: “The Jews went out to meet us with weapons and arms, and a flag with them. Here is their flag that we took from their hands.” They talked about the flag, and the loot included about ten {{em:tallit}} s, and they took one of them and sewed onto it a piece of red silk, and put it on a tall tree, and showed it to the khan and to a prince [a Russian general], while telling them: “Here is a flag of the Jews, and now let us kill all of them with no remnant or residue.”{{fn:57}} And praise be to God, who will neither slumber nor sleep [Psalms 121:4], who has not left us without a guardian-redeemer [based on Ruth 4:14], and there were our brethren [Rabbanites] among us, praise be to God, and they testified before the prince: “This is nothing other than our prayer shawl, that we put on our heads while praying.” The khan was also convinced that this was true: he felt a new seam where they had amalgamated a piece of red silk. (82–90, 2b)
content.comments: [56] In Jewish texts, the Armenians were frequently called Amalekites. Of note, Armenian authors sometimes refer to themselves by this name. Arnauts, or Albanians, were a group from the Balkans among whom Russians settled; they supported the Russian army against the Turks and often conducted punitive operations.
