Albanians were often involved in murder, looting, and pillaging in the Crimea, terrifying its population. | [57] Tatar law permitted the plaintiff to choose either to execute or exact a fine from a defendant found guilty in court.

content.english: We also find evidence that Karaites and Rabbanites in the Crimea worked together to ransom captives in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, such as a letter by Karaite scholar Isaac ben Solomon (see Section 2.5) from Chufut-Kale to the Rabbanite community of Karasubazar. In this letter, Isaac asks the leader of that Rabbanite community, R. David ben Eliezer Lekhno, for help in ransoming the honorable rabbi Barukh Nissim, a messenger from Jerusalem, who “was captured by the hands of uncircumcised gentiles, and you and we must ransom him…”{{fn:58}}
content.comments: [58] Isaac ben Solomon. Letter to Karasubazar. RNL EVR II A, no. 2674, 2b.

content.english: The various sources discussed above reflect the collaboration between Karaites and Rabbanites in ransoming captives, in the use of the same books, and in the joint teaching of children in study halls. This collaboration lasted until the early nineteenth century, but began to unravel under Russian rule when the Russian Karaites started to disconnect from Judaism as they pursued their struggle for emancipation.
{{h2:1.4 The Karaites as a Minority in the Crimean Khanate: Legal Status and Everyday Life}}

According to the Ottoman census of 1529, there were 1,721 Jews in the territory under direct Ottoman rule. By 1545, this number had declined to 1,134.{{fn:59}} However, this information is incomplete and does not reflect the situation across all of Crimea because it is limited to the Ottoman-controlled territories of the coastal area and Mangup and does not include areas, or the Jews living in them, under the rule of the khans. In addition, the proportion of Karaite Jews (among the total Jewish population) is not included in the documents.
content.comments: [59] Alan Fisher. “The Ottoman Crimea in the Sixteenth Century.” {{em:Harvard Ukrainian Studies}} 5.2 (1981): 170.

content.english: As mentioned previously, Bakhchesaray was made the capital of the Crimean Khanate in 1443. Chufut-Kale, a suburb of the capital, began to develop economically.{{fn:60}} Chufut-Kale reached the peak of its prosperity in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and thrived until the Russian conquest in 1783. One of the important testimonies on the Karaite inhabitants of this city is that of the Turkish traveler and official Evliya Çelebi, who visited the Crimea twice between 1641 and 1667. Çelebi provides interesting details about the life of the Karaite communities in Mangup and Chufut-Kale and emphasizes the Jewish character of Chufut-Kale: “There are no Muslims there at all and even the commander of the fortress, the soldiers in the fortress, the guards and gatekeepers are all Jews.”{{fn:61}} Çelebi mentions that there were 1,530 houses of Jews in Chufut-Kale, a probable overestimation—other sources mention 200–300 Karaite houses at most (see details below). According to his testimony, the poor members of the community lived in caves carved out of rock. These caves still exist today, and Hebrew inscriptions can be seen on some of their walls.
content.comments: [60] Chufut-Kale was not under direct Ottoman rule. | [61] Yevgeny Bakhrevsky (transl. and comment.). {{em:Kniga puteshestviya: turetskii avtor Evliya Çelebi o Kryme (1666–1667)}} [The Travel Book: The Turkish Author Evliya Çelebi about the Crimea]. Simferopol: The Crimean Branch of the Institute of Oriental Studies of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, 1999, p. 36.

content.caption: Caves near Chufut-Kale and the house of Firkovich (courtesy of M. Kizilov)

content.english: Çelebi lists “seven whole Jewish quarters” in Mangup, in which there were 1,000 houses. These numbers are also exaggerated. According to data from the 1529 census,{{fn:62}} there were only seventy-six Jewish households; this number fell to sixty-eight by 1649 and to fifty-one by 1662. Therefore, based on the data from the mid-seventeenth century, we can conclude that the Karaite community in Mangup at that time numbered approximately 250 to 380 members. Çelebi also mentions tanning and leatherworking as the main occupations of the Karaites in Mangup. In addition, they ran two butcher shops and one {{em:buza-hane}}—a tavern selling bouza, a Tatar drink made from barley, oats, or millet that has a low alcohol content, hence making it acceptable for Muslims.{{fn:63}}
content.comments: [62] Alan Fisher. “The Ottoman Crimea in the Mid-Seventeenth Century: Some Problems and Preliminary Considerations.” {{em:Harvard Ukrainian Studies}} 3.4 (1979–1980), part 1: 221. Fisher, “Ottoman Crimea in the Sixteenth Century,” p. 151. | [63] Bakhrevsky, ibid.

content.english: From the eighteenth century, we have numerical evidence concerning four communities in the Crimea (Chufut-Kale, Gözleve, Kaffa, and Mangup) from Simḥah Isaac Lutski, one of the great sages of that generation who relocated from Eastern Europe to Chufut-Kale (see Section 2.1). According to Lutski’s testimony,

In all of them{{fn:64}} there are some 500 households, in the holy congregation of Kale there are close to 300. In the holy congregation of Kozlev [Gözleve], some 105 people. In Kaffa, some 50. And in the holy congregation of Mangup, some 40. Further, in the city of Solkhat close to the holy congregation of Kaffa, earlier there had been a great congregation and the synagogue in it was much larger than all other synagogues. And now, there is only a {{em:ḥazzan}} in there who watches over the synagogue… in each of the three congregations there is one regular house of the Torah study, and in each study hall a separate teacher and they study all day from morning till night without a break…{{fn:65}}
content.comments: [64] The Karaite communities in all of the Crimea. | [65] Cited by the friend of Simḥah Isaac Lutski, Isaac ben Isaac from Lutsk, in his letter dated 1755 to Abraham, the judge from Troki. Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, doc. 156, p. 1326.

content.english: Lutski adds that in Chufut-Kale, there were seven study halls, though three of them were not active. He also notes that more than thirty students studied with him in a study hall in Chufut-Kale.

We can compare his testimony with other contemporary sources. In 1769, a German trader named Nikolaus Kleeman visited the Crimea; he writes that there were 120 houses in Chufut-Kale.{{fn:66}} In his book on the Crimea, which he began writing in 1777, Johan Tunmann, professor of philosophy at the University of Halle, also reports this figure of 120 houses.{{fn:67}} Following his visit to Chufut-Kale in 1786, Charles-Gilbert Romme, a French politician and mathe- matician, lists 200 houses and 1,200 inhabitants. In 1799, the traveler Piotr Sumarokov{{fn:68}} notes 227 houses.
content.comments: [66] Nikolaus E. Kleeman. {{em:Puteshestvije iz Veny v Belgrad i novuju Kiliju, tako zh v zemli budzhatskix i nagajskix tatar i vo vesʹ Krym}} [Journey from Vienna to Belgrade and New Kiliya]. Saint Petersburg, 1783, p. 105 (in Russian). | [67] Johan Tunmann. {{em:Krymskoye Khanstvo}} [The Crimean Khanate]. Simferopol, 1991, p. 32 (in Russian). | [68] Piotr Sumarokov. {{em:Puteshestvije po vsemu Krymu i Bessarabii v 1799 g.}} [A Journey Throughout the Crimea and Bessarabia]. Moscow, 1800, pp. 140–141 (in Russian).

content.english: Data on the taxation of the Crimean Karaites or of the Jews in general are limited. The Jews, as well as the Christians in the Crimea, were under the status of {{em:dhimmi}}, meaning “protected person,” a term applied mostly to the Jews and Christians under Muslim rule. These population groups had the right to live (unlike pagans), to practice their religion, and to maintain their communal institutions. However, they were subject to numerous social and economic restrictions (according to the “Laws of Omar”), one of which was payment of the {{em:jizya}}—a special tax designated to purchase {{em:dhimmi}}. Çelebi testifies that the Karaites went each morning to the capital Bakhchesaray with their merchandise, but toward evening, they would have to leave the city. This testimony reflects the ban by Muslims on the settlement of Jews, as {{em:dhimmi}}, in the capital.{{fn:69}} Çelebi gives additional evidence of their status in the context of non-Muslim populations in Karasubazar. He mentions that Jews, Armenians, and Greeks were also obliged to tie bells to their ankles when visiting local bathhouses so that they could be identified as infidels in the baths. Çelebi adds that all the infidels wore hats similar to those of the Tatars, but the Jews attached a yellow patch to theirs and the Christians a blue one.{{fn:70}} He adds that the Jews of Karasubazar who paid {{em:haraj}}{{fn:71}} numbered 300, and if his testimony is correct, about 1,500 Jews lived in this city. It is unclear, however, whether Karaites lived in Karasubazar.
content.comments: [69] Bakhrevsky. {{em:The Travel Book}}, p. 37. | [70] Ibid., pp. 74–75. | [71] A land tax. In the Crimea, it was frequently confused with the {{em:jizya}}.

content.english: The Jewish population in the Crimea (like the Jews in Christian lands) usually received special charters ({{em:yarliq}} s in the Tatar language) granted by the khans that specified their rights and obligations. From such {{em:yarliq}} s{{fn:72}} that were granted to the community of Chufut-Kale, we can learn about the Karaites’ rights within this city. Members of the community were employed by the khan as caretakers and used to guard the fortress of Chufut-Kale (which stood about seven kilometers away from the capital, Bakhchesaray). Hence, they received special benefits: exemption from various taxes, including release from {{em:angaria}} s (forced labor for the authorities), and exclusion from the requirement to house ruling officials and soldiers in their homes and to give them horses, carts, and so on.{{fn:73}} The types of taxes and their rates were determined by the khan, and we find them detailed in the {{em:yarliq}} s. In some of these documents, the khans themselves delineated the boundaries of the lands that belonged to the members of the community, and they prohibited the use of these lands either by the Tatars, including those in the khans’ service, or by Christians living in the vicinity{{fn:74}} for their needs (plowing and pastureland) or for building fences.{{fn:75}} At times, however, some local Tatar nobles (the {{em:beks}}) overruled these privileges. We find, for instance, that the Karaites of Chufut-Kale complained to the khan about newly increased taxes, describing their distress. In light of their complaints, the new taxes{{fn:76}} were annulled. The affliction measures decreed by the {{em:beks}}{{fn:77}} from the fortress, such as {{em:angarias}} and other services, were also annulled. The {{em:bek}} of the city, Ahmad Pasha, was censured and rebuked at the session of the {{em:divan}}{{fn:78}} in the presence of the Jews.{{fn:79}}
content.comments: [72] Zerah Firkovich. {{em:Sbornik starinnyxkh gramot i uzakonenii Rossiiskoj Imperii kasatel prav i sostoyaniya russko-poddannykh karaimov}} [A Collection of Ancient Documents and Laws of the Russian Empire Regarding the Legal Status of the Russian Karaite Citizens]. Saint Petersburg, 1890 (in Russian), pp. 62–66. | [73] Ibid., the {{em:yarliq}} from Salemat Giray Khan in 1608. | [74] The Greek Orthodox monastery, known as the Monastery of Dormition ({{em:Uspenskij skit}}, Russian), which is in the Valley of St. Mary ({{em:Meirem dere}}, in Tatar), is less than a kilometer from Chufut-Kale. | [75] See, for instance, the {{em:yarliq}} from Canibek Giray from 1635. Z. Firkovich. {{em:A Collection}}, pp. 77–79. | [76] The reference is apparently to taxes that the {{em:bek}} s (see the next note) would collect arbitrarily. | [77] {{em:Bek}} or {{em:beg}} was a title of honor in the Ottoman Empire and in the Crimea. | [78] In the Khanate of the Crimea, the {{em:divan}} was the khan’s council (i.e., the government). | [79] Z. Firkovich. {{em:A Collection}}, p. 64.

content.english: However, as can be learned from the Russian and Karaite communal documents of Chufut-Kale, despite the protection of their rights defined in the {{em:yarliqs}}, the Karaites occasionally suffered from the khan’s own arbitrariness. The Russian consul Nikiforov, who was staying in the palace of Khan Qirim Giray before the Russian annexation of the Crimea,{{fn:80}} notes in his report the khan’s mistreatment of the local population. During the construction of the royal palace in Bakhchesaray, Muslims, Christians, and Jews were required to deliver building materials to the khan at their own expense and compelled to work without compensation: “During the construction works, everyday Greeks, Armenians, and Jews worked, 200 … 300 people, and not one {{em:asper}} was paid for their labor.”{{fn:81}} In one of the Karaite documents preserved from the period of Qirim Giray Khan, we are told of a Karaite youth, Joseph Sirkeci, from Chufut-Kale, who was employed in construction on the palace. Upon seeing the young man’s beauty, the khan commanded him to join the dancers in his court and convert to Islam. Joseph, however, refused to convert. Although the end of this episode, which the document describes as “an impure incident,” is unknown, it is one of the many cases of the arbitrariness of the Tatar rulers; as the document says, “this theft was one of a thousand.”{{fn:82}}
content.comments: [80] Qirim Giray ruled from 1758 to 1764 and from 1768 to 1769. | [81] Nikolai Murzakevich. “Donesenije rossijskogo rezidenta pri krymskom xane Nikiforova o nizlozhenii Krym Gereja” [A Russian Resident’s Accounts of the Dethronement of Qirim Giray]. {{em:ZOOID}} 1 (1844): 377 (in Russian). | [82] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, n. 3, p. 461.

content.english: Similarly, we learn from the chronicle of Azariah that another Crimean khan also treated the local populations capriciously. According to Azariah, when Khan Selim Giray{{fn:83}} needed money, he did not hesitate to rob the local population:
content.comments: [83] Selim Giray ruled from 1764 to 1767 and from 1770 to 1771; he fled the Crimea after signing a protocol of intent between Russia and the Ottoman Empire.

content.english: In these times, the king Selim Giray sent [his servants who] took a thousand Roman {{em:gurush}} in one night from the community of Chufut-Kale, as well as from Romans [Greeks] and from Amalekites [Armenians]—a thousand from each community. Afterward, he sent the heads of gangs… and let them take from us anything their souls desired, “and none saith, restore!” [Is. 42:22], and they committed outrage. (108–111, 2v){{fn:84}}
content.comments: [84] Akhiezer. “The Events,” p. 337.

content.english: The last Crimean khan, Shahin Giray the Reformer, treated minorities the best as compared with the former khans. He was the first Muslim ruler in the world who tried to cancel the payment of {{em:jizya}}, and he began a process of equating the rights of the {{em:dhimmi}} with those of the Muslim population. However, these and other changes launched by the khan led to a civil war that inflicted death, devastation, and impoverishment on the Crimean population.

Regarding the economic activity and professions of the Crimean Karaites, we have evidence that in Chufut-Kale, they were engaged in commerce and various crafts, such as sheep husbandry, vineyard cultivation, and food production, in addition to the leather business, as previously mentioned. Among the important sources on the Karaite community of Chufut-Kale are tomb inscriptions in its communal cemetery—one of the largest Karaite cemeteries in the world—with about 5,000 tombs dating from the fourteenth to the twentieth centuries. The corpus of these inscriptions, along with selected inscriptions from other Crimean Karaite communities, was published by Abraham Firkovich in his book {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron.}}{{fn:85}}
content.comments: [85] Abraham Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}} [Stones of Remembrance]{{em:.}} Vilna, 1872 (in Hebrew).

content.english: In addition to the names of the deceased, some of these inscriptions contain additional data concerning the employment of community members, including professions and offices within the community, such as {{em:ḥazzan}}, {{em:melamed}} (elementary school teacher), Torah teacher, or {{em:gabbai}}. A number of officeholders within the community held additional professions that were not necessarily in the service of the community. These included several physicians or those with functions (it is mostly unclear which ones) in the khans’ courts. Three generations of the Aga family were appointed to work in the royal mint.

Some of the biographical facts, circumstances of death, and origins presented in these inscriptions reveal interesting details of personal or community life. The tomb of Isaac ben Mordecai ({{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 327, d. 1656), for example, mentions that he was a scribe and that he “navigated around all the Land of Israel, and saw the splendor of its community, as well as of the Damascene and Egyptian communities, when they still were in existence.” Mordecai ben Elijah, who originated in Mangup, was beaten and wounded during his visit to Gözleve “when the oppressors came to Gözleve, and he came here in order to be treated” (no. 316, d. 1607). Who these oppressors were is unclear. We can surmise that they were Cossacks from Zaporozhie and Don, who, during the seventeenth century, systematically raided the Crimea, including the area under direct Ottoman rule. Cossacks destroyed Crimean towns and villages, disregarding the religion of their inhabitants and often murdering them in cruel ways while inflicting severe economic damage on the area. An inscription from 1629 in the cemetery in Mangup reflects this reality: “Mamuq the wife of the Rabbi… Isaac, the unhappy, from the holy congregation of Kale, when there came shaven heads [Cossacks] in the city of Mangup they smote her with lead, and she passed away on Sunday, the twenty-seventh of Iyyar…” ({{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 53, p. 214).

As a result of the Cossack incursions, the Crimean population drastically declined. The number of non-Muslims fell by seventy percent in less than a hundred years. The number of Jews declined by seventy-five percent—more than any other population group.{{fn:86}} Jews and Christians may have been murdered more than Muslim populations because, as {{em:dhimmi}}, they were forbidden from carrying weapons and could not protect themselves.
content.comments: [86] Fisher. “The Ottoman Crimea in the Mid-Seventeenth Century,” p. 219. The existing statistics pertain only to the territories under direct Ottoman rule.

content.caption: Karaite couple by A. Dokuchaev (courtesy of M. Kizilov)

content.english: Beginning in the seventeenth century, the Turkicization of Karaite society accelerated, so much so that approximately two centuries later, we find many Turkic names, particularly for women, in Abraham Firkovich’s {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}} (see Section 2.9.1). These names include Akbike, Mamuq, Sultan, Altin, and Shumluq. The prevalence of Turkic names among Karaite women should be understood as part of a general Jewish phenomenon in diverse places and times (in both the Rabbanite and Karaite communities) in which non-Jewish names were given more frequently to women than to men.

To be certain, it is likely that men acculturated to Tatar society more rapidly and profoundly than women, as women generally kept to their homes. The extent of the integration of male community members can be assessed from the fact that no small number of them found employment in the courts of the khans. We find, for instance, an inscription on a tomb: “and he was an expert doctor, and well-known, in the gates of kings he was desired” (no. 470, d. 1756). In addition, Karaite men bore Turkish titles, such as {{em:çelebi}} and {{em:pasha}}. Acculturated and affluent Karaites arose during this time period, and at least until the eighteenth century, they used their newly found status to defend the interests of the Karaite community. This can be seen in the inscription on the tomb of Isaac ben Jacob Yerushalmi: “He stood at the breach before ministers, occupied with all the needs of our community” (no. 474, d. 1757).

During the Tatar revolt against the last Crimean khan, Shahin Giray the Reformer, and until the Russian annexation of the Crimea (1776–1783), Karaites and other groups experienced traumatic events, some of which are depicted in the aforementioned chronicle of Azariah ben Elijah. Azariah recounts a tragedy that befell the Chufut-Kale community during the war. The Karaites and the Tatars had fled Chufut-Kale in fear of the oncoming Russian forces, who had been purging local villages in the process of looking for Tatar rebels without trying to distinguish between them and other ethnic groups. Some members of the Karaite community who had fled to nearby villages were captured by the Russian soldiers, who misidentified them as rebels. These individuals fell victim to the purge; they were despoiled of their possessions, and some were executed on suspicion of collaboration with the Tatar rebels:

110The first attack [of the Russian army] was on the Great Uzen Bash, where about 60 families from the community of Israel lived. It was scary there two hours before sunrise. And they rose at night, and there was a great cry among them, and they rushed to escape in the night. Some escaped to the mountains, while others rushed to the road leading to Kale, and everything was mixed up. One shouts: “Where are my son and daughters?!” Another asks: “Where is my wife?!” Some remained in the village, bewildered, amid the horror, about where to turn. And they [soldiers] captured several Israelites, women and men, children, young people and sucklings at the breast, and tormented everyone, demanding to show them the houses where the prey is hidden. And they [soldiers] took away their [the Karaites’ own] gold and silver… And after that they burned down the houses of those who had found things from the khan’s storage. All those who were not among the inhabitants of this village were assigned to the commander and on his order, they were beaten and then executed for leaving their homes and coming to seek refuge from the rebels. The same fate befell those who remained in the village, not having had time to escape. (54–65, 2r){{fn:87}}
content.comments: [87] Akhiezer. “The Events,” pp. 333–334.

content.english: Azariah goes on to say that about twenty-seven people were murdered and buried in Chufut-Kale, with others suffering an unknown fate.

These tragic events were also described by a witness who was among these refugees but had escaped death. We find an emotional depiction in a letter (1778) written by Hillel ben Isaac Qirimi, one of the leaders of the Chufut-Kale community; the letter was sent to his brother and mother in Kaffa. Hillel tells them that he and his family members, including his son Jacob, and other Karaite refugees were attacked by Arnauts. They had gone back to the village of Uzun Bash in order

to take my father-in-law, honorable old Simḥah who suffered from pains in his legs, from home where he stayed. When they{{fn:88}} heard that the enemies were near, they locked the door. The villains pounded on the door, and then honorable Isaac Pastak opened it, while holding a purse full of silver in his hand, and told them: “We are Jews, and obey those who will rule us.” They shot him right in the heart with deadly lead, and he died on the spot. Afterward, they broke into the house to empty it, with a weapon… My father-in-law, and his son Berakhah, my wife Leah, her sister, and her [sister’s] children—all huddled in a corner of the house, and not a single bullet hit them. Everyone started begging them for mercy by telling them: “After all, we obey anyone who will rule us…! Have mercy on us!” And the soldiers answered: “If you are telling the truth, why then did you leave your homes and go to live among our enemies?” Despite this, they did not kill them, and ordered to take them all to the commander in chief… On the way, where they led us, the honorable Berakhah had got a stick, and when he saw them tormenting his father, who could not walk, he attacked one of the villains. It is unknown if then they beat him to death, but eventually everyone was murdered by the villains: my father-in-law, the honorable old Simḥah, and his son, the honorable young Berakhah, his sister Shushka, and her children. No one was left alive except a woman who grabbed one child and ran away… My wife Leah with my little son Abraham came back, beaten and wounded, and died here in Kaleh. And only I remained with my son Jacob and the venerable David, the son of my father-in-law, and I will weep day and night.{{fn:89}}
content.comments: [88] Some of Hillel’s relatives, who came with him to this house. | [89] Hillel Qirimi. Letter. RNL EVR I, doc. 74, 1v, l. 1–30; 2r, l. 1–2.

content.english: These dramatic events are supplemented by another Karaite letter from the same chaotic days. The letter was written in 1779 by Sar-Shalom ben Samuel, possibly one of the community leaders in Kaffa, and sent to the Chufut-Kale community leader, Benjamin Aga (see Section 2.2). Sar-Shalom says that because of the war, the connection between Kaffa and Chufut-Kale had been severed, and he recounts the recent incidents in the Kaffa community:

On Shabbat, enemies suddenly came to us, villains—Arnauts broke doors, robbed and took away all our money, leaving nothing in our houses. And they did not leave any house where the door was not broken down, and only our souls survived, praise to His great holy Name. God gave—God took…{{fn:90}}
content.comments: [90] Simḥah Assaf. “Biqoret ʿal sifro shel Mann” [A Review of the Book by Mann]. {{em:Tarbitz}} 7 (1936): 237 (in Hebrew).

content.english: In his letter, Sar-Shalom tells of the murder of two community leaders by Arnauts. He also reports on a young Karaite captive named Solomon ben Naḥamu Koen, taken to Kaffa by Arnauts, and perhaps four other Karaite prisoners who were seen by non-Jews in Perekop Fortress. According to Sar-Shalom, these prisoners appeared to be from Chufut-Kale and were possibly among those community members who disappeared during the aforementioned massacre of Karaite refugees in Uzen Bash. Sar-Shalom also reports on two Karaite captives in the city of Karasubazar, who were mentioned by Rabbanites from this city during their visit to Kaffa. He recommends to Benjamin Aga that if the Chufut-Kale community took steps to rescue its captives, he should personally submit a petition to the commander in chief, the Russian Prince Prozorovsky, who was in the Crimea at the time. Sar-Shalom also asks Benjamin Aga to keep him informed about the names of the members of the Chufut-Kale community who were captured and of those already rescued.

The chronicle of Azariah includes an intriguing and more optimistic story that occurred within the Karaite community of Kaffa during the same civil war in the Crimea. Azariah heavily emphasizes the motif of community members’ powerful faith and their consequent deliverance by God from the dangers that beset them. When the warships of the Russian navy approached the shores of Gözleve, the Tatar population began fleeing the city out of fear of an artillery bombardment.

The mayor of Kaffa came to the Karaite synagogue on the Sabbath to announce that the city was in danger and its residents had to flee immediately. The Karaites responded, however, that they were unwilling to desecrate the Sabbath. To this, the mayor replied that he knew they were permitted to do so in this instance because of the threat to their lives (he was apparently referring to the relevant rabbinic law),{{fn:91}} and if they insisted on remaining, it was because they were supporters of Shahin Giray the Reformer. However, the members of the community who decided to remain convinced the others to wait until Saturday night to make their escape, arguing that if they refrained from violating the sanctity of the Sabbath, God would save them from danger. In practice, stresses Azariah, this is precisely what happened.{{fn:92}}
content.comments: [91] To what extent the Karaites in the Crimea concurred with the principle that a potentially lethal danger supersedes Sabbath observance is unclear, notwithstanding the argument by Elijah Bashyachi that one may violate the Sabbath if a life is endangered (see Bashyachi. {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}}, pp. 111–112). | [92] Akhiezer. “The Events,” pp. 11–21, 7a; 349–350.

content.english: This chronicle pays special attention to interethnic relations. In addition to the horror inflicted on Karaite communities by the Arnauts’ constant raids, Azariah mentions more than once, as noted earlier, the conflicts between the Karaites and the Armenians, including the aforementioned phenomenon of Armenian libels against the Karaites. The nature of these conflicts is unclear. Possibly, the tension between the two communities stemmed from intense economic competition; although both groups had the same legal status of {{em:dhimmi}}, both were involved in commerce and strived to obtain the best possible charters from the authorities.

A short, anonymous chronicle dated 1778 recounts that after the Tatar rebellion against the khan had been suppressed, the Armenians accused two Karaites of murder. The khan permitted the accusers to have these Karaites executed, and they were subsequently hanged (12–16, 3a):

In 5538 from the creation [1778] Ezra Bebesh was hanged. His executioner was Shahin Giray Khan. The reason for this came from the Amalekites [Armenians] who invented a false accusation against him… and it happened in Bakhchesaray… Also, in Gözleve one Jew was hanged, also named Ezra, nicknamed Kisir Achki, following the libel of the Amalekites, may God avenge his blood… And I will tell you about why they were hanged on the tree. There lived in Gözleve an Amalekite, the most important among the Amalekites and the richest among them. During the war between Muscovy [Russia] and the Crimean people, Ishmaelites [Muslims] killed that important Amalekite, and Ibrahim, the chief among the Ishmaelites, was the one who did it. At that time there were two Jews who used to visit the tavern of Ibrahim Aga. Seeing how they entered and left, the Amalekites thought that these Jews were responsible for that [Amalekite’s] death. Thus, they found a pretext [to blame the Jews], and said to the king so-and-so. Because of their slander, those [two Jews] were hanged. May their death be an atonement for them, amen!{{fn:93}}

Although we find no direct indication that these two Jews were Karaites, this short chronicle was written by a member of the Chufut-Kale community. In addition, these two names are common among the Karaite community and do not appear among the Crimean Rabbanites.

Azariah also mentions this sad story in his chronicle but with some divergences from this text. According to his version, the Armenians falsely accused two Jews of Gözleve of various transgressions before the khan. They claimed that these Jews had slandered them before Ishmaelites, had secretly visited a Tugar (Turkish) ship during the war, had taken 100 {{em:gurush}} from Turks, and had been spying on behalf of the Ottomans. The Armenians begged the khan, who suggested that they ask of him anything they desired (possibly in return for some service—Azariah does not explain), to let them kill these two Karaites, and the khan gave them his consent.
{{h3:1.4.1 {{em:Women in the Karaite Community}}}}

Although it is important to consider the status of women at this time in the Crimean Karaite communities, the documentation on this topic is scarce, so we must draw conclusions from fragmentary sources. One of the earliest documents dealing with women’s activities is a deed of sale from fourteenth-century Solkhat:

This is the testimony we, the undersigned, received, on the fifth day of the week, in the month of Second Adar 17, in 5090 [1330] of the Creation. Shulamit bat Shemaryah came with her daughter-in-law, Malkah, and her son Samuel, and this Malkah, the wife of Abraham ben Shemaryah, testified that she sold to this Shulamit the book {{em:Midrash ha-Ḥokhmot}}, which remained from her [late] husband Abraham, for 120 coins…{{fn:94}}
content.comments: [94] This book was written in Arabic around 1247 by Judah ben Shlomo ibn Matka of Toledo, who translated it afterward into Hebrew. This was the first Jewish encyclopedia of scientific and philosophical knowledge. See Judah ben Solomon ha-Kohen. {{em:Midrash ha-Ḥokhmah}}. MS Mich. 551, Bodl. colophon 210r.

content.english: We find here an interesting case of a transaction between two women—an unusual occurrence, especially in Oriental communities. The purpose of the deal is undisclosed, but we can cautiously suggest that Shulamit purchased this book to study on her own. This assumption is strengthened by other documents showing that women in Crimean communities were quite active in other spheres of community life, such as charitable donations. For instance, in a list of thirteen people who donated money for the support of the Jerusalem Karaite community, we find the names of two women.{{fn:95}}
content.comments: [95] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 457–458.

content.caption: {{em:Portrait of Empress Catherine II by Fedor Rokotov}} (1763, Tretyakov Gallery)
Karaite woman with jewelry and amulets (courtesy of V. Elyashevich)

content.english: Another sphere of women’s activities was the consecration of books for synagogues and study halls. This was a common practice in Oriental communities, especially in Egypt, as we know from the documents of the Cairo Genizah, but less so in Europe.{{fn:96}} The books (both Torah scrolls and books of various genres) were usually donated by men and women for the atonement of their sins, in the hopes of recovering from disease or illness, or in memory of their family members. For instance, this consecration note is dated 1677:
content.comments: [96] Haggai Ben-Shammai. “ʿAl daʿat ha-kahal: sifriyot ṣiburiyot be-kehilot Israel ba-Mizraḥ bi-yemei ha-beinaim” [Public Opinion: Public Libraries in Jewish Communities in the East in the Middle Ages.]. {{em:ʿEt-Mol}} 232 (2014): 1–4 (in Hebrew).

content.english: This Torah scroll consecrated to the God of Israel, was donated to the synagogue of the holy community of Kaffa by Mrs. Altyn, the daughter of honorable R. Judah the old, of blessed memory, and [she is] the wife of R. Elijah ha-Maskil… the son of honorable R. Solomon… for atonement for the souls of her father and mother…{{fn:97}}
content.comments: [97] Abraham Harkavy and Herman L. Strack. {{em:Catalog der hebräischen Bibelhandschriften der Kaiserlichen öffentlishen Bibliothek in Saint Petersburg}}. Saint Petersburg, 1875, no. A 25, pp. 215–217.

content.english: This phenomenon, also widespread in the Crimea, was an important factor in the creation of public libraries in synagogues and study halls. These books could be used by community members, but their removal was forbidden.
We also find an interesting document from seventeenth-century Mangup that reflects contemporary practices regarding contact between men and women:

This agreement will explain that we have seen a bad custom in our community in our times; that is, men and women are sitting together during community events. And that is a great sin, common among gentiles, and a transgression of the commandment “Do not covet,” which is forbidden by [our] law and a sign of harlotry that shakes the foundations of the Torah. For these reasons, we had to put an end to this bad practice among us, in every nook and cranny, to uproot it completely, so that men and women would not sit together either in the course of the festive meal or on a happy or an unhappy occasion. This is the condition established by the learned men of our honorable community council, may God preserve it, in the town of Mangup, may God preserve it. And the Jews accepted this [condition] for themselves and their offspring, and he who disobeys and transgresses a religious enactment will be severely punished. [This document is] valid and in effect. Friday, 13 of Second Adar, year 1642. And I am the scribe Jacob ben Mordecai may his soul be bound into the knot of life.{{fn:98}}
content.comments: [98] Enactment of the Mangup Karaite Community. RNL EVR II 13 D 12. The text was initially published by Daria Vasyutinskaya. “Mangup-Qaleh Jewish Community Documents in the First Firkowicz Collection.” In Artiom Fedorchuk and Svetlana Chlenova (eds.). {{em:Studia Antropologica: A Festschrift in Honour of Michael Chlenov.}} Moscow—Jerusalem: Gesharim, 2010, pp. 193–220.

content.english: This document indicates that, unlike in most Oriental Jewish communities, the practice in the Mangup Karaite community was quite liberal: during community events, men and women could meet each other, sit together, and possibly talk to each other. We do not have similar data on this subject from other documents in the context of other Karaite communities, including those in the Crimea. Presumably, this practice existed in Mangup due to the influence of the non-Jewish—Greek and Gothian Christian—milieu in this location. This document also reflects a change in this regard: an abrupt rejection of this practice initiated by the community authorities; they surprisingly define it as “a transgression of the commandment ‘Do not covet,’ which is forbidden by [our] law and a sign of harlotry.” This change in Karaite society can be attributed to the intensive process of “Turkicization” that accompanied the alignment with Muslim society from the mid-sixteenth to seventeenth centuries.
{{h2:1.5 The Connections between the Crimean Karaite Communities and Jerusalem}}

The community of Chufut-Kale approached the apogee of its economic prosperity by the mid-eighteenth century and regularly pro-vided assistance to other communities, such as those of Lutsk, Troki, Damascus, and Istanbul. For instance, in 1774, the Karaite synagogue of Hasköy{{fn:99}} was burned, and the leaders of the Karaite community of Istanbul asked for help from the communities of Kaffa, Chufut-Kale, Mangup, and Gözleve.{{fn:100}}
content.comments: [99] One of the quarters of Istanbul. | [100] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 353–358.

content.english: The Crimean Karaites assigned much importance to supporting the community of Jerusalem,{{fn:101}} with which they maintained close relations and family ties. The Karaite community had lived continuously in the Land of Israel since the late ninth century, with centers existing in different periods in Jerusalem, Ramle, Safed, and Hebron. Sources, mainly from the seventeenth century onward, testify to the connections between the Karaite community of Jerusalem and those of the Crimea (primarily of Chufut-Kale), although such connections may have existed at an earlier date.
content.comments: [101] Ibid., pp. 125–127, 321–132; Mordecai Wilensky. “Rabbi Elija Afeda Bagi and the Karaite Community of Jerusalem.” {{em:PAAJAR}} XL (1972): 109–146; Golda Akhiezer. “Ziqat Qaraʾei Qrym li-Yrushalayim u-bittuyah be-maṣevot sefer ʾAvnei Zikkaron” [The Ties of the Crimean Karaites with Jerusalem and Their Reflection in ʾAvnei Zikkaron]. In Dan Shapira (ed.). {{em:The Tombstones of the Cemetery of the Karaite Jews in Çufut-Qaleh (the Crimea): Report of the Ben-Zvi Institute Expedition—A Collection of Studies.}} Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute, 2008, pp. 300–311 (in Hebrew).

content.english: A unique feature of the Crimean Karaite communities was that, compared with Rabbanite and other Karaite communities, they made unusually frequent pilgrimages to the Land of Israel. The Crimean Karaites saw the pilgrimage to Jerusalem as a way to obtain purification from sins, ennobling an individual, his family, and the entire community. Anyone returning from such a pilgrimage appended to his forename the word Yerushalmi (commonly abbreviated as Yeru)—“of Jerusalem”—and this title was passed down through the generations in his family. In the nineteenth century, this appellation became a family name. This name was preserved even in the Soviet period, during which the Russian Karaites were cut off from their cultural and religious roots as a result of the Soviet assimilation policy, and most of the Karaites called Yeru no longer understood the meaning of their name.

Some of these pilgrims wanted to memorialize their journey to the Holy Land as a significant event in the lives of both family and community and to preserve it in collective memory. Hence, they left detailed accounts of their journeys to the Land of Israel and other lands. Four such diaries were written by Samuel ben David of Chufut-Kale (on his travels from 1641–1642); Moses ben Elijah ha-Levi (1654–1655); Naḥamu ben Solomon of Chufut-Kale (1794–1795);{{fn:102}} and Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan (1785–1786), a prominent scholar and leader of the Gözleve community (see Section 2.6).{{fn:103}} These authors describe their departure from the Crimea, the course of their travels between cities, the people they met along the way, the hardships of the journey, and their return to the Crimea. Each of their steps is precisely documented and dated, with special consideration of the holy sites of the Land of Israel. The authors describe the Karaite communities they visited in Jerusalem, Hebron, Cairo, and Damascus. These diaries constitute unique evidence of the size of these communities, their economic conditions, their leaders, and their relations with the Rabbanites and the governing authorities.
content.comments: [102] See Section 1.4 on the tomb inscription of his great-grandfather, Isaac ben Mordecai, who visited the Land of Israel, Damascus, and Egypt. | [103] Many Karaite travel diaries have been published. See Yaari. {{em:Masaʿot}}, pp. 221–267, 305–323, 459–478; A. Karp (ed.). “Sefer ‘Derekh ha-qoddesh’ meʾet Naḥamu ben Shlomo be-ʿir Qaleh” [The Book {{em:The Holy Way}} by Naḥamu ben Solomon from the City of Qaleh]. {{em:Koveṣ ʿAl-Yad}} 8.18 (1976): 481–497 (in Hebrew).

content.english: From these diaries, as well as other sources, we know details about the Karaite community of Ottoman Jerusalem, which was reestablished by David ben Jeshuah of Cairo from 1625 to 1627 and numbered twenty-seven people. During the Ottoman period, all the Jewish communities in the Land of Israel suffered high taxes, often with unexpected tax increases or the introduction of new taxes. The small Karaite community desperately struggled to survive and constantly needed support from the Diaspora communities. When the community was unable to pay its taxes, the authorities arrested and tortured its leaders and confiscated communal property. David ben Jeshuah was imprisoned for this reason. After his release, he requested support from the Crimean communities and traveled to Eastern Europe to collect donations from local Karaites. However, he died unexpectedly in Lutsk in 1647, and the Jerusalem community lapsed into economic crisis because of its debts.

An effort by the Crimean Karaites to help the Jerusalem community following the death of David ben Jeshuah is depicted in a note found in the book {{em:Meʾirat ʿEnayim}}, written by the aforementioned Eastern European eighteenth-century Karaite scholar Simḥah Isaac ben Moses Lutski, who relocated from Lutsk to Chufut-Kale (see Section 2.1). Lutski reports the deeds of his great-grandfather, Joseph ben Jeshuah, specifically his activity in collecting donations for the Jerusalem Karaite community. Joseph ben Jeshuah was {{em:ḥazzan}} of the town of Derazhne, near Lutsk. When this town was destroyed by Cossacks, Joseph lost his family in the massacre but was able to escape. On his way to the Crimea (where he arrived in 1666), he began gathering alms for Jerusalem. He intended to complete the donation fund during his stay in Chufut-Kale and then bring it to Jerusalem, but he encountered a serious obstacle:

The king of Kedar [the khan of the Crimea] took all of the charitable funds for his royal household [and chained Joseph] in chains of iron for three months. Afterward, following entreaties and the efforts of the notable men of the community, the king released him from his imprisonment. Nevertheless, [the king] did not give back to him any of the confiscated alms, and therefore he did not pursue his journey to his intended destination, the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, but instead remained there in their study hall for three years and occupied himself with the study of Torah and the sciences and copied many books of the works of our sages of blessed memory…{{fn:104}}
content.comments: [104] Simḥah Isaac Lutski. {{em:Sefer meʾirat ʿenayim}}. Yosef Algamil (ed.). 2 vols. Ashdod: Mekhon Tifʾeret Yosef le-Ḥeqer ha-Yahadut ha-Qaraʾit, 2001–2002, pp. 146–147.

content.english: As this passage indicates, delivering money to the Land of Israel was a difficult task. In addition to the dangers of robbery on the way, the messengers who collected and delivered the donations were often subjected to extortion by the Crimean rulers themselves.

In the eighteenth century, the community of Jerusalem was reorganized by Samuel Levi, who had migrated there from Damascus with twenty-four of his family members in 1744. He succeeded in reviving the Karaite community and was even able to repurchase some of the community’s property, which had been sold to the Rabbanites to pay the community’s debts. However, a few years later, due to extortion by the Ottoman administration, this small community found itself once again in heavy debt. Although Samuel Levi traveled to Egypt to collect donations, the economic situation of the community there did not enable its members to provide substantial financial support for the Karaites of Jerusalem, and they appealed to the Crimea.

Important information on the extent of the financial support sent by the Crimean Karaite communities is found in a letter from the community of Chufut-Kale to the community of Jerusalem, dated 1775.{{fn:105}} From this letter, we can assess the differences in the economic state of the Crimean communities according to the value of their contributions: Chufut-Kale contributed the largest sum, 686 {{em:gurush}} and 26 pieces;{{fn:106}} Gözleve contributed 343 {{em:gurush}} and 14 pieces; Mangup provided 40 {{em:gurush;}} and Kaffa donated 30 {{em:gurush}}. This letter also states that the Chufut-Kale community demanded that the Egyptian community contribute a sum of 300 {{em:gurush}} and asked for 100 {{em:gurush}} from the community of Istanbul. Damascus is absent from the list because it was economically dependent on the Crimean communities at that time. Hence, it appears that Chufut-Kale, enjoying relative economic stability, served as a center for the collection of donations for Jerusalem and of support for other communities.
content.comments: [105] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, n. 1, p. 455. | [106] “Piece,” a small coin. Forty pieces were equal to one {{em:piastre}}.

content.english: Due to the war between Russia and the Ottomans, the donations detailed in the letter did not arrive in the Land of Israel. Therefore, Mordecai ben Samuel Levi, who became the Jerusalem community’s leader after his father’s death, traveled by himself to the Crimea to save his community from liquidation. He did not succeed in collecting the necessary amount in the Crimea. When he returned to Jerusalem, his nephew Berakhah, a grandson of Samuel Levi, who worked as a synagogue assistant ({{em:shamash}}), was tortured and put in jail by the authorities as punishment for the debts of the community. Rendered desperate by these events and by the communal debt of 4,000 {{em:gurush}}, Mordecai ben Samuel Levi asserted that unless all the Karaite communities helped them, he would leave Jerusalem with his family. His nephew Berakhah, after his release from jail, arrived in Chufut-Kale to collect donations with his mother, who was of Crimean origin. Having been impressed by life in this community, Berakhah considered relocating to Chufut-Kale. Eventually, however, after the community leaders promised to cover his living expenses with 1,000 {{em:gurush}} for two years, he agreed to return to Jerusalem. He had no other source of income there but did not want to be dependent on his uncles.{{fn:107}}
content.comments: [107] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 329.

content.english: There was also a Karaite community in Hebron during different periods. The existence of a small community is attested to in the eleventh century, as is the presence of three Karaite families in the sixteenth century. The aforementioned Crimean leader of the Gözleve community, Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan, who made a pilgrimage to the Land of Israel in 1785–1786, testifies that during his visit to Hebron, he saw a Karaite cemetery there. He mentions that he and other Crimean pilgrims had stayed at Rabbanite houses that had previously belonged to the Karaite community. Rabbi Malkiel Ashkenazi, who arrived in Hebron in 1540 and established a Rabbanite community there, reports that he bought a large courtyard from the Karaites that “was fortified by the stone walls of their high three- and four-story houses.”{{fn:108}}
content.comments: [108] Oded Avisar (ed.). {{em:Sefer Hebron: ʿIr ha-ʾavot ve yishuvah be-reʾi ha-dorot}} [The City of Forefathers and its Settlement through the Eyes of the Generations]. Jerusalem: Keter, 1970 (in Hebrew), p. 43.

content.english: We find further evidence of the Crimean Karaites’ support of the Rabbanite community of Hebron. In 1728, the head of the Crimean Rabbanite community of Karasubazar, R. David ben Eliezer Lekhno, sent a letter to the Karaite leaders of Kaffa, asking them for support for the Rabbanite community of Hebron, which was plagued with heavy debts. These Karaite leaders—Eliyahu Fuki and Isaac Sinani—expressed their willingness to support the Hebron community, demonstrating a clear collaboration with the Crimean community. This case also demonstrates that there was collaboration between the Crimean Karaites and Rabbanites with respect to donations to the Land of Israel.
{{header:Chapter 2. Karaite Leadership in the Crimea in the Periods of Transition}}

This chapter presents the central figures who led the Karaite communities from the time of the Crimean Khanate until the Crimea became part of the Russian Empire. The sources tell of Karaite leaders’ attempts to save their community from the horrors of war and the outrages of the authorities and their ways of overcoming physical and political threats and dangers while maintaining study halls, synagogues, and all aspects of religious life.

What do we know about the life and activity of the Crimean Karaite community leaders? In addition to their community responsibilities, many of them were teachers, legal decisors, prolific authors, and bibliophiles with large libraries of Karaite and Rabbanite manuscripts and printed books in various genres. One can find evidence of the life and activity of the key figures in the Crimean Karaite communities through private letters, historical chronicles, travelers’ diaries, tomb inscriptions, and oral traditions that circulated in the Crimea. However, most of these sources are from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when the major Karaite centers in the Crimea were in Chufut-Kale and then shifted to the coastal cities of Feodosia (Kaffa), particularly Evpatoria (Gözleve), after the Russian annexation. The community of Mangup ceased to exist after it was invaded by the Russian army in 1703. Some remnants of the Mangup community relocated to neighboring Chufut-Kale, where they established their own synagogue, while others settled in coastal cities.

The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were a period of dramatic transition in Karaite life in the Crimea, as well as in Eastern Europe. The annexation of Lithuania, Volhynia, and Podolia from 1772–1795, after the partitions of Poland between Russia, Prussia, and Austria—and of the Crimea in 1783—meant that most Karaite communities came under a new power during this period. In addition, they all—apart from the Austrian-annexed communities of Galicia in Halich, Lwów, and Kukizów—found themselves within the territory of one state: the Russian Empire.

Until the Russian annexation, the Crimean Karaites lived under the rule of Muslim political entities. First, they lived under the Crimean Tatar Khanate, and after 1475, the residents of the coast and of Mangup lived under direct Ottoman rule. They were subject to restrictive Islamic laws and periodically suffered from arbitrary taxes. After the Russian annexation, they found themselves in a new reality; they now could settle and work anywhere in the peninsula, yet they also encountered a dramatically different governmental policy that harbored both the danger of economic collapse and the threat of the gradual dissipation of their small communities.

The Russian czars had neither a clear idea of which policies to pursue regarding their large Jewish minority (estimated at one million of an estimated total population of thirty-five million at the time of the Polish partitions) nor enough knowledge about Jews and Judaism. They were, however, strongly influenced by the medieval Christian stereotype that the Jews were responsible for the murder of Jesus. Fearing that Jews would migrate to Russian cities and compete economically with the local population, Catherine II introduced new legal restrictions that confined the Jews to the Pale of Settlement, comprising the western governorates of the empire. She subjected Jews to double taxation, and several other restrictive laws were enacted in different periods by subsequent rulers, along with various projects (mostly unsuccessful) to modernize the rapidly growing Jewish population. In this era, the Karaites were perceived as one of the many Jewish communities in the empire.

The old patterns of interaction with the previous authorities, the Crimean khans, no longer worked in this new reality, and Karaite leaders had to develop new forms of interaction. Over the course of three to four decades, they succeeded in forging extensive ties with Russian officials. A turning point for the community came in 1837, when the Russian authorities recognized the Karaites as a distinct religious group independent of the Rabbanite community, resulting in the establishment of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory, which was supported by the government.{{fn:109}} During subsequent years, Karaite leaders succeeded in obtaining the gradual abolition of the discriminatory laws against their community; occupational restrictions were voided, employment in official positions was permitted, and Karaites were allowed to employ Christian domestic workers. In 1852, the Karaites were exempted from the restrictions of the Pale of Settlement, and in 1863, they were granted rights equal to those of the general Russian population in accordance with each individual’s social status. For the Russian Karaites, this opened previously unavailable career opportunities, and new Karaite communities began to emerge in numerous Russian towns and cities—in Novorossia during the first stage and{{fn:110}} later in the capital, Saint Petersburg. However, this success came at a price. After several decades, these newly formed communities began to disappear, as mixed marriages and conversions became increasingly frequent. Under Russian rule, Karaite leaders had successfully protected their community from discriminatory decrees but were unable to stop the process of assimilation.
content.comments: [109] Phillip E. Miller. {{em:Karaite Separatism in Nineteenth-Century Russia}}. Cincinnati: Hebrew Union College Press, 1993, pp. 43–45. | [110] New Russia, or South Russia, which lay north of the Black Sea. It was formed as a new imperial province of Russia (Novorossiya Governorate), with its largest cities—Odessa and Nikolaev—being a project of Russian colonization; therefore, Jews were allowed to settle there.

content.english: {{h2:2.1 Simḥah Isaac ben Moses Lutski: The Karaite Kabbalist}}

The connection between the Crimean and Polish–Lithuanian communities was established during the settlement of the Solkhat Karaites in Lithuania and was maintained throughout the history of these communities, as evidenced by the prolific correspondence between them dating back to the fifteenth century. During the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, several Karaite families and individuals, mostly from the learned class, relocated from Poland–Lithuania to the Crimea. Some became teachers and spiritual leaders of the Crimean Karaite communities and had a considerable impact on their language, thought, and education. Crimean communities copied and studied books authored by scholars from Poland and Lithuania.

One such leader was R. Simḥah Isaac ben Moses Lutski (1716–1761), who was also called ʿOlam Ṣair (literally, “microcosm”—an acronym based on the gematria of his name) and who belonged to the dynasty of scholars from Eastern Europe. He was one of the greatest eighteenth-century Karaite scholars and legal decisors from Eastern Europe and the author of numerous books in various genres.{{fn:111}} In his native Lutsk (Volhynia, presently in Ukraine), he copied books (among other activities), but this occupation did not provide him a steady income. Lutski authored a wealth of his own books on a range of topics, including scriptural exegesis, {{em:halakhah}}, astronomy, philosophy, and Kabbalah. His epitaph states that he wrote twenty-four books.{{fn:112}} Following an invitation from Mordecai ben Berakhah, the head of the Chufut-Kale community, Lutski relocated to the Crimea with his wife, Batsheva, and some of his children from Lutsk in 1753–1754 and settled in Chufut-Kale. His student, Simḥah ben Solomon Kusdini (see Section 2.4), who came from Evpatoria to Chufut-Kale to participate in Lutski’s study hall, likewise attests to Lutski’s twenty-four books and provides some details about his master’s relocation. Kusdini complains in a letter to Benjamin Aga that the small Karaite community in the Crimea had lost its wisdom because of the meager number of true sages, but he asserts that Simḥah Isaac Lutski considerably improved the local Karaites’ intellectual level. Simḥah Kusdini testifies as follows:
content.comments: [111] See Daniel Lasker. {{em:The Sage Simḥah Isaac Lutski: An Eighteenth-Century Karaite Rabbi—Selected Writings}}. Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute for the Study of Jewish Communities in the East and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, 2015 (in Hebrew); Golda Akhiezer and Daniel Lasker. “{{em:Sefer Elon More}}: qatekhisis le-ḥinnukh qaraʾi me-hammeʾah ha-shemoneh ʿesreh” [{{em:Sefer Elon More}}: An Eighteenth-Century Karaite Educational Catechism]. {{em:Dor le-Dor}} 27 (2006): 7–38 (in Hebrew). | [112] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 483, pp. 149–150.

content.english: My master composed about 24 various books and even more, which teach good judgment and knowledge [Psalm 119:66] in splendid divine wisdom… and composed a number of books on the true Kabbalah… Mordecai ben Berakhah, the loyal minister, a virtuous person, having been modest, tried to honor the Torah teachers and to support them so that they would not need anything. And he, be his memory blessed, spent gold currency, and brought books, and consecrated them to the study halls for the sons of poor people. But when he [Mordecai ben Berakhah] went to Jerusalem… on his way back he died on the island called Skiz [Chios], and was buried there with great honors made by the King of Kedar [the Tatar khan Shahin Giray] who was there at the time. And after this minister’s demise, he [Lutski] was supported by Samuel Aga, the loyal minister, who gave more and more to my master… and he didn’t need anything until the day of his death… He [Samuel Aga] also supported all the students, and spent much money on them, and consecrated many books, and built a new building for an additional {{em:beit midrash}} from hewn stones… and put there a teacher, and assigned 400 {{em:gurush}} as a fund in order to pay this teacher, in addition to students’ stipends. After the death of my master and teacher, the honorable Rav Simḥah Isaac… some years later an impure incident befell our loyal minister, God will avenge his blood…{{fn:113}}
content.comments: [113] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 375–376.

content.english: This passage clarifies that the leaders of the Chufut-Kale community—Mordecai ben Berakhah, and after his unexpected death, Samuel Aga (see Section 2.2)—supported Simḥah Lutski, along with the entire educational system in their community. Lutski’s relocation to Chufut-Kale significantly improved his financial situation; he became the dean of the study hall until his death and had numerous students.

Lutski composed, among other works, the historiographical book {{em:Oraḥ Ṣaddiqim}} (The Way of the Righteous), which deals with the Karaite–Rabbanite schism. In the “Third Path” of this book, Lutski gives an alphabetical bibliography of the Karaite works known to him, including abstracts and the names of the authors. Although this lengthy list is incomplete, it includes the names of Karaite authors and treatises known from no other source and is therefore of great importance.

Lutski gained renown largely because of his interest in Kabbalah. He viewed it as a truly valuable discipline even for Karaites, and authored six works on the subject.{{fn:114}} His writings on Kabbalah also shed light on his view of the history of Karaite and Rabbanite tradition. Unlike other Karaite authors, he regards the Kabbalistic tradition as part of the true wisdom given to Moses on Mount Sinai and transmitted to Joshua and then others. According to his view, after the destruction of the Second Temple, the Rabbanites, who had preserved the Kabbalistic tradition, were unwilling to share it with the Karaites, and for this reason, the Karaites were no longer exposed to it. In his book {{em:Livnat ha-Sappir}} (1756), Lutski defendsthe study of Kabbalah, explains its concepts, and discusses the stages of its transmission. He maintains that Kabbalah studies, unlike philosophy, are of supreme importance to the Karaites and are a common Karaite and Rabbanite pursuit.
content.comments: [114] Lasker{{em:. The Sage Simḥah Isaac Lutski}}, p. 10.

content.english: Lutski was to some extent a tragic figure because no group among his Karaite and Rabbanite contemporaries shared his views. His attempts to contact Rabbanites in Volhynia, borrow books from them, and study Kabbalah from them were rejected because he was a Karaite. As he recounts: “I have not had the privilege that I desired of studying {{em:Sefer ʿEṣ Ḥayyim}}, the work of the master R. Ḥayyim Vital, the consummate student and most senior steward of the holy Ari [i.e., Isaac Luria], of blessed memory… because they [Rabbanites] did not deign to permit me to read or study a whit of it.”{{fn:115}}
content.comments: [115] Simḥah Isaac Lutski. {{em:Livnat ha-Sappir.}} Yosef Algamil (ed.). Ashdod: Mekhon Tifʾeret Yosef le-Ḥeqer ha-Yahadut ha-Qaraʾit, 2002, p. 65 (in Hebrew).

content.english: At the same time, Lutski complains that many of his Karaite contemporaries, due to faulty understanding, objected to his studying of Kabbalah: “They said that all the wisdom of the Kabbalah, both theoretical and practical, is contrived, false, and void, and they saw fit to argue against me and protest against me that I had departed from the fold of the sages of the Karaites.”{{fn:116}} He was active as a teacher in his native Lutsk during the late 1740s and early 1750s, but we have no evidence that any of his students continued the teaching of Kabbalah after his relocation to the Crimea.

In Chufut-Kale, too, there was no special interest in Kabbalah among the members of the community.{{fn:117}} That does not mean, however, that no Karaites studied Kabbalah. Lutski claims that Lithuanian Karaite scholars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries studied Kabbalah, and he provides a list of the names of these scholars, asserting that they excelled in both theoretical and practical Kabbalah. According to him, hundreds of Lithuanian Karaite scholars studied the subject (this number may have been slightly exaggerated).{{fn:118}} In addition, it is unclear to what extent these learned Karaites were deeply involved in this subject or whether they had only superficial knowledge of Kabbalistic concepts, nor is it even certain that they possessed Kabbalistic texts. In the Crimea, we also find dozens of manuscripts on Kabbalah in private Karaite libraries, including those of the community leaders. However, despite their interest in this sphere, we do not find any Kabbalist scholar other than Lutski in either Poland–Lithuania or the Crimea.

Notwithstanding the rejection or ignoring of his Kabbalistic interest by his Karaite milieu, Lutski was a highly esteemed Karaite sage. He died in 1861 in Chufut-Kale, and Firkovich published the epitaph on his grave.{{fn:119}}
content.comments: [119] Firkovich. {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 483, pp. 149–150.

content.english: {{h2:2.2 The Aga Family in the Crimean Khanate}}

The role of a community leader was sometimes transmitted from a father to his son. One example was the Aga dynasty, which led the Chufut-Kale community for over three generations. The first well-known figure of this family (which was not yet called Aga) was Abraham ben Josiah Yerushalmi (c. 1685–after 1734), who was a spiritual leader, a prominent scholar, and the most important author of his time in the Crimea.{{fn:120}} He served as a {{em:ḥazzan}} and a teacher of Torah in the Chufut-Kale community. Although the agnomen Yerushalmi indicates that his father, Josiah, made the pilgrimage to Jerusalem, we have no details about the journey. According to the Karaite oral tradition, Abraham ben Josiah was appointed to serve in the mint of the Crimean khan.
content.comments: [120] See more about him and his book in Samuel Abraham Poznanski (ed.). {{em:Ha-Qaraʾi Avraham ben Yoshiyahu Yerushalmi}}. Berdichev, 1894 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Abraham ben Josiah’s religious-philosophical treatise {{em:Emunah Omen}}, written in 1712 and published in 1846 in Evpatoria, is devoted to the divine origin and the eternity of the Torah and to the questionof whether the Jewish tradition permits the study of the secular sciences. His book is somewhat polemical; one of his main topics is whether the Karaite or Rabbanite religion is the true one. Abraham ben Josiah defends the Karaite conception of the Torah, arguing that the differences between the rabbinic conception and the Karaite view of the fulfillment of the commandments were insignificant. He even shows respect for the Talmudic authorities and later Rabbanite scholars, with whose works he was well acquainted, although he did not accept their positions as obligatory. Abraham ben Josiah opposes the study of the secular sciences, except in the service of the Torah.He was familiar with both Karaite and Rabbanite philosophical and scientific literature. His numerous other works comprise homiletical discourses, liturgical poetry included in the Karaite prayer book, and {{em:Shaʾol Shaʾal}}, a treatise on the laws of ritual slaughter.{{fn:121}}
content.comments: [121] Abraham ben Josiah. {{em:Shaʾol Shaʾal}}. RNL EVR II A 322. This treatise has never been published and is preserved in manuscript.

content.english: The first person to bear the name Aga{{fn:122}} was his son, Samuel ben Abraham (1717–1770). Samuel, who lived in Chufut-Kale and was the leader of the community, was also known by the title Rosh ha-Golah (Exilarch), and he was an expert on Karaite law and an authority on calendrical issues. He was also a “court Jew” in the court of the Tatar khan Qirim Giray, who appointed Samuel to mint coins for the khanate in 1768, and defended the interests of his community before government officials. Samuel wrote a number of liturgical poems, some of which were included in the Karaite {{em:siddurim}}.
content.comments: [122] In Turkic languages—lord, minister.

content.english: There are at least two oral traditions about Samuel Aga that shed some light on his biography. One is the aforementioned popular story (see Section 1.2.1) of how Khan Qirim Giray demanded that Samuel Aga convert to Islam. Samuel rejected this demand, demonstrating his loyalty to his faith, and the khan, after initially exiling him, called him back to the court and appointed him chief courtier.

Another source on Samuel Aga was the Crimean Karaite {{em:maskil}} Samuel Pigit (1849–1911). He based biographical information about Samuel Aga on the testimonies of local, elderly Karaites.{{fn:123}} In recounting the history of Samuel Aga’s life, Pigit says that Samuel’s father died when he was a young child, and his mother, an educated woman, found good teachers for him. An exceptionally gifted student, Samuel became a rabbi when he was eighteen and started teaching disciples in the local study hall. At this time, the leader of the Chufut-Kale community was Çelebi,{{fn:124}} whom the khan appointed to manage his mint. The community members feared Çelebi because of his numerous arbitrary edicts. Among others, he forbade people from passing near his house on carts so that the noise would not wake him. One day, Samuel punished Çelebi’s son, who attended his study hall. When the father heard about this act, he came to the study hall and severely insulted Samuel in the presence of his students. Samuel, in turn, incited his disciples against Çelebi, who beat Çelebi. Afterward, Samuel was forced to flee; he took leave of his mother and went to Kaffa. During the years he lived there, he met an old Karaite who introduced him to the “king,”{{fn:125}} and Samuel made a successful career in his court. Samuel returned to Chufut-Kale a very rich man, and with a recommendation letter from his master on behalf of the khan of Bakhchesaray, he immediately became a leader of the community.
content.comments: [123] See his book, Samuel Pigit. {{em:ʾIggeret nidḥei Shmuʾel}} [Epistle of the Scattered of Samuel]. Saint Petersburg, 1894, pp. 5–10 (in Hebrew). | [124] Pigit does not mention his given name. | [125] It is unclear who this king was. The Crimean khans lived in Bakhchesaray, and Kaffa was under the direct rule of the Ottoman Empire. If this story is true, this person may have been the representative of the Ottoman administration.

content.english: These were hard times for Çelebi, especially in light of Samuel’s systematic cancellation of his rulings and prohibitions. For instance, according to Pigit, Samuel ordered a Karaite funeral procession to pass near Çelebi’s house, despite his stern objection, instead of going through the fields as the community members had practiced previously. He also canceled the custom that had been invented and enforced by Çelebi compelling the Rav to personally serve the people around the table at festive meals.{{fn:126}}
content.comments: [126] Pigit. {{em:Epistle}}, p. 9.

content.english: This confrontation between the two community leaders eventually came to a sad end. One day, Samuel Aga was murdered on his way home to Chufut-Kale from the khan’s court in Bakhchesaray. According to Pigit’s informants, the murder was instigated by Çelebi.

Pigit’s version of Samuel’s biography does not include the story about an attempt by Khan Qirim Giray to convert Samuel to Islam. This biography was drawn from the testimonies of the elders of the Karaite community in Chufut-Kale, and we cannot be sure about the veracity of its details. However, this story reflects important aspects, some of them also appearing in other sources.{{fn:127}} The story also demonstrates the intensity of competition and conflict in the community and the positive activity of Samuel Aga; however, we know little from other sources about Çelebi’s achievements.
content.comments: [127] See his tomb inscription, Firkovich. {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 498, pp. 156–157. In this inscription, he is described as “a good counselor and an excellent judge, and the Head of the Bet Din… over all the congregations he is like a candle.” It also states that he was murdered: “his blood crying out from the earth to a jealous God who takes vengeance.”

content.english: Samuel Aga had three sons: Eliezer, Benjamin, and Simḥah. After Samuel’s death, his son Benjamin Aga (d. 1824) became a leader and intercessor for the community of Chufut-Kale. When the last Crimean khan, Shahin Giray the Reformer, rose to power and decided to carry out a series of economic and political reforms, Benjamin became one of the khan’s unofficial court advisers. Benjamin, like his father, was also appointed to mint coins for the khanate in the court of Shahin Giray, and in 1781, he leased the customs duties on the sale of wine.

Like his father, Benjamin protected his community’s interests. He was active during the period of the civil war in the Crimea from 1776 to 1783. The civil war arose owing to the Tatar population’s rebellion against the Russian invasion of the region; the appointment of Shahin Giray as the new khan by the Russian empress Catherine II; and an attempt by Shahin Giray, who had a European education, to implement liberal reforms in the Islamic society of the Crimea. Benjamin was loyal to Shahin Giray until the very end of his rule. He lent Shahin Giray money for his reform project, sent him taxes from Crimea when he was already in exile, and visited him when the khan moved to Russia after his enthronement by the Russian authorities.{{fn:128}}
content.comments: [128] The fate of this important figure in Crimean history was quite tragic. The Russian empress Catherine decided, before the annexation of the Crimea, that she no longer needed Shahin Giray and dethroned him. The former khan was forced to move to Russia with his family and retinue, receiving a pension from the Russian authorities. After a number of years, the khan decided to relocate to Turkey, where he was executed by order of the sultan for his collaboration with the Russian enemy.

content.english: We find information about the events during the civil war in the Crimea, including the suffering of the Karaites, in the aforementioned chronicle of Azariah ben Elijah. Azariah describes Benjamin Aga as having played a central role in the communal affairs of this period and makes clear that on more than one occasion, he used his status as a court Jew to save his community from oppressive policies. According to Azariah, Devlet Giray seized the throne in 1777 and falsely accused the Karaites of Chufut-Kale, as well as the Orthodox monks from the neighboring monastery, of stealing the khan’s money. This khan attempted to extort from the Karaites (and the Orthodox monks) a huge sum of money that they were unable to pay, but Benjamin found a way to annul the evil decree:

In the month of Adar, Devlet Giray Khan raised a false accusation against the holy community of Kale, and against the uncircumcised, living in Miriam,{{fn:129}} and began to oppress us, rob us, and deprive us of property, saying: “You found a vessel filled with gold on the border of the monastery!” and ordered us to fill [such] a vessel of gold [and give it to him]. Our community was in great sorrow, and all the men of the monastery, from small to large, were captured, placed in jail, and tormented with severe tortures… The reason for this accusation was some empty vessels near the well, which were abandoned long ago… A few days later, the matter [concerning the vessels] reached the khan, who looked for a pretext [for accusation], anticipating that he would not retain the throne and he would need money for travel expenses. Under these circumstances, he resorted to wiles. And two of the top officials and the commander of the police squad… arrived in Kaleh. The gates of the city were locked, and the heads of the [Karaite] community gathered in the house of Rabbi Benjamin, who served as a dignitary in the khan’s court at that time. The [officials] declared the demand of the khan to fill [the vessel] with gold to the brim. This vessel could hold about 100 ounces of water, and we didn’t know what to do. Even if we had given all our property and houses, we would not have been able to pay a thousandth of this amount. Unable to pay at the request of the khan—and a king does not consult with mortals—the whole community asked for mercy from these officials… But they answered us arrogantly and impolitely and ordered the expulsion of our entire community with everyone in iron chains, unless we obeyed the decree. Blessed be God, that he did not leave us without a deliverer… And our great nobleman rose, faithful and wise, Benjamin “stood up in the breach”… and appeared before the khan thereby endangering his own life, and begged his consent for 1,200 silver {{em:gurush}}. Each of our community donated according to his condition, and the Supreme One should double their reward…{{fn:130}}
content.comments: [129] The Greek Orthodox monks, who lived in the monastery of Maria’s Dormition near Chufut-Kale. | [130] Akhiezer. “The Events,” pp. 318–320, 1r, 17–40.

content.english: Benjamin Aga was very active in promoting the well-being of the Karaite Crimean communities and in supporting the community of Jerusalem.{{fn:131}} He corresponded with Karaite leaders in Poland, Lithuania, Istanbul, and Jerusalem and financially supported their communities in times of distress. After the Russian annexation of the Crimea, he continued to serve as head of the community.
content.comments: [131] His name heads a list of donors to the Karaite community of Jerusalem that was appended to a letter from 1775 from the community of Chufut-Kale to members of the Jerusalemite community. Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 457.

content.english: In addition to being a successful community leader, Benjamin Aga was a learned person. He was an expert in Karaite {{em:halakhah}} and an authority on the Karaite calendar, and he had a large library of Karaite and Rabbanite books. This library may have belonged to his father, Samuel, or even his grandfather, Abraham ben Josiah, author of the book {{em:ʾEmunah ʾOmen}}. We know about the existence of the Aga family’s library from the testimony of Abraham Firkovich, who mentions that during his visit to Chufut-Kale in 1838, he bought “a cartload of books… for a high price” from the books of the Aga family.{{fn:132}} In addition, an ownership note on one of the books records that Benjamin Aga himself sold some books of his library to the Karaite community of Gözleve: “These are the titles of books which the Karaite Holy Community of Gözleve bought from Benjamin Aga, the loyal minister and the excellent judge, for 800 Russian coins.”{{fn:133}} This note provides a list of various Karaite books and one Rabbanite book.
content.comments: [132] Firkovich. {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 5. | [133] Ownership note on the {{em:Sefer Dinim}} by Benjamin Nahavendi, IOS C 101, 259r.

content.english: With his brother Simḥah, Benjamin Aga reestablished a publishing house in Chufut-Kale, marking the second time a printing press had functioned in the town.{{fn:134}} The first printers appeared during the time of his grandfather, Abraham ben Josiah Yerushalmi.
