These were the brothers Afeda and Shabbetai Yeraqa, who were invited by another community leader at that time, Isaac Sinani. This Sinani may have been a rival of Samuel Aga, but we have no information on his life and activity. The Yeraqa brothers came from Istanbul in 1733 and remained in Chufut-Kale, where they established a publishing house and published miscellaneous works, including {{em:haftarot}} and prayers. In 1737, they published an entire liturgy and, in 1741, a book of blessings entitled {{em:Meqabeṣ Nidḥei Yisrael}}. We have no evidence for why their press stopped printing after that year. In Benjamin’s time, the Karaite press functioned in Chufut-Kale from 1804 to 1806, publishing the revised versions of the liturgy and {{em:Meqabeṣ Nidḥei Yisrael}} as well as two tracts on calendrical issues. After this press went out of business, Karaite books were published in Christian or Rabbanite printing houses located in Vienna and Istanbul. This situation lasted until the reopening of the publishing house by Abraham Firkovich in 1830 in Evpatoria, where the majority of Karaite books from the Crimea and Eastern Europe were published. One of the major problems concerning book consumption was that small Karaite communities could not permit themselves the luxury of maintaining such an expensive business and printed only limited numbers of copies; in addition, some Rabbanite printers were not prepared to publish Karaite books. For this reason, into the twentieth century, Karaites of the Crimea and Eastern Europe continued to transcribe books by hand. Nevertheless, the situation changed for the better during the nineteenth century—in addition to the publishing house in Evpatoria, several volumes were published by Rabbanite presses in Vilna, Odessa, and Zhitomir.
content.comments: [134] On the Karaite press, see Walfish. “Karaite Press and Printing,” pp. 925–962.

content.english: 97Following Russia’s annexation of the Crimea, Benjamin Aga managed to serve as head of the community, although the Russian authorities, because of their disapproval of him, did not grant him any official status. The reason for their disapproval of Benjamin is not entirely clear. As one story goes, during Catherine II’s visit to the Crimea in 1787, Benjamin, who represented his community before the empress, asked her to permit the Karaite community to leave the Crimea and follow the exiled khan Shahin Giray to Turkey. His request created an awkward situation, and the empress reprimanded Benjamin for showing ingratitude to the Russian authorities. This story was recounted by Simon Shyszman{{fn:135}} without referring to its source. It could be part of an oral tradition that does not match historical reality; indeed, there is some reason to doubt the story. According to the existing practice in the Russian Empire, such an impudent request would not have gone unpunished. Instead, however, Benjamin kept his position and even visited Russian authorities in Saint Petersburg after this alleged incident. We can presume that this story was part of local folklore and designed to demonstrate Benjamin’s loyalty to the Crimean khan while possibly reflecting dissatisfaction with a new power.
content.comments: [135] Simon Szyszman. {{em:Le Karaïsme: Ses doctrines et son histoire}}. Lausanne: Éd. l’Âge d’Homme, 1980, p. 104; Miller. {{em:Karaite Separatism}}, n. 41, p. 56.

content.english: Having been appointed head of a special delegation to the government, Benjamin traveled to Saint Petersburg in 1795 with two other community leaders of the Crimean Karaites: Isaac ben Solomon, the {{em:ḥazzan}} of the community, and Solomon ben Naḥamu Babovich, a wealthy merchant from Evpatoria (Gözleve). Their task was to request an exemption for their community from legal restrictions imposed on the entire Jewish population of the Russian Empire. The delegation obtained from Catherine II an exemption for Crimean Karaites from double taxation and from the billeting of soldiers in their homes at the expense of their owners. In addition, the Karaite communities were permitted to purchase immovable property and employ Christian servants. Isaac ben Solomon wrote a short account of their mission. Their journey to the Russian capital lasted about three months, and the son of Solomon ben Naḥamu Babovich, Naḥamu, even claimed that the delegation stayed there for six months and that his father studied astronomy during this time. If so, what did Benjamin do during his stay at the capital? Philip Miller suggests that he tried to find a way to be reimbursed by the authorities for the huge sums that he had lent to Shahin Giray.{{fn:136}}
Benjamin Aga died in 1824 and left at least two sons, Assaf and Elijah, whose fates are unknown. After Benjamin’s demise, another dynasty came to power in the Crimea: namely, the Babovich family.
{{h2:2.3 Joseph Aga: A Chronicler of a New Era}}

95In the days of Benjamin Aga, educated leadership also arose in Evpatoria (Gözleve). After the Russian conquest, this coastal city (which developed during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries under direct Ottoman rule) gradually became the largest Karaite center. The significance of Chufut-Kale, and its population, declined at the beginning of the nineteenth century. The Karaite leaders of Evpatoria maintained constant contact with other Crimean communities, especially Chufut-Kale. They coordinated their policy, collaborating to collect donations for the Karaites of Jerusalem, Damascus, Istanbul, and Eastern Europe when these communities experienced difficult periods. At the same time, the learned leaders and scholars waged fierce polemics on calendrical and other issues of Karaite {{em:halakhah}}, both by correspondence and in special meetings.

One of the leaders of the Evpatoria community was referred to in the sources as Joseph, or Yassaf, Aga. Although he was not from the same family as Benjamin, he enjoyed elevated status in the khan’s court. The background of his identity can be pieced together from various sources. This is apparently the same person who was mentioned in the charter ({{em:yarliq}}) of Shahin Giray Khan in 1778. According to its text, this charter was given to the head of the mint, Yassaf Aga, who is called “the loyal minister.” The document states that the khan gave Joseph Aga instructions about minting the coins.

The aforementioned chronicle of Azariah ben Elijah ascribes to Joseph a central role with Benjamin Aga, and by virtue of being “court Jews,” they often saved members of the Karaite community from disturbances. Azariah adds that “the loyal minister” Joseph Aga and Benjamin Aga, two community leaders, were summoned by the Tatar administration after the khan’s tax reform to ask them which system of tax payment each preferred for their community. It remains unclear how these two leaders shared their functions in the khan’s mint.

Possibly (and this is the opinion of Samuel Abraham Poznanski),{{fn:137}} Joseph is also referred to as “the loyal minister” on one of the tomb inscriptions from Gözleve, dated 1797 and published by Firkovich: “This sign on the grave of the dear honorable Joseph, the son of honorable Barukh, the loyal minister, of blessed memory, died in the month of Shevat, in 5557 [1797].”{{fn:138}}
content.comments: [137] Samuel Abraham Poznanski. “Joseph Aga.” {{em:Encyclopedia of Bnei Mikraʾ}}. Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute (unpublished digital version). | [138] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 32, p. 227.

content.english: However, there is additional evidence of Joseph Aga that chronologically contradicts this inscription. During my archival work with Karaite manuscripts, I uncovered a lengthy Hebrew chronicle of Crimean origin written in Evpatoria by Joseph Aga.{{fn:139}} In a short note before the text of this chronicle, an anonymous person writes that it was written in the Tatar language by “Joseph Aga, the loyal minister, who was appointed on the khan’s mint in the days of Shahin Giray.” This person translates this chronicle into Hebrew and arranges all the events according to their dates (because Joseph Aga was not accurate regarding chronological order). The events depicted in this chronicle occurred from 1790 to 1821, and according to the tomb inscription published by Firkovich, Joseph Aga died in Evpatoria in 1797. Based on this information, it is possible that (a) this epitaph belongs to someone else because of its date and because it is too short and modest for someone of such importance, (b) Firkovich was mistaken about the date that he gave this epitaph, or (c) the events in this chronicle after 1797 were written by another author.
content.comments: [139] Joseph Aga. {{em:Chronicle}}. HC 484, op. 1, no. 1479.

content.english: The text of the chronicle by Joseph Aga, which is available today only in its Hebrew translation, is quite interesting from a historical standpoint, and to some extent reflects everyday life in the Crimea, including the affairs of the Karaite community. The chronicle describes the events that followed the Russian conquest in various Crimean cities, focusing on Joseph Aga’s home city of Gözleve. The chronicle discusses the aforementioned 1795 Karaite delegation to Catherine II headed by Benjamin Aga, taxation, commodity prices, the succession of czars in Russia, damage to the economy due to natural disasters, epidemics, and the lives and deaths of some Karaite community members. Joseph Aga also expresses curiosity about the questions asked by Napoleon to the Jews of France to verify their loyalty to the state.{{fn:140}} Interestingly, the Crimean Karaites were well informed about Jewish affairs in France at this time. Joseph Aga includes his personal (and sometimes quite emotional) reactions to the events he recounts, which he also accompanies with ethical comments titled “Ethics of the Wise Philosophers.”
content.comments: [140] The event discussed is the Assembly of Jewish Notables convened in 1806 by Napoleon in Paris, at which the Jews were enjoined to answer twelve questions concerning the position of Jewish law on intermarriage, the French motherland, compliance with civil law, and the business of interest-bearing loans.

content.english: {{h2:2.4 Simḥah ben Solomon Kusdini: From Gözleve to Istanbul}}

One of the intellectual leaders of the Evpatoria community was Simḥah ben Solomon, also called Kusdini after his emigration to Istanbul. Simḥah Kusdini was one of the outstanding students of the aforementioned Simḥah Isaac ben Moses Lutski. When Lutski came to Chufut-Kale and began teaching at the study hall, Simḥah Kusdini reflects:{{fn:141}} “When I heard in the city of Gözleve that the great sage and Rav came to us, I immediately left my father and mother and my native place, and went to the city of Qirq-Yer [Chufut- Kale], and I studied under his guidance about three years, day and night.” Simḥah Kusdini pursued his studies under Simḥah Lutski until Lutski’s death in 1766. After that, he joined the students under the guidance of Samuel ben Abraham, the {{em:ḥazzan}} of the Chufut-Kale community. His new teacher was known as the author of the books {{em:Ner Shemuel}} and {{em:Iggeret Kiddush ha-Hodesh}} and a number of epistles on Karaite faith and law. In addition to Torah studies, Simḥah’s instructor gave him ordination ({{em:semikhah}}) for {{em:sheḥitah}}. Eventually, Simḥah returned to his native Evpatoria, where he wrote the book {{em:Derekh Selulah}} (also called {{em:ʾOraḥ Ḥayyim}}), a commentary on {{em:ʿEṣ Ḥayyim}} by Aaron ben Elijah.
content.comments: [141] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 375.

content.english: In 1772, following the Russian invasion of the Crimea, Simḥah Kusdini departed with his family to Istanbul. There, he settled in the district of Hasköy, where the Jewish population was concentrated. He lived there until his death in 1811. His correspondence with the Crimean leaders—Benjamin Aga, Chufut-Kale scholar Isaac ben Solomon (author of {{em:ʾOr ha-Levanah}}), and others—indicates that his life after emigration was full of trials. Although he was chosen as a {{em:ḥakham}} of the local community, he had no salary. A short time after relocating, Simḥah lost his wife, Berukhah, and two sons, Solomon and Judah. In 1774, two years after Simḥah’s immigration, the Hasköy Karaite synagogue was burned as a result of a conflagration—a frequent occurrence in the city. Because the Jews and other minorities were forbidden from erecting stone buildings, many of them were built of wood and burned easily. When this disaster occurred, the indigent Karaite community, whose homes were also damaged by the conflagration, was unable to rebuild the synagogue at its own expense. In his letter to the Cairo Karaite community, Simḥah writes about this tragedy in poetic language:

There was a great conflagration in the village of Hasköy, a place of our residence. And it was burned with no one to douse it [based on Jeremiah 21:12], for with fire God executed judgment on us [based on Isaiah 66:16]. Thousands of homes burned down, and 13 communities [and] Rabbanite synagogues, and our holy house was burned among them—a little temple in our Exile. And one district [{{em:mahala}}] of the Karaites burned down, and not even one house remained, and we took our vessels for going to Exile [based on Ezekiel 12:3] of desert and forests, saving our sons and daughters. Half of our community lost their homes, and they are sitting in the yards… And we remained deprived of all good and lacking all.{{fn:142}}
content.comments: [142] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 367.

content.english: 90According to his accounts, he lived in poverty under heavy debt and had to work very hard without having time to study the Torah or write. Simḥah was forced to take loans, but because he did not succeed in his business, he could not repay them. He asks for support in his letter to Benjamin Aga, who tried to help him return to the Crimea, but the Istanbul community objected to this plan because they needed Simḥah as {{em:ḥakham}}. Due to his inability to pay back his Muslim creditors, he was imprisoned. However, after a period, he was redeemed thanks to the efforts of his daughter’s husband, Mor­decai, from Chufut-Kale, and was finally released from prison.

Simḥah felt isolated in Istanbul and regarded the intellectual level of the local community as lower than that in the Crimea. He expressed regret about leaving the Crimea, to which he wished to return; however, the difficulties of life in Istanbul and the distance prevented him from doing so. He nostalgically recalled that in the Crimea, he would read books with other sages.{{fn:143}} However, his claim about the lower intellectual level of the local community is questionable. This perception may have resulted from his distressed state of mind amid the miseries he endured and from his difficult circumstances, which did not enable him to get acquainted with the various persons and intellectual trends of this vast city. The scholar Benjamin Duvan who was from Simḥah’s native Evpatoria (see Section 2.6), visited Simḥah in Istanbul and took the opposite view. In one of his letters to Simḥah, in which he discusses calendrical matters, Duvan writes, “My beloved [Simḥah] lives in the land of the gentle Kusdina, where sophisticated sages from the seven climates live,{{fn:144}} including the Rabbanite sages, and among them can be found significant wisdom. Apparently, my beloved can hear from these wondrous wisdom…”{{fn:145}}
content.comments: [143] See, for instance, Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 350–353. | [144] From all over the world. Benjamin Duvan uses the division of the world into seven climates with subsequent subdivisions, which is common in medieval Muslim geographical literature, based on the works of Aristotle and Ptolemy. | [145] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 436.

content.english: Despite all these difficult circumstances, Simḥah managed to be active in various spheres of communal and intellectual life. He wrote a number of books, among them {{em:Zivḥei Shelemim}}, which includes 250 responsa about {{em:sheḥitah}} and is based on the book {{em:Gan ʿEden}} by Aaron ben Elijah of Nicomedia; ʿ{{em:Ed ʾEmunah}} on the principles of Karaite faith; {{em:Miqraeʾi Qodesh}}, a set of sermons on Torah portions, which includes, in brief, the reasons for the commandments; and responsa on astronomy and philosophy. None of these treatises, which were used by Turkish and Crimean Karaites, was ever published; they were preserved only in manuscripts. Simḥah also copied several books for his own use.

Simḥah was also actively involved in corresponding with most of the largest Karaite communities of his time. We find his letters to the Damascene community leaders, Amaṣia ha-Nasi and his son Solomon Yedidya Simḥah. Because Simḥah was an expert in astronomical and calendrical issues, they asked him to send them accu-rate and proven astronomical tables of new moons ({{em:moladot}}). Simḥah prepared tables for fifty-one years and sent them to the communities of Damascus, Cairo, and Hit (Samarra, about 125 kilometers north of Baghdad) in Mesopotamia—the last Karaite community of Persia, which disappeared in the late nineteenth century. He added time differences between their geographical regions and advised these communities not to rely only on the tables ({{em:daʿat ha-haqravah}}) but to follow primarily the practice of the observation of the moon ({{em:daʿat ha-berur}}), and they accepted his instructions.

Simḥah played a central role as an intermediary between the Karaite communities on behalf of the Istanbul community’s reconstruction after the conflagration. He immediately applied to the Crimean communities of Chufut-Kale, Evpatoria, Mangup, and Feodosia and to the Cairo community. The synagogue was rebuilt in 1800.

Donations for the Jerusalem Karaite community passed through Istanbul, and Simḥah became an intermediary among Karaite communities capable of supporting Jerusalem—primarily the Crimean ones. He corresponded with their leaders and was involved in the process of transferring money to Jerusalem. The safest practice used by Karaite communities was to rely on the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate as a conduit: the Istanbul leaders collected donations from their community and those brought from the Crimea; they then gave the funds to the Patriarchate in the capital, while the Karaite community of Jerusalem received the same amount from the local Greek Patriarchate.{{fn:146}} According to the Karaite documents, this practice (in addition to the direct transmission of money) existed from at least the eighteenth century, when Samuel ben Abraham Aga was involved in this process. Donations for the poor Damascene community were transferred in the same fashion to Jerusalem and delivered to envoys from Damascus.

All the occurrences that directly affected the Karaite commu- nities—the conflagration in Istanbul, the financial crises of the Jeru- salem community during the wars between the Russian and Otto- man empires (1768–1774, 1788–1792), and Napoleon’s 1799 invasion of the Land of Israel—are mentioned in Simḥah’s correspondence with other communities. During these years, there was a famine in Istanbul, and the Crimean population suffered from the Russian invasion of the Crimea in 1776, which was followed by the civil war in the peninsula. These occurrences prevented the free navigation of ships on the sea, with routes being closed most of the time. Such circumstances made contact (as well as money transfers) between the Crimean, Istanbul, and Jerusalem communities difficult—and in some periods impossible—resulting in the economic decline of the Istanbul and Jerusalem communities.

Despite these occurrences, Simḥah tried to support the small Jerusalem community, which desperately struggled for survival and was on the verge of complete ruin owing to its chronic debts, various exactions, and the tyranny of the local administration. He met with the Jerusalem community’s leader, Mordecai Halevi, who succeeded in reaching Istanbul before 1788 and helped obtain donations during his visit. Simḥah was also involved in subsequently transferring the donations to Jerusalem.

Six years later, Mordecai’s nephew, Berakhah Halevi (see Section 1.5), came with his wife to Istanbul to collect donations. During Berakhah’s stay in the city, Simḥah managed to collect a considerable sum of money in cash and securities for the Jerusalem community. However, Berakhah was forced to remain in the capital for an indefinite period because ships had ceased sailing, and no one knew when they would resume.

One day, Simḥah went to the market and heard people saying that a ship would depart on that day in a short time. He hurried to the house where Berakhah and his wife were staying and told them to hasten to the port. When they arrived, they saw the ship receding from shore. On which day or in which month the next ship would appear, no one knew. One Rabbanite Jew offered to take the frustrated couple in his fishing boat to reach the ship that had just left. This Jewish fisherman kept his word and delivered them to their destination; however, the money collected for the Jerusalem community remained in Istanbul. This story is recounted by Simḥah in his letter to Mordecai Halevi, who was enraged by the fact that he did not receive this money from Berakhah, who had traveled to Istanbul for that purpose. Simḥah tried to placate Halevi, and his words indicate that in a previous letter, Halevi had made unfair claims about Simḥah and other community leaders who had tried to help the Jerusalem community. Simḥah rebukes him:

Why, my beloved, do you not think good things about the Istanbul community, and always judge [them] unfavorably…? And why shall you not say to them “Be blessed before God,” for they stood in the breach for you in times of trouble and distress, and they sent you thousands of {{em:gurush}} [which were collected from] the Crimean communities in times when all the routes were closed, so that even a bird could not fly through! But instead you remained ungrateful, and paid them back with evil for good. And if, God forbid, the doors of the sea were not open yet, the Istanbul community nonetheless thought to send you all this money to save you from your troubles and debts, with God’s help…{{fn:147}}

In addition to organizing support for Jerusalem and other communities, Simḥah corresponded with the Crimean leaders and scholars, discussing issues of philosophy, Karaite faith, and calendrical and other issues of Karaite {{em:halakhah}}.

He sent one of his letters to the head of the Rabbanite community of Chios, Abraham Tariqa, on behalf of a Crimean pilgrim from Chufut-Kale, Berakhah ben Mordecai, who visited Jerusalem and stayed in Istanbul. This Berakhah was a son of the aforementioned Mordecai ben Berakhah (see Section 2.1), who established a study hall and brought the scholar Simḥah Lutski to Chufut-Kale but died and was buried in Chios on his way from Jerusalem to Crimea. His son Berakhah, unable to reach Chios to visit his father’s grave, asked Simḥah Kusdini to apply to Rabbi Tariqa to find somebody in the Rabbanite community to take care of the grave.{{fn:148}} This case illustrates the strong relations between the two communities that prevailed in this period, in both Turkey and the Crimea.
content.comments: [148] See this letter, ibid., pp. 358–360.

content.english: Simḥah was also involved in halakhic decisions concerning various situations related to the community members. In one such situation, Simḥah, along with other leaders of the Istanbul community, consulted by correspondence with Benjamin Aga and other authorities in Chufut-Kale.{{fn:149}} Simḥah’s letter states that an orphaned girl in Istanbul, Sarah bat Barukh, was engaged, but her intended husband had left the capital. About ten years “from the day of his departure no one knew whether he was still alive or dead, or converted … or possibly was captured—there was no evidence, and his wife was sad and suffering, and remained an {{em:agunah}}.”

Later, the story (in Simḥah’s version) takes an unexpected turn. A year earlier, two people from “our brethren Rabbanites,” a merchant and a servant, had come to the Karaite community of Istanbul and presented their evidence to two community members. The Rabbanites said that they were in a small town (apparently in the Ottoman Empire), and one day, a Greek came to their store wanting to buy bread and meat. They gave him what he wanted, and he ate before them. He spoke Turkish, Greek, and Spanish. They were surprised that, in such a small place, he knew all these languages. He asked them, “Do you know me?” “No!” they replied. He added, “I know you. You are from the city of Istanbul, the village of Pera Pasha.{{fn:150}} And I am from the Karaites. I was engaged to a girl, but I have got troubles… and I became Greek.” They responded, “If so, what about your wife? She will be an {{em:agunah}}!” And he answered, “From that day, she should not expect anything from me.” The Rabbanites asked, “Is it possible you will return to the religion of Israel?” He answered that this was impossible.{{fn:151}}
content.comments: [150] A suburb of Istanbul where there was also a Jewish population. | [151] Ibid.

content.english: The question that Simḥah put to the leaders of Chufut-Kale was a question of {{em:halakhah}}: whether the evidence of these Rabbanites about “this damn apostate bridegroom, may his name be erased” could be accepted because they spoke without any intention or interest. Simḥah asked to be given an answer as soon as possible to enable the girl to marry another man.

In this letter, he also writes on a different topic, one seemingly unrelated to this story. He mentions that Abraham Halevi, who was then the head of the Jerusalem community and had been widowed some time ago, was himself looking for a match, preferably from the Crimea. There were no candidates in the small community of Jerusalem, but he categorically rejected any possibility of marriage with a woman from the Damascene community, where, Abraham thought, the people were bad and miserly. He had two unmarried daughters, aged twenty-six and fifteen, and also rejected such a possibility for them because his other daughter had already had a bad experience with her husband from the Damascene community. Simḥah suggests in his letter that if the evidence of the Rabbanites about the apostate from Istanbul were to be accepted, then this woman could possibly be an appropriate match for Abraham Halevi.

Simḥah Kusdini never returned to the Crimea; he died in Istanbul in the autumn of 1811. The vicissitudes of his life, his contacts with a wide range of people—with Karaites from all the major communities and with Rabbanites, Christians, and Muslims—and his activity on behalf of his community all shed light on his epoch and reflect the everyday life of Karaite communities and the doings of their leadership in times of crisis.
{{h2:2.5 Isaac ben Solomon of Chufut-Kale: His Legal Decisions and Calendrical Feuds}}

Isaac ben Solomon was born in Chufut-Kale in 1755 to a merchant family. He became one of the leaders of this community and the greatest legal decisor of his time, leaving his mark on several areas of Karaite {{em:halakhah}}.{{fn:152}} He studied the Torah under the local {{em:ḥazzan}}, Isaac Kalfa, author of the book {{em:Ṣiṣ Nezer ha-Koddesh}}, a work on {{em:sheḥitah}} and on the ten principles of Karaite faith. At age seventeen, Isaac was a secretary to Benjamin Aga, and in 1795, he became part of the delegation to Saint Petersburg headed by Benjamin. Following the completion of the delegation’s task in the capital, Isaac stayed behind for six months to study astronomy with Russian scholars. Unfortunately, we have no details about these studies, but we can assume that he knew Russian. Isaac ben Solomon wrote an account of their mission, which was engraved on a marble tablet erected in the courtyard of the Evpatoria synagogue, where it can still be seen.
content.comments: [152] About him, see Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 468–474, 528–529.

content.english: When Isaac returned to Chufut-Kale, he began to engage in commerce; after some time, he lost his money. Benjamin Aga appointed him as teacher of a Karaite school in Chufut-Kale, and he also became a {{em:ḥazzan}} of the community. Isaac was married to Beim, the daughter of Benjamin’s brother, Jacob Aga. The couple had three sons and seven daughters; during their lives, they lost one son and three daughters.

In 1804, along with Benjamin Aga, Isaac ben Solomon took part in reestablishing the printing press of Chufut-Kale, and he was its first editor. According to Samuel Poznanski,{{fn:153}} Isaac was also a physician who provided services free of charge to poor people, regardless of their religious affiliation. In addition, he represented his community before the Russian authorities.
content.comments: [153] Poznanski. “Isaac ben Solomon.” {{em:Encyclopedia of Bnei Mikraʾ}}.

content.english: Isaac is the author of several works. {{em:Pinnat Yiqrat}}{{fn:154}} (Precious Cornerstone) is a treatise on the ten principles of faith, wherein he explains these principles by means of questions and answers; the book also contains a translation of these principles into Tatar. He prepared tables—{{em:Moladot le-34 Shanim mi-Shenat 5567 ʿad Shnat}} {{em:5600}} (New Moons for the Years 1806–1840)—relevant to the Karaite communities of Jerusalem, Damascus, Cairo, Istanbul, Lithuania, and Galicia. In addition, he left a commentary on the {{em:Song of Songs}}, which exists only in manuscript.
content.comments: [154] Isaac ben Solomon. {{em:Sefer Pinnat Yiqrat}} [Precious Cornerstone]. Gözleve, 1834.

content.english: Isaac was a legal decisor, and some of his decisions were designed to mitigate the halakhic practice. For instance, he permitted marriage during the Ten Days of Repentance and sought to facilitate the process of obtaining a {{em:get}} (writ of divorce). Other decisions, however, were stricter than the existing halakhic practice and aroused strong opposition among some community leaders. For instance, Isaac claimed that gold and silver vessels could be ritually purified only by being carried through fire, he classified pottery plates as impure, and he stipulated that meat salted in a basin was impure because of the possibility of rats. He ruled the same about wine in barrels, and prohibited the carrying of objects in the public domain on Shabbat.{{fn:155}}
content.comments: [155] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 528–529.

content.english: His most far-reaching enactments were in the calendrical laws, which he introduced before the community sages in 1779–1780 and set forth in his preeminent work {{em:ʾOr ha-Levanah}} (Moonlight), written in 1799.{{fn:156}} These laws amounted to a reform of the calendrical system. Isaac was the first Crimean scholar to formulate a uniform system for calculating the timing of new months, an effort intended to put an end to the ongoing debate on this subject. He writes:
content.comments: [156] Isaac ben Solomon. ʾO{{em:r ha-Levanah}} [Moonlight]. Zhitomir, 1872 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Truly, in former days that passed before us, every one of the communities of the Karaites was in great confusion, and in every month that was in doubt they would split into two camps, so much so that in a single city, half would sanctify [a festival] and half would desecrate [it], and each deride the other, so much so that a father would sanctify Sunday and a son Monday. And thus we became an object of scorn and derision for all the nations and the families of the lands, who would mock us and say that they lack clear knowledge of their law and their religion.{{fn:157}}

Isaac proposed a system different from that proposed by Elijah Bashyachi, which he saw as insufficiently precise. Isaac’s system was based on a mathematical calculation that determined the earliest possible appearance of the new moon (nine hours and forty-two minutes after the {{em:molad}}) in the case where there were no clouds in the sky.{{fn:158}} He saw his system, expounded in his book {{em:ʾOr ha-Levanah}}, as marking a new period in the history of the Crimean (and possibly all) Karaites. However, the calendrical debates to which he sought to put an end did not cease but instead turned into fierce feuds that lasted about twenty years, and the central figure in these controversies was the {{em:ḥazzan}} of the Evpatoria community, R. Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan (see Section 2.6), whose criticisms sometimes went beyond learned discussion into personal attacks.
content.comments: [158] Magdi, Shamuel. “The Karaite Calendar: Sanctification of the New Moon by Sighting.” In Meira Polliack (ed.). {{em:Karaite Judaism: A Guide to Its History and Literary Sources}}. Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2003, p. 616.

content.english: Unlike the circle of Benjamin Duvan, Benjamin Aga, joined by Solomon Babovich and his son Simḥah, strongly supported the calendrical system of Isaac ben Solomon. After Duvan’s death in 1816 or 1817, new leaders of the Evpatoria community adopted R. Isaac’s method. Isaac’s approach ultimately achieved victory with the declaration in 1872 by the chief {{em:ḥakham}} of the Crimea, Naḥamu ben Solomon Babovich, that Isaac’s book {{em:ʾOr ha-Levanah}} was the authoritative source for calendrical calculations.{{fn:159}}
content.comments: [159] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 478.

content.english: Isaac corresponded with Simḥah Kusdini in Istanbul and with Karaite scholars from Lithuanian and other communities. He also had extensive connections in non-Jewish society. In his reply to the scathing criticism of Benjamin Duvan, Isaac mentions that Ishmaelites (Tatars), too, learned from him (he does not explain what they learned, but he apparently means astronomy). Isaac adds in his letter that the Russian “director of the House of Wisdom” turned to him for consultation, and “I wrote him [about] studies in the Russian language, and I wrote in Russian characters.”{{fn:160}} This remark is surprising. Isaac may be speaking of a Russian statesman, Count Nikolay Novosiltzev (1761–1838), who, among his numerous positions and titles, was president of the Academy of Sciences and curator of the Education Department of the Saint Petersburg district. Possibly, Isaac had met him during his visit to the capital with the aforementioned delegation, and they may have stayed in contact through correspondence. In addition, Isaac’s command of Russian, especially his ability to write texts in the language, was quite unusual for Karaites during this period. Most of his contemporaries, including the learned class of Karaite communities, still could not speak Russian fluently. Isaac was apparently an exception to the rule, and his studies of astronomy in Saint Petersburg may have afforded him this special ability. R. Isaac ben Solomon died in Chufut-Kale in 1826 and, like many other community leaders, was buried in its cemetery.{{fn:161}}
content.comments: [160] Ibid., p. 495. | [161] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 556, p. 192.

content.english: {{h2:2.6 Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan and His Pilgrimage to the Land of Israel}}

Following the Russian annexation of the Crimea, Evpatoria, located on the western coast of the peninsula, began to develop rapidly. In the early nineteenth century, a large port was constructed, and the city’s coastal strip began to develop. The name of this town was officially changed from the Turkish name, Gözleve, to the Greek one, Evpatoria. The Karaite community of Evpatoria grew in size and importance, and Evpatoria became the most important Karaite center in the Crimea.

Born in Evpatoria in 1747, Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan was one of Isaac ben Solomon’s fiercest opponents and eventually became the leader of the community.{{fn:162}} He was one of the major halakhic authorities and a {{em:dayan}} (judge) of the Karaite {{em:bet din}} (court) in this city; we find his name on a number of decisions of this {{em:bet din}}. From 1782–1783, Duvan{{fn:163}} spent time in Istanbul, where he studied astronomy and became acquainted with some astronomical instruments. Duvan also took an interest in Kabbalah and copied several Kabbalistic treatises, apparently for his own use. We know this only from his colophons, in which he writes his name and mentions that he had copied these books on Kabbalah.{{fn:164}} According to the testimony of Abraham Firkovich,{{fn:165}} during his visit to Chufut-Kale in 1838, he bought manuscripts that had belonged to the late Benjamin Duvan. In addition to books on philosophy and Kabbalah, Duvan’s library contained books on astronomy, such as the astronomical tables of Abraham Zacuto (1452–1515) and the book {{em:Ṣurat ha-ʾAreṣ}} on astronomy and geometry by Abraham ben Ḥiyya from twelfth-century Spain.
content.comments: [162] Benjamin wrote the date of his birth at the end of his copy of the book ʾ{{em:Emunah ʾOmen}} by Abraham ben Yoshiyahu. He also mentioned the dates of birth of his son and daughter: Ezra (1784) and Aqbike (1788). See Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan. {{em:Family Records.}} Hebrew Union College Library Cincinnati, OH USA Ms. 840, 127v. | [163] For more about Duvan, see Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 323, 327, 342, 472–474. Concerning his 1785–1786 journey to the Land of Israel, see Yaari. {{em:Masa}}ʿ{{em:ot}}, pp. 459–478. | [164] Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan. {{em:Liqqutim}}, Adler JTS, no. 166. The manuscripts include a transcription by Duvan of {{em:Shefaʿ Tal}}, a Kabbalistic tract by Shabbetai Horwitz, {{em:Novelot Ḥokhma}} and {{em:Miṣraf la-Ḥokhma}} by Joseph Delmedigo, {{em:Sefer Yeṣirah}} with the commentary of Ibn Daʾud, and a list of the books of Kabbalah. | [165] Firkovich. ʾ{{em:Avnei Zikkaron}}, p. 5.

content.english: In 1785, Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan, with a group of pilgrims—four men and one woman from Gözleve and Chufut-Kale and one man from Troki in Lithuania—sailed to the Land of Israel. The Lithuanian Karaite was so poor that he had no money for food, so Benjamin assumed all of the man’s travel expenses, including meals. He saw special importance in the man’s pilgrimage because he aimed to restore connections between the Lithuanian and Jerusa- lem communities, which had eroded about forty years earlier. Benjamin wrote a detailed account of this trip, and his diary is an important source of information on eighteenth-century Karaite life.{{fn:166}}
content.comments: [166] Most Karaite travel diaries have been published; see also Yonah Gurland. {{em:Ginzei Yisrael be-Saint Peterburg}}. Saint Petersburg, part 1, 1865–66, pp. 1–45 (in Hebrew); Yaari. {{em:Masa}}ʿ{{em:ot}}, pp. 221–267, 305–323, 459–478; Karp. “Sefer ‘Derekh ha-Qoddesh.’”

content.english: After asking forgiveness from everyone in their two communities (as was the traditional practice before leaving for the Land of Israel, echoing the well-known custom that takes place on the eve of the Day of Atonement), the pilgrims boarded the ship to Istanbul, where they were welcomed very warmly by the local Karaite community, whose leaders even drew out the Torah scroll from the ark in honor of their guests’ upcoming pilgrimage to Jerusalem. In the capital, they were forced to stay for more than three months due to rumors about the presence of a large pirate ship preying on ships departing from Istanbul and killing their passengers. The last case that Benjamin mentions was an attack on a ship carrying Ishmaelites and Jews. He says that the pirates killed all the Ishmaelites, who had put up armed resistance, and left the Jews alive while seizing all their possessions. It should be noted that in both Muslim and Christian countries, Jews could not engage in armed resistance or protect themselves because they were forbidden from bearing arms by either the Laws of Omar or the decrees of the church councils.

When rumors about the detention of a pirate ship by the sultan’s army reached the capital, the pilgrims set off to Jaffa. Benjamin writes that the ship held only Karaites and Rabbanites—a total of about ninety men and women. (Christian pilgrims also set forth on a trip to the Holy Land at the same time, albeit on a different ship.) Their journey from Istanbul to Jaffa took fifteen days, with the ship stopping at numerous Greek islands along the way. From Jaffa, they went to Jerusalem via Ramle. They rode on mules, paying the Muslims for them, along with {{em:kafar}}, the tax levied for security on the roads. Benjamin depicts the encounters with people, the holy places, and the interesting attractions of Jerusalem, where they strolled around accompanied by Joseph ha-Nasi and his son from the Damascus Karaite community, who arrived to meet them. They also visited Hebron, where they were accommodated by the Rabbanite community in a house previously belonging to the Karaites, who had been forced to sell it to the Rabbanites because of their community’s debts. They also visited the Karaite cemetery in Hebron, which still exists today.

In Jerusalem, the pilgrims spent time with Mordecai ben Samuel Halevi, who then led the small Karaite community in the city. They brought money collected from different communities to pay off their debts. However, the amount was insufficient to cover the debts of all the creditors, and Benjamin requested an additional sum of 900 {{em:gurush}} from the local Greek Patriarchate in Jerusalem, having provided a receipt and promised that the Karaites of Istanbul would return the sum to the Patriarchate in the capital.

Mordecai ben Samuel requested from Benjamin and other members of his group a letter of recommendation for the Karaite community of Cairo, which he planned to visit to find a bride for himself. Benjamin testifies that he heard there had been about 150 Karaite families in Cairo (with possibly about 750 community members), but the previous year, they had suffered an epidemic, and less than half the community had survived.

Benjamin and his friends considered remaining in Jerusalem for an additional month for Passover; however, several factors led them to leave the city. Their prolonged presence in Jerusalem may have provided a pretext for the local administration, who (according to Benjamin’s diary) were “devising plots out of malice” to extort money from the local Karaite community. The local administration was falsely accusing the Karaite community of engaging in illegal construction within the synagogue. Later, the authorities stated that if “guest Jews” gave the community gifts, that would be welcome; otherwise, the authorities might consider harming the community.

In addition to extortion by the Ottoman administration, which was an everyday practice in Jerusalem, Benjamin remarks that there was a famine in the city and that they could not eat meat there. Benjamin makes a statement whose meaning is not quite clear: “We are not permitted to eat sheep and cattle meat, in accordance with the ordinances of our fathers.”{{fn:167}} Supposedly, the Crimean Karaites practiced a custom common among medieval Karaites in Jerusalem known as the Mourners of Zion—refraining from eating meat in Jerusa­lem. Another possible explanation is that this custom was still common among the existing Jerusalem community, although the previous head of the community—Mordecai’s father, Samuel ben Abra­ham Halevi—had permitted the consumption of meat. However, we have no evidence as to whether his decision was supported by the majority, either in Jerusalem or in other communities. Eventually, because of the hostile atmosphere, which was intensified by the local Ottoman administration in Jerusalem, the pilgrims decided to return to Jaffa and, from there, to Istanbul, where they stayed for three months before arriving in Evpatoria in Nissan before Passover.
content.comments: [167] Yaari. {{em:Masa}}ʿ{{em:ot}}, p. 478.

content.english: In addition to Benjamin’s travel account, most details about his activities and views are drawn from his calendrical polemics with R. Isaac ben Solomon. During the controversy between the two leaders, which lasted about twenty years, they exchanged letters with questions, answers, and mutual accusations. In these correspondences, Benjamin accuses Isaac of arbitrary innovations, of ignorance of astronomy, of disrespect for the sages’ opinions, and of rejecting the principles of Karaite faith. Benjamin claims that no one needs Isaac’s astronomical tables and that all existing Karaite communities should reject them, and he levels many other charges of a purely personal nature. Benjamin Duvan had a circle of supporters in Evpatoria, including Eastern European notables; in addition, Simḥah Kusdini of Istanbul sometimes expressed opinions, mostly critical, about Isaac’s system, although in a more restrained manner.

These calendrical feuds took place in person as well. In 1811, a group of dignitaries from Evpatoria, headed by Benjamin Duvan, arrived in Chufut-Kale to contest Isaac’s calendrical system. However, this dispute, as might have been expected, did not result in reconciliation between the two sides. Benjamin insisted that the first day of the month of Tishrei must come one day later than Isaac maintained. As a result, Benjamin and his supporters observed Yom Kippur on Sunday, whereas Isaac and most of the Crimean Karaites did so a day earlier.

At face value, these controversies were about the methods of calculating and defining {{em:moladot}}, but they were even more so a struggle over authority. Despite the harshness and personal nature of these calendrical feuds, the feuds had the positive effect of kindling Karaite interest in astronomy, and they spurred learned Karaites to pursue scientific knowledge of astronomy from all possible sources, be they Karaite, Rabbanite, Christian, or Muslim.

Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan was last mentioned in the year 1816, and he apparently died in that year or the next. Unfortunately, most of the tomb inscriptions in the Karaite cemetery of Evpatoria were not preserved, and we cannot find his epitaph.
{{h2:2.7 The Babovich Family and Russian Policy toward the Karaite Community}}

The first half of the nineteenth century is associated with a great deal of activity by the Chabak-Babovich family, whose leaders were in close contact with the Russian authorities and were able to significantly improve the legal status of the Karaite community. The first of them was Solomon Yerushalmi Babovich (in some documents, another surname, Chabak, appears),{{fn:168}} the son of Naḥamu and Totash, known as “the great minister of Israel.” Solomon Babovich was a wealthy merchant who became one of the community leaders in Evpatoria. In 1795, together with Benjamin Aga and Isaac ben Solomon, he visited Saint Petersburg to improve the legal status of the Karaites, and he wrote an account of their mission.
content.comments: [168] Possibly after the Crimean village Chabak, where a small Karaite community existed.

content.english: After the Russian invasion of the Crimea, Evpatoria, along with other cities in coastal Crimea and New Russia, such as Kherson, Sevastopol, and the newly built Odessa and Nikolaev, became business centers where wealthy Karaites, including the Babovich family, opened their commercial houses.{{fn:169}} In addition, many bought land from the Tatars, who were unwilling to remain under the new power and emigrated en masse to Turkey. The Karaites ceased to be {{em:dhimmi}}, as they had been under Muslim rule, and new economic opportunities opened for them. However, in the first decades after the Russian annexation, they did not know what the future held because the Russian authorities had yet to define their policy toward the Karaite minority.
content.comments: [169] Miller. {{em:Karaite Separatism}}, p. 16.

content.english: Solomon ben Naḥamu died in 1817 on the eve of this dramatic transition in his community and was buried in Evpatoria.{{fn:170}} His son Simḥah, who replaced him in most spheres of activity, was one of the most powerful and admired leaders of the Crimean Karaites of the new era.
content.comments: [170] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 51, p. 250.

content.english: Simḥah ben Solomon Babovich was born in Evpatoria in 1790, seven years after the Russian annexation. Like his father, he was a wealthy merchant in Evpatoria. He was fluent in Russian and was involved in the Black Sea trade both in his native city, where he had two commercial houses, and in Feodosia and Odessa during the first decades of the nineteenth century. His deals did not always go well, but he managed to remain one of the richest Karaites in the Crimea. In the 1820s, he was appointed head of the community of Evpatoria, which became the major center of the Crimean Karaites. Later, Babovich was officially recognized by the Russian authorities as the leader of all the Crimean Karaite communities.

Under the rule of the Tatar khans, the Karaites did not serve in the military because of the ban on non-Muslims bearing arms, according to Islamic law. In the first decades after the Russian annexation, the Jews of the Russian Empire, including the Karaites, paid a special poll tax that exempted them from military service. However, the new czar, Nicholas I, whose reign (1825–1855) was historically the most difficult for Jews because of its numerous discriminatory initiatives, introduced a new military law, the so-called “Statute on Conscription Duty” (1827), which obliged the Jewish population to supply soldiers to the Russian army. According to this new decree, Jewish boys were drafted into military service at the age of twelve. They were enrolled for their six-year military education in special “cantonist” schools. Like all other soldiers, they were required to serve in the Imperial Russian Army for twenty-five years after graduating from these schools. In reality, Jewish boys above the age of six were often considered “suitable to be drafted.” Those who did not die from the severe treatment and harsh living conditions were usually forced to convert to Christianity; their names were changed to Christian ones, and they were completely separated from their families and communities. This law, known as the “cantonist law,” had the purpose of assimilating the Jewish population. Although it was abolished after Nicholas’s death, it had dramatic consequences for Jewish communities.{{fn:171}}
content.comments: [171] For further details about Jewish military service in the Russian Empire, see, for example, Adina Ofek, “Cantonists: Jewish Children as Soldiers in Tsar Nicholas’s Army.” {{em:Modern Judaism}} 13:3 (1993): 277–308; Yohanan Petrovsky-Shtern. {{em:Jews in the Russian Army, 1827–1917: Drafted into Modernity}}. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008.

content.english: Under the cantonist law, the Karaites, like other Jews, were immediately required by the local authorities of the Russian Empire to provide lists of potential soldiers. Although Simḥah Babovich and other leaders of the Crimean Karaite communities tried to resolve this problem with the local administration, they could not stop the process. The administration, now located in the new Crimean capital of Simferopol (which had replaced Bakhchesaray), refused to delay the implementation of the decree. After the leaders of three Crimean communities—Chufut-Kale, Evpatoria, and Feodosia— discussed the issue, they decided to draft a petition to the Russian government in Saint Petersburg and to send a delegation to the imperial capital.{{fn:172}}
content.comments: [172] Maxim Gammal. “Karaimy i imperiya: ocvobozhdenie Karaimov ot rekrutskoi povinnosti, 1827” [Karaites and the Empire: The Exemptions of Karaites from Conscription, 1827]. In Arkadii Kovelʹman (ed.). {{em:Izrailʹ drevii i novyi}}, vyp. 1. Moscow: Indrik, 2015, pp. 143–166 (in Russian).

content.english: The Karaites of Volhynia and Lithuania found themselves in the same position as their Crimean coreligionists. The Crimeans tried to coordinate their activities and decisions with the community of Lutsk, where Abraham Firkovich was an active figure. One of the questions discussed in the correspondence between these communities was what they might do in the event that their delegation failed to obtain an exemption from military service. Because the responsibility for recruiting new soldiers from each community lay with its leaders, they discussed the possibility of sending to the Russian army youngsters with a criminal background or boys from poor families who could not pay taxes{{fn:173}}—a practice that emerged in the Rabbanite communities in the face of this decree. Along with this practice, numerous attempts were made to conceal from the authorities the real number of community members and register some young boys from families with several sons as the single sons of couples who were childless because single sons were not subject to conscription.

Simḥah Babovich was chosen as the head of the delegation that departed for Saint Petersburg in 1827 to obtain the exemption from military service for Karaites. The delegation’s other members were Solomon Michri{{fn:174}} and Joseph Solomon (Yashar) Lutski, {{em:ḥazzan}} and spiritual leader of Evpatoria, who subsequently describes in detail their journey and mission in his {{em:Epistle of Israel’s Deliverance}} ({{em:ʾIggeret Teshuʿat Yisraʾel}}).{{fn:175}} This mission completely changed the status of the Karaite minority in the Russian Empire.
content.comments: [174] This common surname among the Crimean Karaites testifies to the Egyptian roots of some community members. | [175] See its original Hebrew version, the translation by Abraham Firkovich, and the English translation in Miller. {{em:Karaite Separatism}}, pp. 70–244.

content.english: According to Joseph Solomon Lutski’s account, Babovich met the president of the Council of State—Count Victor Pavlovich Kochubei, one of the most influential figures in the Russian govern- ment—who explained to him how and to whom to submit a petition and other letters. During this process, Babovich visited numerous government offices, and he managed to befriend a number of high-ranking officials, including Kochubei himself. The mission of the Karaite delegation was a success, and they were even invited to Kochubei’s home, where a banquet was held with the participation of Czar Nicolas I. Babovich appears as the main hero in this account, and all the developments are presented as a miraculous deliverance of the Karaites from disaster, reminiscent of the deliverance in the book of Esther.

90Although the ultimate law exempting Karaites from military service had not yet been issued, an exemption in this specific case be- an important precedent in distinguishing the status of Karaites from that of all the other Jewish communities. There were additional factors that influenced the distinctive policy toward Karaites in subsequent years. Among them was the Karaites’ rejection of the Talmud, which the rulers, following the common Christian theological view, tended to see as a source of moral corruption for the Jews and the root of the Jews’ rejection of the “Christian truth.” There were also several social and cultural factors at play. For instance, in educated Russian society, the Karaites were viewed as an exotic Oriental people. The Russian annexation of the Crimea and the Caucasus during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries aroused an interest in the peoples of these regions and a romanticization of the mountain dwellers who populated them. These romanticized views and ten- dencies, reflected in contemporary Russian art and literature, generated a certain sympathy for the Karaites. The Russian authorities and intelligentsia found the Karaites to be different from the numerous Ashkenazi Jews who resided in the territory of newly annexed Poland, viewing the Karaites more like the Crimean Tatars in their attire, language, and some of their customs. It should be noted that Tatars were also exempted from military service by the Russian authorities (two of their representatives joined the Karaite delegation from the Crimea and went with them to Saint Petersburg).

In addition, members of the Karaite minority, especially in the Crimea, tended to be wealthy, which encouraged officialdom to see them as a group useful to the state. The ties between wealthy leaders of the Karaite community and local government officials, and, in some cases, courtiers and ministers, played an important role in advancing the goals set by Karaite leaders. These ties had already begun to form during the early period of the Russian annexation of the Crimea.

The modest size of the Karaite population relative to the Rabbanite population of the empire was also a significant factor in their success in improving their status. According to official data, there were 2,400 Karaites in the Crimea following the Russian conquest. According to the imperial census of 1897, the Karaite population of the empire had grown to 12,894, of whom 1,166 resided in the Crimea and the remainder in the western governorates and various other cities of the empire.{{fn:176}} By contrast, the Rabbanite population, mostly Ashkenazi, numbered 5,215,805 (about fifty percent of all the Jews in the world){{fn:177}} in the same year.
content.comments: [176] Veniamin Sinani. “K statistike karaimov.” {{em:KZh}} 1 (1911): 30 (in Russian). | [177] {{em:Bulletin of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics}}. Washington: U.S. Government Printing Office, 1907, vol. XV, p. 488.

content.english: In 1830, Babovich visited the Land of Israel, accompanied by Abraham Firkovich, who was then his personal secretary. A group of Crimean Karaites joined them, accompanied by some community members in Istanbul, from where they sailed to Jaffa. During the pilgrimage, some people died of an epidemic. Epidemics were frequent in nineteenth-century Jerusalem due to poor sanitary conditions and water shortages. However, Babovich and Firkovich returned to Evpatoria in good health.

During the 1830s, Babovich continued contacts and negotiations with the authorities to further improve the legal status of the Karaites. During this period, the governor-general of the Crimea and Novorossia, Count Michael Vorontsov, involved him in the ceremonial receptions of Russian royal persons with their families and of high-ranking officials who visited the Crimea. After its annexation, the Crimea became a major attraction due to its beautiful landscapes and historical sites, as well as the attempt to integrate it into the Russian Empire. The czars came to survey Bakhchesaray, the former capital of the Tatar Khanate, and sometimes visited Chufut-Kale, which, in their eyes, was a tourist attraction and home to an exotic Oriental people. Babovich and other Karaite leaders assigned great importance to such official visits, taking an active part in the preparations for the receptions for the czars. Such receptions for distinguished guests offered an important channel for establishing special relations between the community and high-ranking Russian officials. Before the expected visit of Czar Nicholas I and his retinue to Bakhchesaray, Governor Mikhail Vorontsov decided to restore the old, previously splendid khan’s palace to honor these distinguished guests, sending Babovich to Istanbul to purchase horses and other suitable goods from the Ottoman sultan’s court.{{fn:178}}
content.comments: [178] Miller. {{em:Karaite Separatism}}, p. 43.

content.english: The year 1837 marked a turning point for the Karaites in the Russian Empire. The Russian authorities established the Karaite Spiritual Consistory—the high council of the Karaites.{{fn:179}} Two years later, Babovich was appointed as its head and dubbed “{{em:Ḥakham}} of the Crimea and Odessa.” This position was more political and public than spiritual. Of his two main assistants, one was a {{em:ḥazzan}}, a learned scholar and expert in Karaite law who was responsible for religious life and Torah studies, and the other was a {{em:shamash}}, responsible for maintaining the synagogue and other communal institutions, which became the property of the Spiritual Consistory. This institution, including the salaries of its employees, was funded by the Russian government.

Although the Karaite communities welcomed this change, this reorganization of Karaite spiritual life was intended to make the consistory an instrument of full control of all the ethnic and religious minorities in the empire, including their integration and further assimilation. The leaders of these minorities, whose power was gradually restricted to the religious sphere of life, were expected to serve as a channel for applying governmental policy in their communities. Such a practice was first implemented in France in 1806, when Napoleon established the Jewish Consistoire. In Russia, this measure was applied to the Karaites, accompanied by a gradual extension of their rights. In the short term, the status of Karaites improved greatly; however, these changes ultimately played a role in their assimilation. The authorities were unable to achieve similar results with the large Rabbanite communities in the Russian Empire, whose legal status did not significantly change, despite numerous laws and modernization projects.{{fn:180}}
content.comments: [180] One such project was the establishment of rabbinical schools in Vilna and Zhitomir in 1847, the aim of which was to prepare a new generation of modern teachers and rabbis; however, these institutions were not favorably viewed by the Jewish population because of their assimilationist tendencies and low level of traditional education.

content.english: In 1843, Simḥah Babovich received the status of honorary citizen, which, until that time, was not granted to Jews. It entailed certain privileges, usually pertaining to the upper class. They were exempt from corporal punishment and military service, were allowed to have suburban backyards, gardens, river and ocean vessels, and factories, and could pass this status on to their children.

More than once, Babovich is unfairly described in various testimonies, including scholarly writings, as illiterate and ignorant. Ephraim Deinard even claims that Babovich could not sign his name. Poznanski, in his {{em:Encyclopedia of Bnei Mikraʾ}}, expresses a similar view. However, according to the existing manuscripts, there is no basis for such a claim. The manuscripts reveal that Babovich had his own library and bought books for himself. For instance, we find a list, written by him, of Karaite and Rabbanite books: “This is the list of books which I, Simḥah the son of my father and teacher, honorable Solomon, master and learned person… bought from the loyal minister, and the sage of Torah… the son of honorable Samuel… in 1817…”{{fn:181}} This impressive list of books features treatises on Karaite law, anti-Christian and anti-Rabbanite polemics, exegeses, philosophical works by Aristotle with commentaries by Ibn Rushd, and others.
content.comments: [181] Simḥah Babovich. {{em:A List of Books}}. Oxford: Bodl. MS Opp. Add. Qu. 121, 1r.

content.english: Of similar interest is Babovich’s correspondence with the German Jewish scholar Isaac Markus (Mordecai) Jost.{{fn:182}} This correspondence also demonstrates his intellectual and educational level, showing his acquaintance with modern Jewish literature. Jost, who is considered one of the founding fathers of Jewish history as a discipline, wanted to know more about Karaism and Karaite literature. In one of his letters, he also expresses a desire for closer ties with the Karaites: “Why must we forever fight? Are we not brothers, sons of a single father?” In response to Jost’s request for a list of the books in the Karaite community’s possession, Simḥah Babovich sent a letter to Jost from Evpatoria in 1829 in which Babovich notes the importance of the books of “our master Moses of Dessau{{fn:183}}… for the man Moses is very great… and contributed precious works to every discipline and science, whether in the curriculum and education of the youth of the Children of Israel or in ethics and proper conduct.” To this, Babovich adds that the Karaites were in possession of certain works by Moses Mendelssohn. This passage testifies that in addition to traditional knowledge, Babovich was acquainted with contemporary intellectual trends. Although he apparently did not see himself as a successor to Mendelssohn, he belonged to a traditional society with a burgeoning interest in general knowledge and in Mendelssohn’s writings.{{fn:184}}
content.comments: [182] Jost’s letters to the Karaites Simḥah Babovich and Joseph Solomon ben Moses appear at the end of Isaac ben Solomon’s {{em:Pinnat Yiqrat}}. | [183] Moses Mendelssohn (1729–1786), who was born in Dessau, Germany, is considered the founding father of the Jewish Enlightenment movement ({{em:Haskalah}}) in Europe. | [184] Simḥah Babovich. Letter to Jost. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 1026.

content.english: Babovich was married to Biche Yerushalmit, and they had three sons—Netanel, Immanuel, and Shalom—as well as daughters. Babovich had a house in Evpatoria and one in Karasubazar, which was called Gan Yaffe, where he spent his last days. An archival document that recounts his death also reveals interesting details about Babovich’s financial management aimed at supporting the Karaite communities. This document is a letter{{fn:185}} sent by the {{em:ḥazzan}} of Chufut-Kale, Solomon Beim, following Babovich’s death. According to Beim, Babovich died unexpectedly at the age of sixty-seven on the tenth of Tammuz, 5615 (1855), from a contagious disease, possibly cholera.
content.comments: [185] See Oleg Bely. “New Materials for the Biography of Solomon Beim.” {{em:Materials in the Archaeology, History and Ethnography of Tauria}} 10 (2003): 664–666 (in Russian).

content.english: Beim presents a detailed list of Babovich’s expenditures for the communities when he was still alive and describes how he willed his money for the time after his death. Along with his brother, Babakai Babovich, he donated the income from their mill to the Crimean communities. He left a village granted to him by the authorities, as well as his house with a plot of land numbering 500 {{em:dessiatin}} s,{{fn:186}} in the possession of the Evpatoria synagogue. In addition, he deposited in his son Shalom’s possession one thousand rubles, from which Shalom was to pay the community sixty rubles each year—half for the needs of poor people and half for the community’s cash box. He divided another thousand rubles between the Karaite communities of the Crimea, Novorossia, Lutsk, Istanbul, and Jerusalem, and even the Rabbanite community of Karasubazar.
content.comments: [186] 546 hectares (1,350 acres).

content.english: {{h2:2.8 Eastern European Karaites in the Crimea: A New Leadership}}

As previously mentioned, during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, a considerable number of Eastern European Karaites migrated from Poland–Lithuania to the Crimea, where their coreligionists enjoyed greater prosperity. Some of these immigrants came from the learned class, and many were descendants of great scholars who were also well known in the Crimea. After their relocation, some rose to become leaders of Crimean Karaite communities. Connections between Eastern European and Crimean communities tightened; both found themselves within the borders of the same empire, which facilitated their travel and relocation. Many of these immigrants came from Lutsk, among them the aforementioned Simḥah Isaac Lutski. They usually tried to obtain a position in the Crimean communities, such as {{em:melamed}} or {{em:ḥazzan}}, although there were not enough community positions because the local Karaites also competed for these roles. These newcomers were completely dependent on the support of local community leaders. At the same time, the Crimea opened new economic possibilities for these Karaite immigrants from Poland–Lithuania. Unlike their experiences in Eastern Europe, these Karaites did not have intense business competition from Rabbanites or other ethnic groups. In addition, they were able to purchase land because many places had been abandoned or sold for low prices by the Tatars who had fled to Turkey following the Russian annexation.

Notwithstanding these advantages, the Polish Karaite immi- grants did not integrate well into the local economic system, possibly because they lacked knowledge of the Tatar language and the local cultural codes. However, despite all the difficulties of integration, Eastern European Karaite scholars influenced the Crimean communities by bringing new knowledge, modifying the prevalent educational system, and developing large-scale book printing.
{{h3:2.8.1 {{em:Joseph Solomon (Yashar) Lutski}}}}

Joseph Solomon ben Moses Lutski, also known as Yashar Lutski, was born in 1770 in the Galician town of Kukizów, where he resided in a small Karaite community. This community had resettled from Troki in 1688, as decreed by the Polish king Jan III Sobieski. Upon the decline of this community, Yashar relocated to Lutsk, where he became {{em:ḥazzan}} and {{em:melamed}}. He had command of Polish and Russian and became a member of the local city council. His opinion on halakhic issues was much esteemed and taken into consideration by the Crimean sages, who consulted with him by correspondence about difficult cases. Yashar became one of the central figures of spiritual life in Evpatoria. He was one of the Polish Karaite immigrants who had a great impact on the Crimean communities during the first half of the nineteenth century.

In 1804, Yashar Lutski decided to relocate with his family to Ev-patoria, perhaps with the consent of Solomon ben Naḥamu Babovich. As we learn from Yashar’s correspondence with Firkovich, Yashar’s first years in the Crimea were not easy because he lacked a permanent income, earning money by copying books when he was able. After several years, Solomon Babovich invited Yashar to be a private tutor for his children, and his financial situation improved significantly. Later, Yashar was offered a position as local {{em:ḥazzan}}, and also served as {{em:dayan}} (judge) in the Karaite {{em:bet din}} of Evpatoria.{{fn:187}} His former disciple, Simḥah Babovich, supported him financially. As mentioned earlier, in 1827, when the delegation from the Crimea went to Saint Petersburg to obtain an exemption from military service for Karaites, Simḥah Babovich took Yashar along as one of its members. Yashar describes their journey in detail in his {{em:Epistle of Israel’s Deliverance}} ({{em:ʾIggeret Teshuʿat Yisraʾel}}). Written in very rich and beautiful Hebrew, the book credits Babovich as primarily responsible for the success of their mission.
content.comments: [187] Poznanski. “Lutski, Joseph Solomon (Yashar).” {{em:Encyclopedia of Bnei Mikraʾ}}.

content.english: Despite his stable position in the Evpatoria community, Yashar Lutski decided to relocate to the Land of Israel. In 1831, he departed for Jerusalem with his wife. Sources provide neither an explanation for this unexpected decision nor the exact date of his departure. The only hint is offered by Firkovich, who attests to a scandal in the community related to Yashar’s publication of the book {{em:Zekher Rav}}. This was a grammatical treatise by Benjamin Musafiya, a Sephardic Jew of the seventeenth century. Yashar translated the book into Tatar for Crimean students and had it printed in Istanbul. According to Firkovich, “my teacher and author, the honorable Yashar Yeru[shalmi] … relocated from Gözleve to the Land of Israel to fulfill an oath, which he swore—to die and to be buried in the Holy Land, and after the bitter complaints of many people about his trans- lation of {{em:Zekher Rav}}, his soul was sick and tired of their evil…”{{fn:188}} The nature of these complaints remains unknown. Firkovich adds that during Yashar’s absence from Evpatoria, the Evpatorian community appointed as {{em:ḥazzan}} another Polish Karaite, David ben Mordecai Kukizów (Mordkovich), who was Yashar’s relative. The community leaders, however, were not satisfied with his activity, and they asked Firkovich to come to Evpatoria and take part in a special meeting on the issue. Firkovich, who was living in Istanbul at that time (1830–1832), made the trip to Evpatoria. He explains, “And when my teacher, Yashar, heard about it, he envied me, and returned to Istanbul [from Jerusalem], and came to Gözleve, since he thought that possibly he would be taken back [by the community].”{{fn:189}} Although this passage does not clarify the reasons for the conflict, we know that competition between Polish immigrants in the Crimea sometimes generated friction regarding community positions.
content.comments: [188] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 4. | [189] Ibid.

content.english: In 1834, several Polish Karaite scholars and Simḥah Babovich established a publishing house in Evpatoria. In addition to classical Karaite books and liturgical texts, each partner who had written a book wanted at least some of their own works to be published. For instance, Yashar had written several treatises on Hebrew grammar, {{em:halakhah}}, and exegesis. He and others involved in the publishing activity regarded Aaron ben Joseph’s {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}} as one of the highest-priority works for printing, and they decided to publish it with a commentary by the prominent Eastern European Karaite scholar Mordecai ben Nisan of Kukizów (d. 1709), which was titled {{em:Maʾamar Mordecai}}. However, instead of the initial decision to publish {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}} with {{em:Maʾamar Mordecai}}, Yashar decided to replace the latter with his own book of commentaries on {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}, which was titled {{em:Tirat ha-Kesef}} (The Silver Palace). The abovementioned David Kukizów, who was involved in the publishing process as a proofreader and as one who took part in making decisions, objected to this change. He was unwilling to accept Yashar’s initiative, especially given that David was a great-grandson of Mordecai ben Nisan of Kukizów. Thus, David suggested publishing his own critical commentaries on Yashar’s {{em:Tirat ha-Kesef}}, which he titled {{em:Sukkat David}}, at the end of {{em:Sefer}} {{em:ha-Mivḥar}}. However, Yashar refused and, instead, selected some fragments from David Kukizów’s treatise and published them separately under the title {{em:Shigayon le-David}} (The Whim of David){{fn:190}} with his own responses. David, in futile anger, presented his arguments against Yashar’s views in an unpublished booklet that he called {{em:Shever Yoseph}} (The Failure of Joseph), in reference to Yashar’s given name.{{fn:191}}
content.comments: [190] We find a pun on the word {{em:shigayon}}, which has two meanings: musical instrument and whim. | [191] A pun on the word {{em:shever}}, one of whose meanings is provision. There exist numerous Jewish books with the title {{em:Shever Yoseph}} (such as one by the seventeenth-century Galician Karaite scholar R. Joseph Hamashbir—the Provisor), with the connotation of spiritual food. Other meanings of the word are failure, break, or rift.

content.english: David ben Mordecai Kukizów (originally named Mordkovich) was also among those who influenced the communal and intellectual life of the Crimean Karaites. He was born in Kukizów in 1777 and served as {{em:ḥazzan}} of its community. He moved to Evpatoria in 1822 and was appointed {{em:ḥazzan}} in 1825 and later {{em:shoḥet}} (slaughterer) in Evpatoria by Yashar Lutski. David knew German and Polish, had a rich background in Rabbanite literature, and looked after the community’s interests. Having been appointed a proofreader of Karaite books for the Evpatorian publishing house, he also managed the publishing and printing of works from 1835 to 1845. In 1835, he reprinted {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}} by Elijah Bashyachi, adding to the edition two of his own calendrical treatises, {{em:Yemot ʿOlam}} and {{em:Halikhot ʿOlam}}. He also wrote {{em:Keviʿot Rashei Ḥodashim u-Tekufot ke-Minhag ha-Karaʾim}} and {{em:Maʾamar be-Kiddush ha-Ḥodesh}} (Evpatoria, 1840), which deal with calendation and the calculation of the new moon. In these works, David raises objections to the opinions of some other scholars, specifically rejecting the observation of the moon as inaccurate. His main work, {{em:Ṣemaḥ David}}, was completed in 1848 and published posthumously in Saint Petersburg in 1897. It contains essays on the laws concerning Shabbat, abstinence, a person’s obligations before God, the resurrection of the dead, the determination of the new moon, poems, and elegies, as well as annotations to biblical passages. While still in Kukizów, David was friendly with one of the central figures of the Jewish Enlightenment, Nachman Krochmal.{{fn:192}} In 1854, David left the Crimea because of the Crimean War and moved to the city of Nikolaev, where his sons dwelled. A year later, he died there during a cholera epidemic.
content.comments: [192] Nachman Krochmal, {{em:Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zman}} [Guide for the Perplexed for Our Time]. Berlin, 1923, p. 315 (in Hebrew); Reuven Fahn, {{em:Sefer ha-Qraʾim}} [The Book of Rift]. Lvov, 1929, p. 89 (in Hebrew).

content.english: {{h3:2.8.2 {{em:Eben Yashar}}}}

97The only son of Yashar Lutski was Abraham (b. 1792), also known as Eben Yashar Lutski.{{fn:193}} His father brought him from Lutsk to the Crimea at the age of eleven. When Yashar and others in the delegation headed by Simḥah Babovich secured the Karaites’ exemption from military service in 1827, Eben Yashar composed a poem in honor of Czar Nicholas I, which Karaites sang in their synagogues. Eben Yashar had a good education and became a scholar; however, even though he had suitable qualities, he was not interested in becoming a community leader. He was elected {{em:ḥakham}} of Evpatoria in 1835, but he declined the office, possibly due to his desire for independence. Despite the opportunity to develop his career within his community, Eben Yashar preferred to relocate to Istanbul, where he entered the service of the wealthy Karaite merchant Shabbatai Kviṣo for thirteen years and married his daughter, Esther. In Istanbul, he devoted his free time to studying rabbinic literature, including the Talmud and Mishnah, with Sephardic teachers, and he acquired extensive knowledge of Turkish, Persian, Spanish, Greek, and Italian.
content.comments: [193] Poznanski. “Abraham ben Joseph Solomon (Eben Yashar) Lutski.” {{em:Encyclopedia of Bnei Mikraʾ.}}

content.english: 90Finally, Eben Yashar decided to return to Evpatoria. Although he did not seek a communal office, he did not detach himself from his community. In 1844, at the request of community leaders who were concerned that Eben Yashar was the only great sage in the Crimea and that no one from the young generation could yet replace him, he founded a school in Evpatoria. His school became the most popular educational institution in the Crimea, and he taught there for sixteen years. Some of his students (such as Judah Savuskan, Avraham Yefet, and Elijah Kazaz) became well-known figures of the Crimean Karaite communities. Gifted students from poor families attended this school at the community’s expense. In addition to the classical Karaite books, Eben Yashar taught Hebrew grammar and philosophy.

80Eben Yashar died during a visit to Ekaterinoslav in 1855.
