He left behind a number of works, including {{em:ʾIggeret Zug ve-Nifrad}} (Evpatoria, 1833), a ruling concerning marriage law that mitigates earlier more severe Karaite rulings; {{em:Mishlei Musar}}, a translation of fables into Tatar; and his Tatar translation from Hebrew of Joseph ha-Efrati’s drama {{em:Melukhat Shaul}} (The Reign of Saul). His works in manuscript include {{em:Shoshanim Edut le-Yosef}}, a collection of poems, lamentations, sermons, and obituaries left in the possession of his grandson, Samuel Neeman, in Evpatoria. In addition, he wrote numerous liturgical poems, of which eight are included in the Karaite prayer book.{{fn:194}}
content.comments: [194] {{em:Karaite Prayer Book}}. Vienna, 1854, p. 168ff.

content.english: {{h3:2.8.3 {{em:Mordecai Sultanski as a Transitional Figure of a New Era}}}}

The political transformations of the era, including the reform-minded policies of the government, spurred the Karaites to launch a public campaign for their rights to obtain better legal status than that of the Rabbanites. At this time, there was an additional factor significantly affecting Karaite life and thought: the {{em:Haskalah}} (the Jewish Enlightenment movement). The {{em:Haskalah}} arose in Germany through the activity of Moses Mendelssohn and other Jewish figures and began to spread through Eastern Europe during the final years of the eighteenth century,{{fn:195}} reaching its peak in the Russian Empire during the 1860s. This movement advocated for the integration of Jews into general society, the use of the state language in everyday life, and the teaching of secular subjects in school, while advocating for the preservation of Jewish tradition. The {{em:maskilim}} (exponents of the {{em:Haskalah}}) believed that their efforts to effect these changes would lead to the emancipation of the Jews. Karaite leaders were also influenced by this movement, which arrived in, among other places, the Crimea. They took an interest in non-Jewish literature and science, advocating for the modernization of traditional education and the development of relations with Rabbanite {{em:maskilim}}. At the same time, they tried to convince the authorities that the Karaite community was fundamentally different from the Rabbanites in terms of history, religion, way of life, and occupations.
content.comments: [195] There is extensive literature on the Eastern European {{em:Haskalah}}; see, e.g., Israel Bartal. {{em:The Jews of Eastern Europe, 1772—1881}}. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2005, pp. 90–112; Shmuel Feiner and David Sorkin (eds.). {{em:New Perspectives on the Haskalah}}. London: Littman Library of Jewish Civilization, 2001; Immanuel Etkes. {{em:Ha-dat ve-ha-Ḥayyim: Tenuʿat ha-Haskalah ha-Yehudit be-Mizraḥ Eropah}} [Religion and Life: The Eastern European Jewish Enlightenment]{{em:.}} Jerusalem: Zalman Shazar Center, 1993 (in Hebrew).

content.english: One of the leaders of this epoch was Mordecai ben Joseph Sultanski (1772–1862), who was emblematic of the transitional period from traditional culture to modernity.{{fn:196}} Sultanski was born in Lutsk into the family of the local {{em:ḥazzan}} and was the head of the {{em:bet din}}. He served as a teacher in his native town. The Eastern European and Crimean Karaite communities regarded him as one of the most prominent scholars of his time. He was also well versed in Rabbanite literature. He expresses his view of studying the Talmud in a letter to Isaac ben Solomon of Chufut-Kale, echoing other Karaite sages over the course of history with his statement that Karaites ought to study the Talmud without accepting its authority and that there was a need, as he put it, “to separate the grain from the chaff.”{{fn:197}}
content.comments: [196] Golda Akhiezer. “Mordecai Sultanski: An Outline of His Character and His Historical Writing.” In Dan Shapira and Daniel J. Lasker (eds.). {{em:Eastern European Karaites in the Last Generations}}. Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute and Center for Research on the History and Culture of Polish Jews, 2011, pp. 170–196 (in Hebrew). | [197] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 542.

content.english: In 1817–1818, conflict erupted in the Lutsk community. The conflict was instigated by Abraham Firkovich, a member of the community. Firkovich was a former student of Sultanski, as well as Sultanski’s business partner, and was related to Sultanski by marriage (Sultanski’s son was married to Firkovich’s daughter). Firkovich sought to increase his influence and took over one of Sultanski’s offices in a local study hall. Sultanski, apparently following the great fire that ravaged his home city, had moved to the Crimea, where he was appointed {{em:ḥazzan}} and teacher of the Chufut-Kale community.{{fn:198}} Firkovich, who had visited the Crimea previously and maintained ties with its community leaders, would not leave Sultanski alone. He tried to discredit Sultanski’s name (and even that of Sultanski’s son, Isaac) among the community leaders of the Crimea and Lutsk. Firkovich accused Sultanski of embezzling public money (specifically, sending money belonging to the Chufut-Kale community to the poor people in Lutsk), failing to teach his students in the manner expected, and more. Some leaders of the Lutsk and Crimean communities accepted Firkovich’s allegations against Sultanksi. The Lutsk {{em:bet din}} also accused Sultanski of violating the laws of {{em:halakhah}} and demanded that Sultanski’s authority as a {{em:shoḥet}} be invalidated. During this ordeal, Sultanski was forced to retreat to Lutsk and did not return to the Crimea until the early 1830s.
content.comments: [198] For his biography, see Golda Akhiezer. {{em:Historical Consciousness, Haskalah, and Nationalism among the Karaites of Eastern Europe.}} Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2018{{em:,}} pp. 170–176.

content.english: However, the existing documents, which are preserved in Firkovich’s private archive, cast doubt on the truthfulness of these accusations because the only witness to Sultanski’s “crimes” was Firkovich, who had great ambitions for his own career as a community leader. Sultanski tried to pacify and reason with Firkovich, but struggled for years to justify himself in his numerous letters addressed to Firkovich{{fn:199}} and various community leaders. Sultanski tried to explain that he was being slandered by Firkovich, and in 1821, he demanded that the {{em:bet din}} of Evpatoria be convened on this subject.{{fn:200}} He asked, “How can you reach a guilty verdict without questioning and without hearing the words of two opponents just as it is the duty of the litigants to hear the judges?”{{fn:201}}
content.comments: [199] Correspondence of Sultanski with A. Firkovich. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 737. | [200] Mordecai Sultanski. Letter to Benjamin ben Elija. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 888. | [201] Mordecai Sultanski. Letter from Lutsk to Chufut-Kale. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 1016.

content.english: This case eventually ended in Sultanski’s acquittal. To his credit, Sultanski set aside his bitter feud with Firkovich; however, his troubles did not end there. As we learn from his correspondence with Firkovich, Sultanski had been working hard for many years to repay his debts, some of which had been passed down by his father. In 1828, Sultanski wrote that he had been summoned by the Berdichev police department, probably because he had a guest in his home who lacked a passport (perhaps a Karaite from another community), and Sultanski was interrogated several times. While in the Crimea (1828–1829), he was robbed by a cabman named Gedalyah, who was probably a member of the Evpatoria community. For a number of years, through an appeal to the Evpatoria city council, Sultanski tried to take measures against this criminal and have him taken into custody through the support of the community.

In 1834, he defines his state of affairs in a letter to Firkovich: “I have given up and ended my life in my troubles and have no desire in the world for anything and do not consider myself a living man.” In that same year, Sultanski, in one of his letters to Firkovich, recounts what was happening in his house in Lutsk after his return from the Crimea:

Upon my arrival home, I found all my family members grumpy and desolate on account of my delay, and God added to their grief because of the sins of my youth, and took the light of my eyes, my beloved daughter Shlomit who had been gathered to her people on the first day of Sukkot. And my heart aches also because I left my house having nothing, and there [in the Crimea] I likewise did [not earn] anything… And I said to myself: I will rest after my travels and then put things in order in my home business, my movables, and my real estate, and in addition, during my travels, my two horses died, and now suddenly comes a messenger with a missive [saying that I have] to go to our city to repay my debt of twenty-three rubles in taxes, and I went to the city and repaid the taxes… it is impossible to verbalize all the events that occurred to me when I returned!{{fn:202}}
content.comments: [202] Mordecai Sultanski. Letter to A. Firkovich. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 736.

content.english: Sultanski’s wife had passed away earlier (in a letter from 1821, he calls himself “a widower and a mourner”), and after settling in the Crimea, he married a woman from a privileged Karaite family, which apparently improved his status somewhat. However, life in the Crimea was not easy for him either. In 1831, he wrote to Firkovich that he had been appointed a {{em:melamed}} in Chufut-Kale and wanted to relocate to Evpatoria, but “the Head of Exile” (possibly Simḥah Babovich) had not consented to the move. Sultanski’s motivation to move to Evpatoria may have arisen from feelings of social isolation because Chufut-Kale had been divested of its residents.

Like other Polish Karaites, he saw in the Crimea a land of better opportunities, though his integration did not go smoothly. Thus, even while visiting there for the first time in 1817, Sultanski wrote about moving to the Crimea: “It is difficult for me, for I lived for a while with Meshekh [Slavic people], and I lived among tents of Kedar [in the Tatar region], and until my old age I did not learn their language, and did not get used to writing as they do.”{{fn:203}}
content.comments: [203] Mordecai Sultanski. Correspondence of Sultanski with A. Firkovich. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 737, 18r.

content.english: The Polish Karaites indeed saw themselves as a special and different entity from the Crimean communities. This view was also found in Sultanski’s letter, which uses the phrase “we, Polish [Karaites]” as opposed to the Crimeans. Apparently, for Sultanski, as well as for other Eastern European Karaites who regarded themselves as the intellectual elite of entire Karaite communities, it was difficult to accept their lower social status in a new land, despite having greater religious and general education than that of the Crimean natives. Sultanski and other Eastern European immigrants, despite this lower status, had a great impact on the Crimean educational system. We note a curious practice in the correspondence between Sultanski and Firkovich, one that also typified the Eastern European Karaites. When they did not want the Crimean Karaites to know about specific issues in their letters, they used Yiddish, incorporating some passages in that language.{{fn:204}}
content.comments: [204] Ibid.

content.english: In the early 1830s, Sultanski, along with Firkovich, Yashar, and others, was engaged in publishing Karaite books in the publishing house in Evpatoria, and some of his treatises were also published. Despite all his troubles and vicissitudes, he found time to read books and write his own treatises. Influenced by maskilic trends, Sultanski studied general philosophical and other secular literature and was interested in historical research. In addition, he was personally acquainted with maskilic figures in the Russian Empire, such as Isaac Baer Levinsohn, Peretz Smolenskin, and Ephraim Deinard.

Sultanski wrote a number of works on various subjects. {{em:Tetiv Daʿat}} (Adorn Wisdom){{fn:205}} is an apologia for the Karaite faith, including philosophical arguments and a range of quotations from rabbinic literature. In this book—and especially in another of his books, {{em:Petaḥ Tiqva}} (Door of Hope)—he advocates for a modern approach to education. His {{em:Yalqut Yosef}} (The Compilation of Joseph) is a commentary on the Torah, while his book {{em:Mikhtam Sur me-Raʿ}} (Epigram Turn from Evil) deals with ethical issues.
content.comments: [205] Mordecai Sultanski. {{em:Tetiv Daʿat}}. Gözleve, 1859 (in Hebrew).

content.english: He also wrote two books that contain anti-Rabbanite polemics. One of them, {{em:Sefer ha-Taʿam}} ({{em:The Book of Discernment}}), consists of answers to questions asked of Sultanski by an adviser (named Miller) to Czar Alexander I, which apparently occurred before 1825, concerning the history and customs of the Karaites. The manuscript text of {{em:Sefer ha-Taʿam}} indicates that Sultanski had ties with powerful political officials and had the chance to discuss with them the differences between Karaites and Rabbanites. Most of his works have not been published and are preserved only in manuscript form.

His most famous work, which also contains anti-Rabbanite polemics, is {{em:Memory of the Just}} ({{em:Zekher Ṣaddiqim}}).{{fn:206}} This was the first scholarly attempt by a Karaite author to write a history of the Karaites. As Sultanski testifies, he was inspired to write this book following a visit to the Crimea in 1837 by Czar Nicholas I and his retinue. During their visit, the distinguished guests posed a series of questions to the community leaders about the Karaites, the time of their settlement in the Crimea, documentary sources that shed light on their origins, prominent historical figures, the reasons for the split from the Rabbanites, and the differences between the Karaites and the Rabbanites.{{fn:207}} The community leaders were confused by these questions and did not know how to answer them. Hence, Sultanski decided afterward to provide extended answers in his book, which he intended to title {{em:Hod Malkhut}} ({{em:The Splendor of Kingship}}) and dedicate to the czar, but for reasons that remain unclear, he wrote {{em:Memory of the Just}} instead.
content.comments: [206] Mordecai Sultanski. {{em:Memory of the Just}}. Introduction by Shemuel Abraham Poznanski. Warsaw, 1920 (in Hebrew). | [207] Ibid., pp. 71–72.

content.english: Sultanski saw the writing of this book as an important means of improving the legal status of his community, seeking to create a positive image of the Karaites in the eyes of the Russian authorities. Although he read some books on Jewish and world history in Hebrew and in Polish, most of his claims in these books were not supported by historical fact. He wrote, among other things, about the Karaites’ relationship to the ten lost tribes and about Karaite settlements in Eastern Europe that preceded the crucifixion of Jesus (an event, therefore, in which they had no part). {{em:Memory of the Just}} repeatedly asserts that the authorities in all the lands where the Karaites ever settled appreciated them as useful citizens because of their contribution to these lands’ economic prosperity.

Interestingly, during the period of modernization, enlightened German Jews, who established Jewish studies as a new discipline (known as {{em:Ḥokhmat Israel}}), also tried to present a new Jewish history in a European context. Their writings aimed to demonstrate Jewish contributions to economics, culture, and human civilization in general, thus creating a new, positive image of Jews and convincing Christians that they were worthy of emancipation.{{fn:208}} Despite the differences between these Jews and the Karaites, the same pattern emerges: creating a Jewish history that demonstrates Jews’ contribution to Christian society.
content.comments: [208] Paul R. Mendes-Flohr (ed.). {{em:Ḥokhmat Yisraʾel: Hebbetim Historiyim u-Filosofiyom}} [Modern Jewish Studies: Historical and Philosophical Perspectives]. Jerusalem: Zalman Shazar Center, 1979, pp. 10–12 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Sultanski, like the German and Russian {{em:maskilim}}, was aware of the official agenda for the “improvement” and “productivization” of Jews, which both European and Russian rulers tried to implement starting from the eighteenth century; these improvements took the form of different projects and legislative initiatives. The very notion of productivization was based on a conception{{fn:209}} of the earth and its produce as the major source of wealth, denying the contributions of commerce and banking to the economic development and prosperity of society. This conception, which completely contradicts today’s economic outlook, prevailed in Europe and Russia during this period in the bureaucracies of absolute monarchies. It fostered the perception of Jewish economic activity—such as trade, intermediation, or interest-based lending—as destructive, parasiti- cal, and harmful to one’s character. In Poland and Lithuania, Karaite and Rabbanite Jews ran the taverns of the Polish nobility because they were the only ones who knew how to buy alcohol and manage taverns properly (in the eyes of the Polish nobles).{{fn:210}} After the annexation of parts of Poland, Russian authorities launched a struggle against this occupation, claiming it was immoral and destructive, thus causing many Rabbanite and Karaite Jews (Firkovich among them) to go bankrupt.
content.comments: [209] This is known as physiocratic economic theory. | [210] Glenn Dynner. {{em:Yankel’s Tavern: Jews, Liquor, and Life in the Kingdom of Poland}}. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.

content.english: In Europe and Russia, a series of endeavors was proposed that targeted the “civil and moral improvement of the Jews” and their “productivization” by distancing them from commerce and encouraging them to engage in manual labor and agriculture, which were erroneously viewed as the most beneficial kinds of activity for the economic flourishing of a state.{{fn:211}} One of the contradictions of the governmental policy toward Jews was that even though Jews were forced to engage in agriculture, the authorities were in no hurry to lift the bans on land acquisition by Jews.
content.comments: [211] Christian W. Dohm, a diplomat, economist, and high official under King Friedrich II of Prussia (1740–1786), proposed integrating Jews into general society; see Christian W. Dohm. {{em:Über die bürgerliche Verbesserung der Juden}}. Berlin and Stettin, 1781. Among the better-known programs for “productivizing” the Jews in the Russian Empire was that of poet and senator Gabriel Romanovich Derzhavin (1743–1816), see John D. Klier. {{em:Imperial Russia’s Jewish Question}}, {{em:1855–1881}}. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005, pp. 95–115.

content.english: To fit the official policy, Sultanski repeatedly asserts in his book the usefulness of the Karaites’ economic and other activity in the lands where they had dwelled throughout history. Because of their economic contribution, and the fact that the Christians regarded the Karaite movement as closer than rabbinic Judaism to ancient, biblical Judaism,{{fn:212}} he maintains that there were special relations between Karaites and Christian rulers that had manifested in a long history of protection and special rights granted to Karaite communities.{{fn:213}} To illustrate this point, Sultanski recounts a story about Karaites and the Crusaders not found in any other source. According to Sultanski, when the Crusaders besieged Jerusalem in 1099, they did not—so he claims—kill Karaites because they saw them as “righteous people in their deeds, and honest in their behavior.”{{fn:214}} This claim is in stark contrast to earlier, credible sources that state unequivocally that the Crusaders massacred Rabbanites, Karaites, Muslims, and even Christians in the city. To support his novel claim, Sultanski “quotes” Baldwin I, the first Crusader king of Jerusalem, as saying that Karaites were not to be found in Jerusalem during the Second Temple period and, thus, they did not “hurt Christians” (i.e., did not take part in the crucifixion of Jesus).{{fn:215}} Sultanski adds that Baldwin I, because of his respect and love for Karaites, granted them various rights, including residence charters in Europe and in the Crimea. As we know, in the eleventh century, Karaites did not reside either in Europe or in the Crimea but only in Persia, Egypt, and Byzantium, and Sultanski knew this as well.
content.comments: [212] Akhiezer. {{em:Historical Consciousness}}, pp. 225–228. | [213] Because the authorities tended to refer simply to “Jews” without specifying a denomination, most of the existing charters or other documents do not contain sufficient evidence of which group was intended—Rabbanites, Karaites, or both. | [214] Sultanski. {{em:Memory of the Just}}, p. 104. | [215] The Crusaders massacred the Jewish (as well as Muslim) population in Jerusalem without distinguishing between its communities. Goitein. {{em:Ha-yishuv be-Eretṣ Israʾel}}, p. 233 ff.; Joshua Prawer. {{em:The History of the Jews in the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem}}. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988, pp. 235–236.

content.english: Sultanski presents as historical fact some fictional narratives borrowed from Karaite folklore. However, some of these Karaite oral traditions do contain a historical core, such as those concerning the relocations of Karaites from Solkhat to Lithuania.{{fn:216}} Sultanski emphasizes the early date of the settlement of Karaites in Lithuania when its duke, Vitold, who allegedly brought them from Crimea as captives, granted them special rights and then resettled them in Polish territories. This story, which contains numerous errors of dates and other details, was supposed to demonstrate that the Karaites had been brought to Eastern Europe at the will of the local rulers and granted special privileges, which the Karaite leaders of the nineteenth century also expected to receive from Russian officialdom.
content.comments: [216] Sultanski. {{em:Memory of the Just}}, p. 109.

content.english: Whatever their veracity, the oral traditions describing the transfer of communities from one land to another by local rulers (and the concomitant granting of special privileges) were widespread in other Jewish communities. The tradition of the Jews of Provence, for example, held that Charlemagne had brought them there to develop the country, whereas Egyptian Jewry kept alive a tradition concerning a relative of the exilarch who was brought by the Fatimid ruler to serve as the leader of the community.{{fn:217}}
content.comments: [217] See Abraham Grossman. “Mitos dor ha-meyasdim bi-Tfuṣot Yisraʾel bi-Ymei ha-Beinayim u-mashmaʿuto ha-historit” [The Myth of the Founding Fathers in the Diaspora in the Middle Ages, and Its Historical Meaning]. In Moshe Idel and Ithamar Gruenwald (eds.). {{em:Mitos ba-Yahadut: Historya, hagut, sifrut}}. Jerusalem: Zalman Shazar Center, 2004, p. 126 (in Hebrew).

content.english: The “historical events” in {{em:Memory of the Just}} and some of Sultanski’s other writings incorporate various ahistorical narratives, such as the rescue of the Byzantine emperor, Constantine V, by Rabbi Sangari (whom he arbitrarily identified with the fictional rabbi named “Ḥaver” in Judah Halevi’s philosophical book {{em:The Kuzari}}). According to Sultanksi, Sangari converted the Khazars to Karaism{{fn:218}} and met the Russian prince, Vladimir the Great of Kiev (reigned 980–1015). Other plots, too, are restricted only by the author’s own imagination and his superficial knowledge of general history from Hebrew and Polish sources.
content.comments: [218] Karaism, in its version closer to the present one, emerged in the second half of the ninth century (almost 150 years after ʿAnan ben David), after the presumed conversion of the Khazars to Judaism and before the birth of Vladimir the Great of Kiev (960–1015).

content.english: In addition to clear factual errors and dubious claims, Sultan- ski’s book contains numerous contradictions. For instance, he writes that Karaism appeared in the times of the Second Temple, but elsewhere, he asserts that there were no Karaites in Jerusalem during that same period (thus, as noted, alluding to the fact that they played no role in the crucifixion of Jesus).

It is important to note that Sultanski’s historical writings cannot be judged as if they were written by a modern professional historian, especially considering that in those days, Jewish—and especially Karaite—history was at its very inception as an academic discipline. Sultanski, like other traditional Jewish authors, compiled various texts and passages that were not necessarily related in any way and supplemented them with folkloric or invented stories that illustrated a certain—in this case, social—agenda. This approach differs from modern historical writing, which is based on comparative criticism and analysis. However, we can see some signs of a modern approach that Sultanski appropriated from the maskilic worldview. First, he came to the conclusion that the Karaites had their own history that should be presented through documental sources; second, he saw this documental history as an instrument of social struggle—namely, a campaign for emancipation. This innovative thinking was adopted and expanded by Sultanski’s student, Abraham Firkovich, who, in his writings, explicates many ideas that came from his teacher without mentioning his name.
{{h2:2.9 Abraham ben Samuel Firkovich and His Role in Karaite History}}

The colorful and controversial figure of Abraham ben Samuel Firkovich (1787–1874), perhaps the most famous individual Karaite in history, has provoked scholarly and ideological debates through the present day. He lived an extraordinary life that included travels, encounters with unusual people, historical research and the pursuit of ancient manuscripts, extensive social activity aimed at obtaining emancipation for his community, and forgeries of tomb inscriptions and colophons. His biography is connected to numerous events and processes of the epoch that significantly affected the Karaite community in the Russian Empire, gradually altering its self-identity. These changes resulted largely from Firkovich’s own activity, and contemporary historians offer differing (and even opposing) assessments of his impact.
{{h3:2.9.1 {{em:His Life, Activity, and Enactment of Ideas}}}}

Abraham Firkovich (also known by the acronym Eben Reshef) was a younger contemporary of his teacher Sultanski, who resided in Lutsk. According to most researchers, Firkovich was born in Lutsk and, after his marriage to Hannah in 1808, made his livelihood from a windmill his father-in-law bequeathed to him. However, these scholars based this understanding on Firkovich’s own version of his early life. A recently published document{{fn:219}} demonstrates that he lived in Zalavʹya, a small village near Lutsk where he may also have been born, and, like many other Karaites and Rabbanites in local villages, made a living from running a tavern that sold alcohol to farmers. Sometime in 1809–1810, Firkovich was forced to leave the village along with other Jews expelled by the Russian government, which banned this “distracting” occupation, and went bankrupt. Never again would he mention that he had once been engaged in such a “nonproductive” business.
content.comments: [219] Volodymir Shabarovsky. {{em:Karaimy na Volyni: shtrikhi do portretu zagadkovogo narodu}} [Karaites in Vohlynya: Outlines of the Portrait of a Mysterious People]. Lutsk: Tverdynia, 2012, p. 92 (in Ukrainian).

content.english: Firkovich studied under some rabbinic teachers before he began to study with Mordecai Sultanski, and Firkovich was influenced by several key ideas set forth in Sultanski’s {{em:Memory of the Just}}. These ideas played a critical role in shaping Firkovich’s perception of Karaite history. Several decades later, Firkovich would adapt and reimagine Sultanski’s ideas in his own articles and books, without mentioning Sultanski. As previously noted, in 1822, Firkovich was involved in a conflict with Sultanski and decided to move to Evpatoria, where he was appointed {{em:ḥazzan}}. In 1830, Simḥah Babovich hired Firkovich as a tutor for his sons, and later, Firkovich became Simḥah’s personal secretary. In the same year, he accompanied Simḥah on a pilgrimage to the Land of Israel, including visits to Jerusalem, Hebron, and Cairo. During these travels, Firkovich came into possession of a great number of old manuscripts. Beginning in the mid-1820s, he worked to reestablish the Karaite press of Evpatoria. After some years, he obtained permission from the authorities to open it, and starting in 1834, he became a central figure in book publishing.

content.caption: (Manuscript Department of the Library of the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences, F. 143, call no. 1200)

content.english: In 1839, the governor of Novorossia and the Crimean Peninsula, Count Mikhail Vorontsov, who was favorably disposed toward the Karaites, sought a learned Karaite to fulfill a task that would be of critical importance to the community. The aim was to provide answers, supported by documentary evidence, to six questions formulated by Vorontsov concerning the nature and history of Karaism, its sages and literature, the reasons for the schism with the Rabbanites, and the differences between the two communities.{{fn:220}} This task entailed searching for old Karaite manuscripts and artifacts and subsequently writing a report on their history, literature, and customs (including distinctions from the Rabbanites) that would be presented to the authorities. Firkovich was undoubtedly the best candidate for this role, and he was recruited to carry out this task on Vorontsov’s recommendation. The governor was also the founder of the Imperial Odessa Society of History and Antiquities and of its journal ({{em:ZOOID}}), and he needed to publicize sensational archaeological and historical artifacts from this newly annexed geographic region. The choice of Firkovich was strongly supported by Simḥah Babovich, who had been appointed that year to the top level of the Karaite religious leadership—the head of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory.
content.comments: [220] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 8.

content.english: For this work, Firkovich received financial support from both the government, which had an interest in the collection of antiquities in a region that had been annexed to Russia, and Babovich, whose interest was in advancing the legal status of the Karaites. Babovich applied to other Karaite communities for financial support for Firkovich in his undertaking, which he regarded as an important national project. In his letter to the Crimean community of Perecop, Babovich expresses hope that the antiquities that Firkovich seeks and assembles will help counteract all sorts of prejudice against the Karaites and that their history “will flourish just like that of large, well-educated nations.” Babovich, like many Karaites, expected that Firkovich’s work would help raise the profile of Karaism across the world because, up to that point, they had been relatively unknown, given the small size of the community and the non-existence of a Karaite historical narrative.{{fn:221}} Babovich well understood that composing a glorious history, especially based on ancient documents, could be a powerful means toward achieving emancipation.
content.comments: [221] Simḥah Babovich. Letter to the Karaite Community of Perecop. RNL 946, op. 1, no. 33, 1r-v.

content.english: Having received the appointment, Firkovich traveled to the Crimea and the Caucasus to collect old manuscripts and epitaphs from Karaite cemeteries. Within just a few years of work on this task, Firkovich’s goal was supplanted by one of much greater scope: to create a new history of the Crimean and Eastern European Karaites. For him, this was an opportunity to improve the standing of his community while simultaneously increasing his own stature. Firkovich received assistance from the Russian authorities over the course of his work, during which he initiated contacts with government ministers and officials. He also became personally acquainted with the functionaries responsible for education and censorship who assisted him in publishing books in Hebrew. In 1843, in recognition of his efforts in collecting ancient artifacts, Firkovich was awarded a gold medal by the government for public service. Two years later, Crown Prince Alexander, son of Nicholas I, gifted him a diamond ring. In 1855, Firkovich participated in the coronation of Alexander II, presenting him with a Hebrew poem that he composed in the new czar’s honor. Dozens of individuals, both Karaite and Rabbanite, wrote to Firkovich requesting economic assistance, asking that he help relatives gain admittance to institutions of higher learning, and so forth. Over the span of a few years, the taverner from Volhynia had become a famous public figure with extensive ties to officialdom.

From 1839 to 1858, during his travels to various cities to collect materials of historical interest, Firkovich became acquainted with many figures of the {{em:Haskalah}} movement, such as Samuel Joseph Finn, Simḥah Pinsker, Abraham Ber Gottlober, and Jonah Gurland, and maintained correspondence with them for many years. Some became friends with whom he cooperated in scholarly and historical pursuits. In 1856, while in Saint Petersburg, Firkovich showed Daniel Khvolson, one of the founding fathers of Jewish studies in Russia, some 700 transcriptions of burial monuments and approximately 150 assorted Torah scrolls and manuscripts.

Firkovich’s ties with {{em:maskilim}} were of decisive importance in his life. These individuals opened for him the world of the {{em:Haskalah}} with its scientific, scholarly work and techniques that would enable him to mold his ideas and bring them to the general public. Firkovich also tried to help the {{em:maskilim}} shorten the censorship process that was required for the publication of each book. He was a friend of the influential censor Wolf Tugendhold, an educator and supervisor in a rabbinic seminary in Vilna who, from 1827 to 1864, worked for the Vilna censorship committee.{{fn:222}}
content.comments: [222] Akhiezer. {{em:Historical Consciousness}}, p. 261.

content.english: News of the collections that Firkovich had assembled spread in the 1840s, and enthusiastic articles about his findings began appearing in Russia and abroad in Russian, Hebrew, and German. Thus, Firkovich gained renown in the scholarly world in Eastern and Western Europe. He conducted prolific correspondence with important Jewish scholars and Christian Hebraists from Europe. In their letters, they asked him questions about materials in his possession and requested certain manuscripts for publication. For example, in 1873, Solomon Buber asked for a few manuscripts so that he could publish them. In a letter in 1838, the German scholar Heinrich Friedrich Wilhelm Gesenius expresses admiration for Firkovich’s knowledge of the Hebrew language and its literature.

In 1871, Firkovich, aged eighty-four, and his young wife, aged seventeen, visited the Austrian Empire and received an audience in Vienna with the emperor Franz Joseph II, with whom Firkovich discussed the civil rights of the empire’s Karaite community.{{fn:223}} From Vienna, he traveled to the Karaite community of Halich, where he introduced some legal injunctions intended to highlight the differences between the Karaites and the surrounding Rabbanites and to abolish customs that resembled those of the Rabbanite communities.{{fn:224}} Such separation was apparently an important goal of Firkovich’s activity, helping him ensure the complete emancipation of the Karaites in both the Russian and Austrian empires.
content.comments: [223] Golda Akhiezer. “What Do You Think of Jesus Christ?—A Letter to Abraham Firkovich from the Christened Jew of Vienna.” {{em:Moreshet Israel}} 16 (2018): 24–25 (in Hebrew). | [224] Adolf Jellinek. {{em:Taqqanot ʾEben Reshef li-qehal ha-Qaraʾim be-Halich}} [The Legal Decisions of Eben Reshef for the Halich Karaite community]. Vienna, 1875 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Beginning in 1839, Firkovich was an active member of the Imperial Odessa Society of History and Antiquities, and from 1853 to 1865, while in Vilna, he was an associate member of the Archaeological Committee and the Vilna Museum of Antiquities. In the early 1860s, he took part in the activities of the Imperial Russian Geographical Society in Saint Petersburg and was periodically invited to give lectures and offer his opinions on various topics.

Firkovich, as depicted in the available documents, became famous and well connected, yet lacked a senior government position and a steady salary. Over his considerable lifespan, he served in a wide range of offices and capacities in both the Karaite community and various official institutions. At the same time, however, he was registered as a merchant of the Second Guild and as an educator of the Karaite people. It is possible that Firkovich’s charisma, fame, and innumerable connections left the {{em:maskilim}} and the people in Russian society with an inflated image of the man that did not correspond with reality.

Firkovich authored several books and articles, as well as apologetics for Karaism, in the spirit of medieval Karaite literature. His greatest scholarly work was {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}} (Memorable Stones), a corpus of 769 Karaite burial inscriptions, most from Chufut-Kale, which was published in Vilna some two years after his death. In the introduction to this book, Firkovich describes the process of collecting antiquities and his ideas concerning Karaite history. Two additional books that he considered to be of great importance are {{em:Naḥal Qedumim}} (Stream of the Ancients), which contains lists of the Torah scrolls and Scriptures that he found during his travels (some with forged colophons), and {{em:Yemot ʿOlam}} (Days of Old), which gives a chronological account of the generations from Adam to the time of the author. These books remain unpublished. Firkovich also wrote pamphlets on matters of ritual law and faith, scriptural exegesis, and several articles published in Hebrew periodicals. In addition, Firkovich composed two anti-Rabbanite treatises, {{em:Massah u-Merivah}} (Temptation and Contention) and {{em:Ḥotem Tokhnit}} (Sealing a Program),{{fn:225}} which provoked fierce criticism (particularly the former).
content.comments: [225] Abraham Firkovich. {{em:Ḥotem tokhnit}}. Gözleve, 1834, repr. Ramle, 1977 (in Hebrew); Abraham Firkovich. {{em:Massah u-merivah}}. Gözleve, 1838.

content.english: Firkovich (much more than Sultanski) was familiar with Hebrew maskilic historical literature. In addition, he read Polish and Russian history books. One of the notions that Firkovich adopted from his teacher concerned the antiquity of the Crimean Karaite community. In his view, the proto-Karaites were the descendants of the exiles of Samaria (the ten tribes). He claims that they were brought to the cities of Media following the destruction of Samaria by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser in 720 BCE{{fn:226}} and that in the sixth century, King Cambyses, son of Cyrus, awarded them the Crimean Peninsula for their participation in his campaign against the Scythians. They then ostensibly settled in the Crimean cities of Solkhat (which did not yet exist), Onkhat (which never existed), Sefarad (Firkovich’s name for the yet unestablished city of Kerch), and Chufut-Kale (also not yet founded), among others. Firkovich includes with the exiles of Samaria a group of Judeans (belonging to the tribe of Judah), termed “the captivity of Jerusalem,” “who came to the aid of their brethren from their cities during the war against Samaria.”{{fn:227}} This reflected the special importance of the tribe of Judah in Karaite (as well as in Rabbanite) tradition.
content.comments: [226] Firkovich thus conceived a new calendar, whose epoch was “the exile of Samaria,” which he used in his writings. He also invented “the Crimean reckoning from the Creation” and “the reckoning of Matarkha” (i.e., the city of Tmutarakan, in the Kerch Peninsula), the latter of which is identical to the traditional reckoning “from the creation of the world.” | [227] Deinard. {{em:Massaʾ Qrim,}} p. 46.

content.english: To prove that the local Karaite community had lived in the Crimea before the Christian era, Firkovich had to present historical evidence. Because such documents did not exist, he forged colophons, sale contracts, and ownership or consecration notes using dates, names, and toponyms that he revised or added. Some of these contained a story, such as consecration notes on Torah scrolls or books. For instance, one of them tells how a certain Ḥamu ben Judah consecrated a Torah book to the community of the Khazars in Solkhat. Firkovich did not write a date on this inscription. It is undoubtedly a forgery: Solkhat was established more than 300 years after the Khazar period, and we have no evidence about either the physical presence of Khazars in the Crimea or their use of synagogues in any period of time. As for the burial inscriptions, he would change them by adding an early date to an undated burial monument or altering the numerical values of letters by deleting or changing some of them, such as by turning a {{em:tav}} (400) into a {{em:kof}} (100).{{fn:228}}
content.comments: [228] For further details about Firkovich’s forgeries, see Herman L. Strack. {{em:A. Firkowitsch und seine Entdeckungen: ein Grabstein mit den hebräischen Grabschriften aus der Krim}}. Leipzig, 1876; Abraham Harkavy. {{em:Altjüdische Denkmäler aus der Krim, mitgetheilt von Abraham Firkovisch (1839–1872) und geprüft von Albert Harkavy}}. Mémoires de l’Académie Impériale des sciences de St.-Pétersbourg, série 8, St. Petersbourg, 1876, vol 24, no. 1; Dan Shapira (ed.). {{em:The Tombstones of the Cemetery}}.

content.english: The theories that Firkovich propounded in his various writings on the early Karaite settlement in the Crimea are exemplified by two of his forgeries: the Derbent Document and the Mejelis Document. Both are colophons that Firkovich added to the Torah scrolls that he discovered in 1840 during his travels among the Rabbanite Jewish communities in the Caucasus Mountains, one in the synagogue of Derbent (in the present Republic of Daghestan on the Caspian Sea) and the other in that of the village of Mejelis.{{fn:229}} The Derbent Document was reported to be the work of Judah ben Moses ha-Naqdan Mizraḥi, whom Firkovich describes as a descendant of the exiles of Samaria and of those Israelites who, many years later, had arrived in the Crimea with members of the tribe of Judah.
content.comments: [229] Firkovich submitted them for publication. See Abraham Firkovich. {{em:Nusaḥ ha-reshimah ha-nimṣeʾt be-Mendzhelis ʿal yedei …” Abraham Firkovich … ve-Yiṣḥaq … b. Kevod… Mordekhay… irishkan.}} Istanbul: Y. de Castro, 1844–1845; Deinard. {{em:Massaʾ Qrim}}, p. 46 (Derbent Document). For an analysis of these documents, see Dan Shapira. “Remarks on Avraham Firkowicz and the Hebrew Mejelis ‘Document.”’ {{em:Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae}} 59.2 (2006): 131–180.

content.english: Firkovich understood that somehow he had to incorporate ʿAnan ben David into his theory, so he produced a narrative linking this figure to the Crimean Karaites. A text that he wrote during the 1850s, “Remarks on the Sadducees and the Origins of Eastern European Karaites,”{{fn:230}} links the traditions about the captivity of Samaria and the settlement of the proto-Karaites in the Crimea to the advent of ʿAnan. Firkovich does so with a plot in which ʿAnan sends emissaries to the Crimea to herald the ʿAnanite tradition. These messengers, he claims, gave the Crimean community the name {{em:Karaites}}. However, in the days of ʿAnan, this name did not yet exist; the first to use it was Benjamin Nahavendi, who was active at the end of the eighth and beginning of the ninth centuries.
content.comments: [230] Abraham Firkovich. Remarks on the Sadducees and the Origins of Eastern European Karaites (1850s). RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 387.

content.english: Introducing the narrative about the early Karaite settlement in the Crimea required Firkovich to provide an explanation for the existence of the Karaites’ neighbors, a non-Ashkenazi Crimean Rabbanite community known as the Krymchaks (a cognomen invented by the Russian authorities in the mid-nineteenth century) who resembled the Karaites in language, dress, and certain customs. This similarity raised the question of whether the two communities had a shared origin. Any explanation that assigned the Krymchaks a different origin from the one that Firkovich had attributed to the Karaites would cast doubt on the credibility of his theory. As previously noted, the Rabbanites appeared in the Crimea at about the same time as the Karaites: in the thirteenth century. Firkovich elegantly solved this problem by positing that the Krymchaks were former Karaites. He claims that in the tenth century, motivated by envy of Karaism for its success in the Crimea, a group of Rabbanite missionaries had arrived there from Jerusalem and begun promulgating Talmudic propaganda, which was accepted by some 200 Karaites:

When the Rabbanites witnessed the success of the emissaries of their opponents the Karaites there [i.e., in the Crimea], they sent their own emissaries in the middle of the tenth century… the emissaries, the sages of Jerusalem, arrived, bringing with them the Rabbanite law, weighed down with numerous stringencies in addition to the Law of Moses…{{fn:231}}
content.comments: [231] Ibid. See also his draft article on the history and present condition of the Krymchaks: Abraham Firkovich. Essay on Krymchak History. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 174.

content.english: This theory was intended to prove that Rabbanism was a later phenomenon in the Crimea than the arrival of the Karaites. To support his claim about the “Rabbanization” of some Crimean Karaites, Firkovich created a colophon on a book of the Pentateuch, allegedly written by a certain former Karaite in Kaffa: “This is the end [of the work] that the scribe… copied and completed, I, Noah, in the year… 1038, after accepting Rabbanite faith, here in Kaffa.”{{fn:232}} Again, this date is about 250 years before the establishment of the city of Kaffa by the Genoese. In addition, the book of the Pentateuch itself is written in Sephardic script and, hence, was obviously copied in a Sephardic Rabbanite community outside the Crimea, not in Kaffa, and was brought to the Crimea much later.
content.comments: [232] Harkavy and Strack. {{em:Catalog der hebräischen Bibelhandschriften}}, no. 110, 244v, pp. 143–144.

content.english: Firkovich, like the medieval Karaite authors, placed special emphasis on biblical history and non-Talmudic groups and currents in Judaism, including early Christian ones. His aim was to demonstrate that the Karaites were among these numerous ancient groups and that they were distinct from the Rabbanite Jews. This task im- him to investigate various Jewish and even non-Jewish groups, such as Ethiopian Christians. Among the most important news about which Firkovich writes in his letter from Jerusalem to his son-in-law Gabriel, who was married to his daughter Milca, is that he had received a letter from Egypt from a Christian priest. This priest said that his community wanted to come to Jerusalem, leave Christianity, and “join your brethren, and make sacrifices in the Temple…”{{fn:233}}
content.comments: [233] Abraham Firkovich. Letter to Gabriel. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 605, 9r.

content.english: Firkovich also corresponded with the Armenian patriarch Nersis.{{fn:234}} The patriarch asked him about his historical research and about the Karaite view of Jesus. Avoiding as much as possible a direct answer to the second question, Firkovich asked the patriarch to investigate Armenian sources about the Jewish roots of the Armenian kings. He tried to find a connection between the Armenian royal dynasty and the Karaites, although this could also be seen as distant from historical reality.
content.comments: [234] Abraham Firkovich. Letter to Nersis. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 576, no. 721.

content.english: Another interesting matter is Firkovich’s attitude toward the Rabbanites of Derbent (the mountain Jews), whom he visited during his trip to the Eastern Caucasus. This specific community was not familiar with the Talmud until the nineteenth century, a fact that aroused Firkovich’s interest. As Firkovich writes in his book, he told the leaders of the mountain Jews:

You are of the exile of Samaria and of the exile of the First Temple, having been exiled from Persia, whence you arrived in the provinces and cities of Media and Crimea… And therefore you are speaking Persian… When it becomes known to all that you are not of the exile of the Second Temple, but from previous exiles, the Christians will love you, because your forefathers were not part of the conflicts and strife of the Second Temple [the crucifixion of Jesus]… and they will consider you among the ancient Israelites… and you will find favor in the Russian kingdom, and will dwell safely… under the wings of Russian kings, the kings of grace, just as we, the Karaite community, dwell in the Crimea and Poland and Lithuania…{{fn:235}}
content.comments: [235] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 77.

content.english: Firkovich tried to convince the leaders of this community to accept his version of history, namely, that the mountain Jews were also a non-Talmudic group that passed through the Crimea and settled in the Caucasus. He included this conclusion about the history of the mountain Jews in the colophons he wrote on the scrolls found in synagogues in the Caucasus (in Derbent and Mejelis), attributing it to Judah ben Moses ha-Naqdan Mizraḥi, whose words were allegedly written by a scribe in 890 (Derbent Document). Mizraḥi describes himself as a descendant of the exiles of Samaria, who were taken to Persia and eventually settled in the Crimea. However, Firkovich did not manage to convince the leaders of this community.

Firkovich was also interested in the Samaritans as another non-Talmudic group and as direct descendants of ancient Israelites from the First Temple period. At the time of his second and last trip to the Middle East (1863–1865), during which he visited Jerusalem, Syria, and Egypt and acquired a vast collection of Rabbanite, Karaite, and Samaritan manuscripts, he was a guest of the Samaritan community of Sichem. In 1864, while staying in Jerusalem and before his planned trip to Cairo, he sent a messenger, a local Karaite named David ha-Levi, to Sichem to look into the possibility of obtaining manuscripts from the Samaritan community. Following in ha-Levi’s footsteps, Firkovich went from Jerusalem to Sichem with his grandson, Samuel. After a two-week stay in Sichem, they returned to Jerusalem with four large boxes of Samaritan manuscripts that they had loaded on to two donkeys.{{fn:236}}
content.comments: [236] Golda Akhiezer. “Between Samaritans and Karaites: Abraham Firkovich and His Perception of Samaritanism.” In Jan Dusek (ed.). {{em:The Samaritans in Historical, Cultural and Linguistic Perspectives. Studia Samaritana}} 11, {{em:Studia Judaica}} 110 (2018), pp. 235–244; Tapani Harviainen and Haseeb Shehadeh. “How Did Abraham Firkovich Acquire the Great Collection of Samaritan Manuscripts in Nablus in 1864?” {{em:Studia Orientalia, Societas Orientalis Fennica}} 73 (1994): 167–192.

content.english: The Samaritan community’s priests, who were usually reluctant to sell their manuscripts to strangers, agreed in this particular case. This may have been because Firkovich promised to donate 20,000 or 40,000 {{em:gurush}} to the repair of their synagogue and to build a room there for women. According to an unverified testimony of the aforementioned Russian {{em:maskil}} Ephraim Deinard, Samaritan leaders agreed to sell Firkovich their manuscripts after he promised to bring Karaite brides to Sichem for the young community members (the small community did not have enough women eligible for marriage). Deinard adds that Firkovich had no intention of keeping his promise.

The Samaritan source {{em:New Samaritan Chronicle}} (1900) provides some details about Firkovich’s visit to the Samaritan community and the perceptions and reactions of community members to Firkovich’s visit:

In these days, there came to the city of Sichem from the land of Russia a Jewish Karaite sage, named Abraham, who stayed in the house of Jacob ben Zedaka ha-Danfi. And he loved the Shomrim [Samaritans] with a great love for their truthful [faith] of the Holy Torah, and every Shabbat he prayed in the synagogue with the Shomrim both in the evening and in the morning, and testified that there is no such other truthful community, and he suggested to Amram the Priest, our sage, that the Shomrim and the Karaites were one and the same people. And Amram the Priest, our sage, answered him: “There is a great contradiction between us and you concerning observing the commandments of the Holy Torah. If you will become like us—accept the way of the five books of the Holy Torah—we will be one people.” And the sage Abraham answered him:“I will remember your words, I will return back to my country and gather all the elders of the Karaite tribe so that I may speak these words in their ears, and we shall be one people.”{{fn:237}}
content.comments: [237] Elkan-Nathan Adler and Max Seligsohn. “Une nouvelle chronique samaritaine.” {{em:Revue des études juives}} 46 (1903): 143.

content.english: We cannot be sure that this dialogue between Amram the Priest and Firkovich, or any other detail of this chronicle, completely corresponds to reality. The author claims, for instance, that Firkovich died on his way back to Russia, whereas he was still alive and active over the next ten years. However, in the context of Firkovich’s integrative tendency, combined with his search for common roots and traits in the history of various sects and currents, talk about the unification of the two communities and the recurrent prayer with Samaritans are quite plausible. This probability may also be strengthened by the fact that the Samaritan community leaders agreed to sell him their vast collection of manuscripts. This passage from the {{em:New Samaritan Chronicle}} reflects a certain degree of trust that could even have enabled some dialogue about unification.

According to Deinard, the Karaites were influenced by the Samaritans and, therefore, had a number of similar laws and cus- toms, such as strictly observing the laws concerning ritual impurity, refraining from using candles lit before Shabbat, and observation of the new moon.{{fn:238}} This claim about the direct impact of the Samaritans on the Karaites, however, is not based on any documentary proof. Instead, this similarity reflects some common views and perceptions that are typical of certain groups that, for various historical and ideological reasons, did not practice the oral tradition and tended toward a literal interpretation of the Scriptures. The crucial point in this context is that these similarities between the Karaites and the Samaritans were apparently used by Firkovich to gain the sympathy and trust of the Samaritan community—without, however, seeking to merge the communities.
content.comments: [238] Deinard. {{em:Massaʾ Qrim}}, pp. 100–101.

content.english: Firkovich also invented historical figures—sages and heroes from Karaite history whose names he linked to existing inscriptions in the cemetery of Chufut-Kale. In some cases, he produced “ancient” burial inscriptions, such as that of Sangari, whom he identified with the figure of the rabbi named “Ḥaver” in Judah Halevi’s philosophical book {{em:The Kuzari}}. According to Firkovich, following Sultanski’s aforementioned story, Sangari was a Karaite who had converted the Khazars and died in Chufut-Kale.{{fn:239}} Firkovich claimed the identification of this tomb inscription as his own “scientific discovery.” Moreover, he engraved another inscription next to that of Sangari, using the name Sangarit to denote Sangari’s late wife.
content.comments: [239] The name Sangari, however, does not appear in {{em:The Kuzari}}; it is given as the name of the {{em:ḥaver}} in the book. Nahmanides appears to be the first to refer to Isaac Sangari; see Moses Nahmanides. {{em:Kitvei ha-Ramban.}} Ed. Chavel Charles Ber (Haim Dov). Jerusalem: Mosad Harav Kook, 1962–1963. Vol. 1, 1:151.

content.english: In his letter to Babovich, Firkovich tells a story of the conversion of the Khazar king and supports his argument that the Khazars converted to Karaism by invoking Halevi’s words in {{em:The Kuzari}}: “In the beginning of the second essay it says that God inspired the king of the Khazars to go to the forests of Khersones and that he would there find what he sought.”{{fn:240}} To associate the Khazar king’s conversion to Judaism in Crimea, where, according to Firkovich, Sangari lived, he replaces the word “Varasan,” which appears in Halevi’s text,{{fn:241}} with the word “Khersones” (a city in the Crimea). Firkovich claims that Sangari wrote the original text of {{em:Sefer ha-Kuzari}} and accuses Halevi of corrupting the original text because Sangari was (according to Sultanski and Firkovich) a Karaite:
content.comments: [240] Deinard. {{em:Massaʾ Qrim}}, p. 28. | [241] Judah Halevi. {{em:Sefer ha-Kuzari}}. Trans. Judah Even Shemuel. Tel Aviv: Dvir, 1972, p. 47.

content.english: The companion of the king of the Khazars was R. Isaac Sangari… R. Isaac Sangari compiled all of the questions and answers, and the work fell into the hands of R. Judah Halevi. He saw that this work was contrary to the faith of the Rabbanites and altered it and transcribed it into Arabic, being unable to publish it in its original state… Inasmuch as the king of the Khazars accepted upon himself the faith of the Jews of the Crimea, it may be the case that he also intermarried with them. Perhaps there are yet among us today members of his family.{{fn:242}}
content.comments: [242] Deinard. {{em:Massaʾ Qrim}}, p. 28.

content.english: In meetings with representatives of the Russian government in the Crimea, Firkovich continued to claim a connection between the Khazars and the Karaites,{{fn:243}} although he did not state unequivocally that the Karaites were the direct descendants of the Khazars. However, his words were interpreted as such by subsequent generations of Karaite leaders and scholars who sought to create distance from Judaism and its historical narrative.
content.comments: [243] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 37.

content.english: Firkovich also constructed family trees for some communal leaders of Lithuania and the Crimea to prove the continuity of the Karaite community in these areas since ancient times and to distinguish the families of these leaders. For instance, he created a figure who allegedly established the Chufut-Kale community, named Sinan Bey or Moses ben Joseph Sinani Çelebi. According to Firkovich, Sinan came from Persia in 1501 and found favor with Khan Mengli Giray after he healed the khan’s ailing daughter. The khan permitted him to gather all the Benei Mikraʾ from the area (who lived among other nations and even intermarried with them) and resettle them in Qirq-Yer (Chufut-Kale). Sinan did so, taught them the Torah, and turned them from Benei Mikraʾ into Karaites. Firkovich also claims that Sinan built the palace for the khan in Bakhchesaray after it became the capital of the khanate.{{fn:244}} Firkovich writes about Sinan as an ancestor of the dynasty and he assigns Abraham ben Josiah (grandfather of Benjamin Aga) to this clan. As can be reconstructed from the sources, although we find the Sinani and Çelebi families in the Crimea mentioned in the documents and burial inscriptions, a Karaite figure named Sinan Bey never existed in Chufut-Kale.{{fn:245}} Firkovich invented this figure by drawing on the biographical details of two different people from Istanbul. One of them was the Karaite scholar Joseph ben Moses Raviṣi, also called by the Turkish name Sinan Çelebi, and the other was Hoja Maamar Sinan Bey, a Christian who converted to Islam and became one of the greatest architects of the Ottoman Empire.{{fn:246}} Firkovich claims that he found the biography of Sinan Bey in a fragment of an old book that was later lost or stolen.
content.comments: [244] Ibid., p. 206. | [245] There is not even a burial inscription of Sinan Bey in the cemetery of Chufut-Kale. | [246] Dan Shapira. “Sinan.” In Dan Shapira (ed.). {{em:The Tombstones of the Cemetery of the Karaite Jews in Çufut-Qaleh (the Crimea): Report of the Ben-Zvi Institute Expedition—A Collection of Studies}}. Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute, 2008 (in Hebrew), pp. 233–246.

content.english: The publication of the documents in his possession, both authentic and forged, was a key tool for the promotion of his ideas and the advancement of his goals. However, because he was an autodidact, Firkovich was not proficient in academic writing and would seek scholarly advice from experts, frequently availing himself of their assistance in formulating and publishing his ideas. In addition, he was unable to publish the thousands of manuscripts preserved in his collections. However, he occasionally selected some to transcribe and submit to famous scholars. He expected that the transcriptions’ publication by well-known figures would gain him renown and enhance his collections’ scientific and financial value.

The peak of the {{em:Haskalah}} movement in Russia was also the period in which Hebrew maskilic periodicals emerged, and Firkovich and other educated Karaites published their articles and poems in them. Sometimes, Firkovich provided editors with information and materials about Karaism, and some of his maskilic friends (such as Samuel Finn or Abraham Gottlover) published them{{em:.}} These articles appeared in the pages of {{em:Zion}}, {{em:Ha-Karmel}}, {{em:Ha-Maggid}}, {{em:Ha-Meliṣ}}, and {{em:Ha-Shaḥar}}, with whose editors Firkovich was personally acquainted and corresponded.

For some Rabbanite {{em:maskilim}} who advocated rapprochement between the various streams of Judaism, this was an opportunity to promote unification. Simḥah Pinsker, a {{em:maskil}} and scholar, was a friend of Firkovich, with whom he corresponded until the end of his life, and Pinsker published his fundamental book {{em:Liqqutei Qadmoniyot}}, which is based on manuscripts from Firkovich’s collections.{{fn:247}} Pinsker viewed Firkovich’s work as the fulfillment of a pan-national task that was common to Karaites and Rabbanites: “Most manuscripts that I used in this book came to my hands through the grace and faith of my longtime friend, adviser, and intimate, the sage and scholar who exerts himself in the search for the antiquities of our people.”{{fn:248}} Firkovich, however, was far from following the universalist pan-Judaism agenda advocated by {{em:maskilim}}. Over the course of several decades, the {{em:Haskalah}} served as a common ground for the cultivation of closer relations, the development of mutual interests, and literary and scholarly cooperation between Karaites and Rabbanites. However, as trends toward separatism from Judaism grew stronger among Eastern European and Crimean Karaites, this common ground eroded and declined to the point of insignificance.
content.comments: [247] This book includes numerous medieval Karaite texts that were published and analyzed by the author for the first time. See Simḥah Pinsker. {{em:Liqqutei Qadmoniyyot}} [Selected Antiquities]. Vienna, 1860; repr. in 2 vols. in Jerusalem, 1967–68 (in Hebrew). His son, Judah Leib Pinsker (1821–1891), a {{em:maskil}} from Odessa, became famous for his book {{em:Auto-Emancipation}}, in which he urges the Jewish people to strive for national consciousness and political independence, laying the foundation for the Russian Zionist movement {{em:Hovevei Zion}}. | [248] S. Pinsker. {{em:Liqqutei}}, p. ix.

content.english: Even in Firkovich’s lifetime, and especially after his passing, an increasing number of critical voices were raised about his research activity and his sensational discoveries. One of these voices was that of the {{em:maskil}} Ephraim Deinard (1846–1930), who was Firkovich’s personal secretary during the 1860s. Deinard, like Firkovich, was a collector of manuscripts and a self-educated scholar; he researched Crimean, Karaite, and Krymchak history, traveled frequently, and published numerous books and articles. In two of his books, {{em:Massaʾ Qrym}} and {{em:Toldot Eben Reshef}}, Deinard harshly criticizes Firkovich’s historical theories and analyzes the methods he used to produce his forgeries. The scholar Daniel Khvolson, who initially expressed excitement at Firkovich’s discoveries and published a number of works based on his materials and theories, was forced to publish acknowledgments that Firkovich had indeed forged some tomb inscriptions and colophons. The most comprehensive analysis of Firkovich’s work is by Abraham Harkavy (1835–1919), one of the greatest scholars among the pioneers of Jewish studies in Russia. Harkavy describes Firkovich’s method of forging documents{{fn:249}} and refutes his historical theories. Hermann Strack, a Christian Lutheran scholar from Leipzig, spent two months in the Crimea and published his own book{{fn:250}} containing an analysis of Firkovich’s forgeries. In 1874, after Firkovich’s death, Harkavy was invited to Chufut-Kale with Strack to evaluate his second collection, which his descendants suggested selling to the Imperial Public Library. Considerable scholarship on Firkovich has been published over the past two decades.{{fn:251}}
content.comments: [249] For the most significant book that he published on the matter, in conjunction with Hermann Strack, a Lutheran Hebraist from Leipzig, see Harkavy. {{em:Altjüdische Denkmäler}}. | [250] Strack. {{em:Firkowitsch und seine Entdeckungen}}. | [251] See, for instance, Akhiezer. {{em:Historical Consciousness}}, pp. 256–301; Mikhail Kizilov and Tatyana Shchegoleva. “Osen$’$ karaimskogo patriarkha. Avraham Firkovich po opisaniyam ochevidtzev i sovremennikov” [The Autumn of the Karaite Patriarch, Avraham Firkovich, in the Memoirs by Eyewitnesses and Contemporaries]. {{em:Paralleli}} 2–3 (2003): 319–362 (in Russian); Dan Shapira. “Yitshaq Sangari, Sangarit, Bezalel Stern, and Avraham Firkowicz: Notes on Two Forged Inscriptions.” {{em:Archivum Eurasiae Medii Aevi}} 12 (2002-03): 223–260; Daria Vasyutinskaya. “When Copyright Was Different: Avraham Firkowicz and the Rehabilitation of Daniel Chwolson.” In Dan D. Y. Shapira and Daniel J. Lasker (eds.). {{em:Eastern European Karaites in the Last Generations.}} Jerusalem: Ben-Zvi Institute, 2011, pp. 123–130.

content.english: {{h3:2.9.2 {{em:Collecting Ancient Manuscripts}}}}

Notwithstanding Firkovich’s dozens of forged colophons, with which he tried to make manuscripts more ancient and congruent with his theories, one should not dismiss his contributions to Karaite, Rabbanite, and general studies and culture by assembling his manuscript collections. Combined, his manuscripts constitute the second largest collection in the world (after the documents of the Cairo Genizah), and they include Karaite, Rabbanite, and Samaritan documents; Torah codices and scrolls (among the most ancient in the world); and manuscripts and printed books from various genres, including {{em:halakhah}}, exegesis, astronomy, astrology, medicine, philosophy, poetry, grammar, historical chronicles, Kabbalah, and others in Hebrew, Arabic, Aramaic, Persian, Greek, Tatar, Polish, and Russian.{{fn:252}} He collected manuscripts from his youth until his death, obtaining them in various ways.
content.comments: [252] Golda Akhiezer. “Rabbanite Manuscripts in Karaite Hands: Findings from the Crimean Genizot and Libraries.” {{em:Journal of Jewish Studies}} 70.2 (2019): 332–356; Olga Vasilyeva. “The Firkovich Odessa Collection, the History of Its Acquisition and Research, Present Condition and Historical Value.” {{em:Studia Orientalia}} 95 (2003): 45–53.

content.english: As part of his project, Firkovich traveled around the Crimea in 1838–1839. His most important task was to examine tomb inscriptions in the cemeteries and {{em:genizot}} of existing synagogues and study halls; these {{em:genizot}} contained the most ancient manuscripts, scrolls, and books. As noted previously, Firkovich carried out this work in the Caucasus, Sichem, and other places. Such interest was also one of the new trends of {{em:Haskalah}}; these and other antiquities became historical sources and objects of research and were used as evidence to support national or social agendas.

According to Firkovich’s testimony, in October 1838, he came to the Rabbanite synagogue of Feodosia (Kaffa) to take their manuscripts from the upper {{em:genizah}} in the attic (a second {{em:genizah}} was behind the Torah Ark). In the synagogue, he asked the community leaders to show him the ancient manuscripts, but they categorically refused. These leaders feared that he had come to appropriate their synagogue for the Karaite community. At that time, there was a controversy over this synagogue; the Karaites, including Firkovich, claimed that it belonged to their community.{{fn:253}} Firkovich showed them a document from Mikhail Vorontsov, the governor of Novo­ros­sia Province and the Crimea, which authorized him to confiscate ancient Jewish—Rabbanite and Karaite—manuscripts. When the community leaders cast doubt on its authenticity, Firkovich returned accompanied by policemen and Karaite students to help him fulfill this task.{{fn:254}} Firkovich testifies that there were cartloads of manuscripts in the attic and that bundles of them were thrown down by the Karaite students, who climbed up on ladders. Firkovich states that he took only a small part of this treasure—those manus­cripts in the best condition and those he assessed as the most valuable.
content.comments: [253] Ilya Farfel. {{em:Drevniaya evreiskaya sinagoga naidennaya v gorode Feodosii}} [An Ancient Jewish Synagogue Found in the City of Feodosia]. Odessa, 1918, p. 119. | [254] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 22.

content.english: In addition to Feodosia, Firkovich visited the Karaite synagogue of Chufut-Kale and the Rabbanite (Krymchak) one in Karasubazar, which was the Crimea’s main center for Rabbanite Jews in this period. In every synagogue, he asked to be shown ancient books, which he sometimes proposed exchanging with modern, beautiful, and convenient editions. In many cases, the leaders of these synagogues agreed, not understanding the value of the ancient manuscripts. After visiting the Karasubazar synagogue, where the Rabbanites showed him some valuable books, Firkovich examined the entire structure, including the study hall. Unexpectedly, he discovered that in the wall between the study hall and the synagogue, there was a large {{em:genizah}}, and he demanded that it be opened. The community members categorically protested; they feared that opening the {{em:genizah}} would bring a curse upon the community. Their fear was probably rooted in the warning inscriptions that appeared in numerous manuscripts threatening a curse upon anyone who might take for themselves a certain book or Torah scroll that was in the community’s possession. Firkovich did not give up; he brought policemen and workers. When these workers, both Muslim and Christian, came to carry out the order of the police and heard the Jews’ claim about the curse, they refused to open the {{em:genizah}}. Firkovich himself had to take an ax and strike the wall.

97He reports that he confiscated a full cartload of manuscripts from the Karasubazar community.{{fn:255}} His aforementioned theory that the Crimean Rabbanites were previously Karaites was partially designed to justify the confiscation of Rabbanite-owned manuscripts. At the same time, he tried to help the Krymchaks, even sending his own recommendation to Count Mikhail Vorontsov on behalf of high officials when this community tried to obtain an exemption from military service and have some other restrictions overturned. In his recommendation, Firkovich tried to convince Russian authorities that the Krymchaks were closer to the Karaites than to Polish Ashkenazim: “The antiquities were discovered in the repository adjacent to their synagogue, and it became known to the monarchy that they are not of the families of the [Rabbanite] Jews, but of the families of the ten tribes…”{{fn:256}} However, Firkovich was unable to ameliorate the conditions of this small and impoverished community.
content.comments: [255] Ibid., pp. 16–17. | [256] Firkovich. Essay on Krymchak History, 1v.

content.english: Firkovich also purchased books from individuals, and, like many passionate collectors, he was ready to pay any sum for them. As he mentions in his {{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, during his visit to Chufut-Kale in 1838, he bought manuscripts from the descendants of Rabbanite leader David Lekhno and from Benjamin Duvan. After Duvan’s demise, Firkovich acquired some additional books from this library from Benjamin’s grandson, Isaac Duvan.{{fn:257}} In addition, Firkovich purchased a section of the library that belonged to Samuel ben Abraham from the Aga family: “a cartload of books from the bequest of his late father for a high price.”{{fn:258}} His Crimean finds numbered more than 1,500 Karaite and Rabbanite manuscripts and formed his so-called First Collection, which he sold to the Russian Imperial Public Library (currently known as the National Library of Russia) in Saint Petersburg in 1862 for an unprecedented sum of 125,000 rubles.
content.comments: [257] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, p. 5. | [258] Ibid.

content.english: His Second Collection of manuscripts, numbering 17,000, was assembled during his travels in the Middle East. He bought numerous manuscripts in Jerusalem from Karaites and Rabbanites and managed to bring a vast number of manuscripts from the {{em:genizah}} of the Moussa Darʿi Karaite synagogue in Cairo and some items from the {{em:genizah}} of the Ben Ezra synagogue (the “Cairo Genizah”) before the scholar Solomon Schechter transferred its contents to the University of Cambridge. Firkovich visited Aleppo and was one of the few people permitted to see the Aleppo Codex (see Section 1.3), but he was unable to convince its guardians from the local Rabbanite community to sell it to him. If he had done so, it is possible that this unique Pentateuch codex from the tenth century, which passed between Karaite and Rabbanite hands several times, would be complete and in better condition today. He also brought a number of other manuscripts from Istanbul. This Second Collection was sold to the Russian Imperial Public Library by Firkovich’s children in 1876 for 50,000 rubles.

In Sichem, Firkovich acquired from the Samaritan community a manuscript collection consisting of 1,341 items (about 18,250 pages) and a number of Samaritan antiquities that were sold to the Russian Imperial Public Library in 1870 for 9,500 rubles. These became the world’s largest collection of Samaritan manuscripts. He also amassed some manuscripts in Lithuania and Poland, among them communal Karaite documents, charters given to Karaites by Lithuanian dukes, correspondence, and numerous treatises by Eastern European Karaites.{{fn:259}} Despite the number of forgeries, Firko- vich’s collections, which are considered among the largest collections of Jewish (and especially Karaite) manuscripts in the world, had a crucial impact on Karaite studies and changed many established conceptions, providing numerous discoveries in this field.
content.comments: [259] Boris Zaykovsky and Anastasia Romanova. “‘Pol’skie documenty’ sobraniya A.S. Firkovicha.” [‘Polish Documents’ in the A. Firkovich Collection]. {{em:Vostochnyj Sbornik}} 6 (2003): 36–51.

content.english: {{h3:2.9.3 {{em:A Long-Term Perspective on Firkovich’s Mission}}}}

When he was not traveling, Firkovich spent the last decades of his life in Chufut-Kale. Although this previously important Karaite center became depleted of its inhabitants due to the abandonment of the former khan’s capital of Bakhchesaray and because the city’s water sources began to dry up, Firkovich sought to restore the city to its former glory. In addition to setting a personal example by purchasing a house and settling there, Firkovich conceived and proposed a grand project aimed at changing the lives of the Karaites. His private archive contains a draft of a letter written in 1863 to Grigory Vasilyevich Zhukovsky, the military governor of Simferopol, recommending the transfer of the Karaites of Lithuania and Volhynia to Chufut-Kale.{{fn:260}} Firkovich pointed out that the mass emigration to Turkey by the Crimean Tatars had left the region de- populated and in need of rehabilitation. He claimed that the Karaites of Lithuania and Volhynia were good agricultural workers and that Chufut-Kale, being the Karaites’ historical place of residence, ought to be resettled and developed. He further maintained that frequent visits to the Crimea by royalty and high-ranking officials made the rehabilitation of the city imperative. This project, which emphasized Karaite “productivity,” sought to nullify the Karaite leadership in Lithuania and Volhynia by gathering all the members of these communities in Chufut-Kale, thus leaving Firkovich the sole leader of all Karaites in the Russian Empire. He also planned to move the publishing house from Evpatoria to Chufut-Kale and establish a research journal that would operate there, in which the leading scholars of Russia and Europe would publish the texts from Firkovich’s collections. In his zeal, Firkovich went so far as to offer 6,000 rubles of his own for the project’s implementation. However, the Russian government was not interested, and the plan was never carried out. Firkovich died in Chufut-Kale in 1874 and was buried in its cemetery.
content.comments: [260] Abraham Firkovich. Letter to Simferopol Military Governor Grigory Vasilyevich Zhukovsky (1863). RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 41.

content.english: Despite Firkovich’s forcible confiscation of manuscripts from the Rabbanite communities of Feodosia and Karasubazar (which caused their members distress and were seen as immoral acts), from a long-term perspective, his activities may paradoxically be viewed as positive. A considerable number of manuscripts have disappeared since the Crimean Rabbanite community was almost completely exterminated by the Nazis—their ancient synagogue in Feodosia was destroyed by Nazi bombardments—and other collections were lost during the Soviet period. However, Firkovich’s collections are still available today in Russian and Ukrainian libraries. It is also important to note that Karaite private libraries, which Firkovich purchased as well, were an important factor in the survival of many rare medieval and later Rabbanite manuscripts.
