His numerous forgeries, especially in the manuscripts found in the Crimea—colophons, sale contracts, and ownership or consecration notes, with dates, names, and toponyms altered or added by him to demonstrate the Karaites’ presence in the Crimea before the Christian era and their origin from the ten lost tribes—sowed confusion in the academic world. It took more than 150 years for scholars to distinguish some of the forged inscriptions from the real ones. Unfortunately, in many cases, it is impossible to reach clear-cut conclusions about the authenticity of the inscriptions because Firkovich would smear a chemical substance he invented on many of them. Over the years, this substance made text illegible and destroyed parchment or paper, rendering the basic identification of manuscripts impossible.

However, his forgeries also had a positive side: with his activity in the field of Karaite history, Firkovich succeeded in attracting the attention of Jewish and Christian scholars in Russia and Europe. The furious debates that broke out around his theories and findings while he was still alive, and even more so following his death, contributed significantly to the development of academic Jewish studies, particularly in the Russian Empire, resulting in numerous studies of the Karaites, the Krymchaks, the Khazars, and the Jews of Slavic lands.

In addition to his collecting and research activities, Firkovich saw himself as a spiritual leader ushering the members of his small community into a new historical era. He succeeded in bringing the Karaite question into public and scholarly discourses, thus producing a social change: Karaite emancipation. This traditional Karaite, who maintained strict observance of the Torah’s commandments during his long life, successfully fostered a new reality, for which his ideas were used as the building material. This process eventually led to the emergence of a new identity for Eastern European and Crimean Karaites—an identity without the basic principles of Karaism and Judaism in general, as the next chapter demonstrates.
{{header:Chapter 3. The Karaite Educational System and Cultural Life: The Advent of Modernization and Enlightenment}}

Karaite communities regarded their educational system, including elementary schools and advanced study halls, as their most important communal institution. Education played a central role in creating and preserving the Karaites’ unique identity from the Middle Ages to the modern era. The Austro-Hungarian Empire and especially the Russian Empire were the regions where Karaite education, culture, and identity, as well as the other spheres of Karaite life, underwent dramatic changes following the partitions of Poland (1772–1795) and the Russian annexation of the Crimea (1783). These changes were accelerated by modernization processes occurring in Christian society and by the Jewish {{em:Haskalah}} movement, which had a considerable impact on Karaite communities, especially at its peak in the 1860s.

At the same time, the gradual removal of legal restrictions, followed in 1863 by obtaining civil rights equal to those of the Russian population, became decisive factors not only in the lives of the Russian Karaites but also in their self-identity. The nineteenth century saw the greatest transitions in the Karaite community. In less than a hundred years, the Karaites went from a growing and flourishing traditional community to one that had almost completely lost its religious and national identity and whose very existence was under threat of mass assimilation.

In this short period, the Russian Karaite community succeeded in establishing new communal and educational institutions and composing and printing a large number of literary works in various gen- res, including secular literature. Numerous new communities spread all over the Russian Empire, their members gradually integrating into Russian society. However, this period of cultural flourishing gave way to a sharp decline, which was manifested in the closure of educational institutions due to a lack of demand, the weakening of the community’s authority, and, ultimately, its disintegration. These events, among others, eventually led to assimilation. This gradual decline of Karaite religious and national life in the Russian (as well as the Austro-Hungarian) Empire had its roots in the emergence of deep changes in the Karaite perception of their identity. This chapter analyzes the Karaites’ cultural achievements during this epoch and the reasons for this decline.
{{h2:3.1 Karaite Education}}
{{h3:3.1.1 {{em:Traditional Karaite Learning Practices Prior to the Modern Period: General Survey}}}}

There is very poor documentation of the Karaite educational system of the Middle Ages, including its curriculum, the functioning of its institutions, the methods of teaching, and other details regarding the activity of teachers and pupils.{{fn:261}} Fragmentary statements by early Karaite scholars indicate some tendencies of Karaite approaches to Torah studies and education. The well-known statement by ʿAnan ben David—“Search the Scriptures well, and don’t rely on my opinion”—gave scholars an impetus to study, investigate, and comment on the Scriptures. This was followed by the emergence of rich Karaite exegetical literature, mostly focusing on {{em:peshat}} commentary.
content.comments: [261] Barry D. Walfish. “Karaite Education in the Middle Ages.” {{em:Dor Ledor}} 5 (1992): 1–25 (in Hebrew).

content.english: An important characteristic that distinguishes the Karaites’ approach to study from that of the Rabbanites is that their education centered exclusively on the Tanakh. The main source of information on Karaite education is Elijah Bashyachi.{{fn:262}} He asserts that children should begin to study from the age of six (by contrast, the Rabbanites began teaching children at the age of five). The curriculum usually consisted of rote learning of large portions (or the whole text) of the Tanakh, with the teacher training the children to recite the texts in the classrooms. The texts were orally translated (the translation being called {{em:tafsir}}) so that their meaning would be understood by pupils. The children were also taught prayers so that they could participate in the various synagogal services (be they daily, Shabbat, or holiday services). Older children who could afford to continue their education or exceptionally talented children supported by the community also studied the principles of interpretation of the Tanakh.
content.comments: [262] Elijah Bashyachi. ʾ{{em:Adderet Eliyahu}}, pp. 252–256.

content.english: Another specific aspect of Karaite education was the notion that Hebrew, as the language of the Tanakh, must be studied as a separate subject, including its grammar and vocabulary. Evidence of this approach is found as early as the twelfth century. The Byzantine Karaite scholar Judah Hadassi, who was the first to define the principles of Karaite faith, made knowledge of the Hebrew language a requirement, and this requirement was strongly supported by other Karaite scholars. Elijah Bashyachi shared this approach and ascribed great importance to the knowledge of Hebrew in the educational context:

Forasmuch as our Divine law was written in this language, every believer should study the law in this same language, and not another, although the meaning of the law can be understood well in other languages, He who revealed it, cannot be understood thoroughly as in its own language. In addition, the proper names in the law cannot be translated, and there are various metaphors in every language, which cannot be exactly rendered into other languages… This being so, every person of the holy seed of Israel is obliged to study the holy language and must teach his children to know the language of our law… and of the words of the Prophets in a proper and fitting manner…{{fn:263}}
content.comments: [263] Elijah Bashyachi. {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}}. In Leon Nemoy (ed.). {{em:Karaite Anthology: Excerpts from the Early Literature.}} New Haven and London: Yale University Press, 1952, vol. 7, pp. 251–252.

content.english: Therefore, studying Hebrew was part of the elementary Karaite curriculum, and for this purpose, medieval Hebrew grammatical works by Rabbanite authors were used, while the Karaites also produced their own grammars and textbooks. The educational level of a given community depended on numerous factors, such as its social and economic conditions, the presence of books and educated teachers, and its connections with other communities. The traditional Karaite educational system had the same shortcomings as the Rabbanite system: there was no division of pupils by age groups, the level of difficulty of the studied material was not always taken into consideration, and corporal punishment was common. Despite the amount of time dedicated to studying the Hebrew language, teaching was frequently reduced to rote learning of the texts, without considering whether the children understood their meaning. For these reasons, only gifted children who could contend with this system progressed to higher education, eventually becoming part of the intellectual elite of the communities. Notwithstanding these limitations, one distinctive trait of Jewish education (both Karaite and Rabbanite) was that it was provided at a mass level, which set Jewish communities apart from other populations, in which illiteracy and ignorance of the Scriptures among the laypeople were considered normal in the Middle Ages and even in the early modern period.

Wealthy Karaite (as well as Rabbanite) families preferred to hire private tutors for their sons, who also taught them writing skills and secular subjects that would be important for their future employment. We have no evidence of the existence of formal modes of female education in the Karaite communities. Apparently, this began only following modernization and the spread of the {{em:Haskalah}} movement under Russian imperial rule, a period that saw significant changes in the practice of Karaite (and, to a large extent, Rabbanite) education, with the introduction of secular studies and Russian language as compulsory subjects in schools.
{{h3:3.1.2 {{em:The Karaite School System in the Crimea}}}}

Most testimonies on Karaite education in the Crimea—regarding schools, teachers, curriculum, and the maintenance of institutions—are found in memoirs written by maskilic Karaites in the late nineteenth century. The earlier period is not documented, with the exception of scarce and fragmentary testimonies by some community members, mainly in the eighteenth century before the Russian annexation of the Crimea.

One of these testimonies was left by Samuel Yefet from Chufut-Kale, who speaks of the achievements of his classmates in the years 1751 to 1753. This manuscript contains a comprehensive list of the names of the students in the study hall ({{em:bet midrash}}) and of the elementary education subjects they studied there. His account clearly describes how the younger pupils focused on studying the Tanakh and practicing Tatar translation. Samuel also mentions the study of Hebrew grammar. The following fragment from his account reflects several important aspects of Karaite education as well as the Karaites’ relations with the Crimean Rabbanites:

I praise the name of God and glorify Him in this year of “hope,”{{fn:264}} this being the year 5511, the first year of my sitting in this study [hall] with the permission of heaven… I, the young Samuel Yefet. On the New Moon of “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine” [i.e., the month of Elul],{{fn:265}}… by the grace of Him who teaches man wisdom, two students began reading the Book of Joshua… these being the sons of my friend Yefet and his colleague Moses the student, son of the pleasant [and] honorable R. Jacob Kefeli… On Sunday, the eighth of Elul, the student Jacob son of the honorable R. Samuel the tutor, of blessed memory, began reading a translation of the Torah… On Wednesday, the seventh of this month [of Ḥeshvan 5532, 1772], two students began reading {{em:Sefer Mikhlol}} [Book of Splendor],{{fn:266}} which is [also] called {{em:Diqduq}} [Grammar], these being Raphael and Samuel… And prior to these three, Simḥah the student, son of the honorable R. Samuel the wise master… began reading the translation of the Torah called {{em:tafsir}}. On Monday, the twenty-fifth of Ḥeshvan, two students, these being Isaac son of the honorable Aaron, of blessed memory, and Jacob ibn Solomon of the Rabbanite community, began reading the book of the Former Prophets… On Sunday, the 10th of Kislev, David ben Joseph… son of Rabbi David… began reading {{em:tafsir}}. Furthermore, the student Joseph son of Isaac… son of the honorable Joseph Çelebi Sinani, of blessed memory, also began in this month… On Tuesday, the ninth of Sivan, two students, these being David and Joseph, of the community of the Rabbanite brethren, began reading the Five Books of the Torah. May it be His will that He make them great in the Torah… On Sunday, the fourth of Kislev, two students began reading the Torah of God. The name of the first is Joseph ben Abraham Sirkeci, of blessed memory, and the name of the second is Benjamin ben Elijah Duvan, may his Rock keep and safeguard him…{{fn:267}}
content.comments: [264] Heb. {{he:תקוה}}, the numerical value of which is 511. | [265] This name for a month ({{he:אלול}}) is the acronym of the passage cited (Song 6:3 {{he:אני לדודי ודודי לי}}). | [266] A book on Hebrew grammar by David Kimḥi (1160–1235). | [267] For the full text, see Akhiezer. {{em:Historical Consciousness}}, pp. 326–330.

content.english: This excerpt indicates the various stages of elementary education, including the reading of Torah books, their translation into Tatar, and the study of Hebrew grammar according to the medieval {{em:Sefer ha-Mikhlol}} (Book of Splendor) by R. David Kimḥi. This account contains unique evidence of the presence of at least three pupils from the Rabbanite community who studied in this Karaite school in Chufut-Kale. This phenomenon may be an indication of a Rabbanite community that lived in this town or of the absence of a Rabbanite communal elementary school there. In any case, the passage testifies to healthy and strong relations between the two communities.

Another important piece of evidence regarding Karaite education in the Crimea is a manuscript dated 1777, written by Joseph Kusdini of Chufut-Kale, who later wrote {{em:Perush ʿal ʿAsarah ʿIqqarim}} (Commentary on the Ten Principles). His report contains impor- tant data about the advanced stages of “traditional Karaite higher education”; he describes his own studies at the study hall, including its subjects and duration:

I set my intentions and the thoughts of my mind to inscribe the year of my entrance into the study hall of R. Hillel the Sage of the Torah, may his Rock keep and safeguard him, and indeed the year of my entrance into his study hall was the year 5537 from Creation [1777 CE]. I sat in his study hall one-and-a-half years, and subsequently I departed the study hall and entered the study hall of the exalted sage R. Isaac Qalfa,{{fn:268}} may his Rock keep and safeguard him, and I sat in his study hall likewise one-and-a-half years, for a total of three years. In the space of these three years, I read {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}, {{em:Sefer ʿEṣ Ḥayyim}}, {{em:Sefer ha-Moreh}},{{fn:269}} {{em:Sefer ha-Miṣvot}}, and {{em:Sefer ha-ʾAdderet}},{{fn:270}} and I further read in the space of these three years some three hundred books, among them compositions of our scholars both ancient and recent, among them compositions of Rabbanites, may they rest in peace. When I entered the study hall I was eighteen years old, and when I departed I was twenty-one years old. Afterward I joined my father to study the science of medicine [120b].{{fn:271}}
content.comments: [268] Isaac Qalfa was a renowned scholar, {{em:ḥazzan}}, and teacher in Chufut-Kale (his epithet is a Tatar word for “teacher’s assistant”). See his tomb inscription in Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}, no. 533. Qalfa was the author of {{em:Ṣiṣ Nezer ha-Qodesh}} (The Frontlet of the Holy Diadem), a work on the laws of ritual slaughter and the ten principles of faith. His name appears among the signatures on a letter of 1775 sent from Chufut-Kale to Jerusalem, regarding which see Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, p. 458. | [269] Maimonides’s {{em:Moreh Nevukhim}}. | [270] {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}} by Elijah Bashyachi. | [271] The full text is published in Akhiezer. {{em:Historical Consciousness}}, pp. 159–160.

content.english: According to this account, the author attended the study hall starting from the age of seventeen, after the completion of his studies at the elementary school. He began his professional studies after three years in the study hall, during which his father, who was a physician, probably supported him. Students from less wealthy families may have studied and worked concurrently. The range of books used in the study hall clearly evinces a tendency to combine classical Karaite works with Rabbanite literature. Joseph mentions a book by Maimonides, whose works were widespread among the Karaite scholars of Poland–Lithuania and the Crimea.

Another testimony, possibly less than twenty years earlier, is from the aforementioned scholar Simḥah ben Solomon Kusdini about his studies in Chufut-Kale (to which he relocated from Evpatoria). He reports his studies under the famous R. Simḥah Isaac Lutski, who relocated from Lutsk and was appointed by his patron, Mordecai ben Berakhah, to be the head of the local study hall. Simḥah Kusdini mentions that Mordecai ben Berakhah “spent gold currency, and brought books, and consecrated them to the study halls for the sons of poor people.” When he died, Simḥah Isaac Lutski

was supported by Samuel Aga, the loyal minister, who gave more and more to my master… and he [Samuel Aga] also supported all the students, and spent for them much money, and consecrated many books, and built a new building for an additional {{em:bet midrash}} from hewn stones… and appointed there a teacher, and assigned 400 gurush as a fund in order to pay to this teacher, in addition to the students’ stipends. After the death of my master and teacher, the honorable rav Simḥah Isaac… some years later took place an impure outrage against our loyal minister, God will avenge his blood…{{fn:272}}
content.comments: [272] Mann. {{em:Texts and Studies}}, pp. 374–375. The author hints at the murder of Samuel Aga.

content.english: Simḥah Kusdini focuses on establishing and maintaining the educational institutions and on supporting their students, including with generous stipends. As the above excerpt indicates, this support (including subsidizing the teacher, Simḥah Isaac Lutski) was possible only through the personal donations of the two community leaders. This phenomenon was a common practice among the Crimean Karaites. Also typical was the case of Simḥah Babovich, who supported the communities using his own money and, in his will, dedicated part of his wealth for this purpose.

Until the 1860s, when changes gradually emerged in the Karaite educational system, most of its institutions retained their traditional form. Children entered a study hall at the age of six and continued their studies for seven to nine years. Their curriculum was similar to the one described in the aforementioned documents. There were many small study halls; these were opened by teachers, some of whom were important scholars, whereas others could only read and translate the biblical text and had limited knowledge of Karaite texts. Many of these teachers were assisted by their advanced students; however, children graduating after all those years in the study halls often had only poor and superficial knowledge. This problem also existed in the Rabbanite school, which children attended for a shorter period.

We also learn some details about Karaite education from the aforementioned book by Samuel Pigit, who offers autobiographical reminiscences from his childhood in Chufut-Kale, where he was born in 1849. Pigit writes that his grandfather, Moses Koylü (grandson of Simḥah Isaac Lutski), told him that when Moses was young, there were a number of study halls in Chufut-Kale. Pigit adds that the halls were located in every part of the town, the teachers received a salary from the community, and that all the children from poor families attended them to study Tanakh with translation. If there were any gifted children whose parents wanted them to learn Hebrew grammar, Karaite books, and other subjects, they were sent to well-known scholars. Pigit also recalls that for the festival of Purim, the pupils would go from one house to another, and all the people—both rich and poor—would give them as much as they could. The pupils then gave this money to their teachers at the study halls as an annual tuition fee for their teaching, in addition to the fees paid from the community budget.{{fn:273}}
content.comments: [273] This custom was called “a love of Purim.” Pigit. {{em:Epistle}}, p. 10.

content.english: The dozens of study halls spread all over the Crimea during this period were funded by private individuals, both parents and philanthropists, as well as by the communities. There was no central supervision of these schools. We have no exact statistics regarding these study halls, but some partial data provide insights about the conditions and processes of Karaite education during this period. For instance, in 1858, there were two study halls in the Feodosia community, where two teachers, Mordecai Hojash and Moses Kefeli, taught a total of 73 students. This Karaite community had 891 members.{{fn:274}}
content.comments: [274] All data were provided by Hojash in his letter to the {{em:ḥakham}} Babakai Babovich (the brother of Simkhah). See Viacheslav Eliashevich. “Karaite Primary Schools (Midrashi) in Feodosia in the Mid-Nineteenth and Early Twentieth Centuries.” In Viacheslav Eliashevich and Mikhail Kizilov (eds.). {{em:The Karaites of Feodosia: History, Religion, Culture}}. Simferopol–Feodosia: Tavrida, pp. 32–33 (in Russian).

content.english: The full course of Hojash’s curriculum was nine years. The children began at the age of six or seven in the ninth class (which was the first level of study), where they learned to pronounce Hebrew words. In the eighth class, the pupils, aged seven or eight, learned to read. By the age of eight or nine, they joined the seventh class, where they studied the translation of the book of Genesis. At the age of ten, in the sixth class, they translated Leviticus. Aged eleven or twelve, in the fifth and fourth classes, they studied the Prophets. The last three classes were for children between thirteen and fifteen. In the fourth and third classes, they studied the book of Psalms; in the second, they learned Hebrew grammar; and in the first class, they read {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}} and {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}. In addition, the teacher taught them basic arithmetic and writing in Hebrew, which was not typical in traditional study halls. Thirty-one pupils studied there under Mordecai Hojash.

The teacher of the second school in Feodosia, Moses Kefeli, had forty-two pupils and a slightly different curriculum. Studies with him lasted only seven years and began from the seventh and sixth classes, called “Alef Bet,” where reading was taught. The fifth one was dedicated to studying the Tanakh, the fourth to the translation of the book of Genesis, the third to the translation of Exodus, the second to the translation of Deuteronomy, and the first (and last) class to the translation of the book of Psalms. Thus, despite the emphasis on Tanakh reading and translation in the education of these children, the curriculum included other texts in some cases, and the duration of studies varied by teacher. With the emergence of the {{em:Haskalah}} and modernization, an increasing number of differences appeared between the study halls.

The Crimean War (1853–1856), which was fought between the Russian Empire and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, France, Britain, and Sardinia, had a huge impact on the Crimean communities. Due to military actions, the Karaites (like the other populations of the Crimea) had to flee from Evpatoria and Sevastopol to Novorossia or Chufut-Kale. The war not only disrupted the normal course of life but also damaged community structures, including schools, many of which closed during this period.
{{h3:3.1.3 {{em:The Modernization of Karaite Education}}}}

Karaite education underwent initial changes under the influence of Karaite immigrants of Polish origin. These Karaites had main- closer contact with Rabbanite intellectuals and had been more extensively exposed to the new trends of public thought and to the maskilic literature. They felt that traditional Karaite education was in urgent need of modernization. For instance, in a letter to Firko­vich, Mordecai Sultanski expresses his criticisms of problematic aspects of Karaite education in the Crimea that he encountered as a teacher:

You also know that in Poland we are not accustomed to study the {{em:miṣvot}} from {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}} only, but when I arrived here [the Crimea], and started teaching the young children, the greatest Crimean scholars did not imagine that one of these students could study {{em:halakhah}} under my guidance, as they keep telling nonsense about us, such as that we, Polish rabbis, are just poets and garrulous speakers, but the truth is that they themselves don’t understand the texts. And presently a number of students, who are candidates for the title of rabbi, came to study {{em:halakhah}}, and because it appeared that they lacked basic knowledge, I had to send them back to learn basic principles. Similarly, even the best among the children who engage in basic learning with me are not yet ready to study the {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}. My rule is not to let [pupils] jump to the study of the {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}} before they complete the study of [other] appropriate texts.{{fn:275}}
content.comments: [275] Mordecai Sultanski. Correspondence with A. Firkovich. RNL f 946, op. 1, no. 737, 40r.

content.english: Sultanski further reports that one of his students, after studying some chapters of the {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}, left school to start a trade and earn his living. Sultanski adds that such events were frequent among Crimean Karaite students. Beyond the irony evinced by his comments on the intellectual level of “the greatest Crimean scholars,” his criticisms, even if influenced to some extent by personal motives, reflect the problems of traditional Karaite education—the lack of systematized teaching and learning and the limited know­ledge of the teachers. Some of these problems may have also been prevalent in the Eastern European communities, but the Crimean educational institutions were in urgent need of drastic changes to adequately prepare the next generation of teachers and learned leaders. To address this challenge, Sultanski, Yashar Lutski, David Kukizów, and other Karaite intellectuals wrote new books and grammars to make the classical, medieval Karaite texts more understandable.

Firkovich shared Sultanski’s approach and tried to initiate some changes in the Crimean Karaite educational system. Another advocate for change was Babovich, who even published a letter on this issue, which was addressed to the Crimean Karaite communities. In this letter, written in Hebrew and Tatar, he criticizes the local Karaite education and proposes the establishment of a new school in Evpatoria{{fn:276}} that would be modeled on those established by {{em:maskilim}} in Germany and Galicia. Such schools were just beginning to appear in Russia; the first was established in Odessa in 1826 and headed by Rabbanite {{em:maskil}} Bezalel Shtern, who was on friendly terms with Firkovich and other Karaite leaders. These modern schools included in their curriculum a combination of traditional Torah studies and secular subjects, including the language of the state and vocational training. The Russian authorities usually supported these schools as part of their policy of Jewish “productivization” and partial integration into general society. The reforms proposed by Simḥah Babovich, who lived in the Crimea during an early stage of the establishment of Russian rule, were an attempt to comply with this policy and reflect the influence of the {{em:Haskalah}} ideology, apparently resulting from personal contacts with some of its adherents. As previously mentioned, Babovich was familiar with the writings of Moses Men­dels­sohn. In addition, he corresponded with the German Jewish scholar Isaac Mar­kus Jost, and was closely associated with Firkovich, who had extensive connections with important maskilic figures.
content.comments: [276] Simḥah Babovich. {{em:Mesirat Modʿaa}} [Publishing an Advertisment]. Evpatoria, 1836, p. 1r-2v (in Hebrew).

content.english: In his letter concerning Karaite education, Babovich discusses the aims of the new study hall in Evpatoria and its operating principles. He begins by describing the existing problems of this Karaite education: numerous low-level study halls with an inadequate number of teachers who were unable to dedicate enough time to their students, where books were in short supply, and where everyone who could read and had a little knowledge was called “teacher,” even though those who could legitimately be called “teacher” were few. In his own words, the students “entered [a study hall] without anything, and went out without anything.”{{fn:277}} He further reports that many people in the Karaite communities could not even sign their own names.

In his description of a new school model, Babovich suggests gathering all the Karaite students who were dispersed among the existing study halls throughout the Crimea at the new institution, which would be able to accommodate 400 students with a suitable number of teachers. The classes would be categorized according to levels of knowledge, and emphasis would be placed on taking an individual approach to each student. As was typical of Jewish maskilic schools, Babovich presents the main direction of the curriculum without going into detail beyond the study of the Russian and Hebrew languages and other secular sciences and crafts. Babovich also suggests including a library, a printing office, and a special hall for conducting examinations, events and meetings of community leaders, and receptions for officials. He saw the last point as especially important because he hoped for the support of the authorities and even the personal involvement of Czar Nicholas I in this visionary project. Babovich’s proposal, though unrealistic in terms of the potential number of students and teachers, was in line with the official policy of the czar. Despite its attractiveness, for undisclosed reasons (possibly financial ones or the lack of official support), this project was not implemented.

A few decades later, the first modern Karaite school in the Crimea was opened in Chufut-Kale by the Karaite {{em:maskil}} Solomon Beim from Odessa. As previously mentioned, the first modern maskilic Jewish school in Russia had been established in Odessa in 1826 and was headed by Bezalel Shern. Odessa, in the Novorossia Province on the Black Sea, had been designated by the authorities as part of the Pale of Settlement. A cosmopolitan port city with large trade and business opportunities, Odessa had grown rapidly since its foundation in 1794.{{fn:278}} Odessa had become the site of the largest Rabbanite community in the Russian Empire and one of the major centers of the {{em:Haskalah}}. Beginning in the 1880s, it became one of the major centers of Zionism.
content.comments: [278] Steven J. Zipperstein. {{em:The Jews of Odessa: A Cultural History, 1794–1881}}. Stanford: Stanford University Press, 1985.

content.english: The Karaite community had been established in Odessa early in the nineteenth century, and most of its members were wealthy Karaite families of Crimean origin. An interesting testimony about Karaite education in Odessa can be found in {{em:Memoirs and Travels}}, written by the prominent {{em:maskil}} Abraham Ber Gottlober (1811–1899). A writer, Hebrew and Yiddish poet, journalist, historian, and pedagogue from Volhynia, Gottlober lived for some time in Odessa and was on friendly terms with the Karaites there, especially the Beim family. Gottlober later became associated with Firkovich, and published a book on the history of the Karaites, titled {{em:Bikoret le-Toldot ha-Karaim}} (Critique of the Karaite History, 1865). In his {{em:Memoirs,}} Gottlober recalls his visit to the Beim family, who originally came from Chufut-Kale, settled in Bakhchesaray, and later lived in Odessa. Abraham Beim and his son Solomon were the leaders of the Karaite community in Odessa, being the first Karaite {{em:maskilim}} there.{{fn:279}}
content.comments: [279] Abraham Ber Gottlober. {{em:Zikhronot u-masaʿot}} [Memories and Travels]. Jerusalem: Mosad Bialik, vol. 2, pp. 170–172 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Gottlober’s acquaintance with Karaism, which aroused his curiosity, began with his visit to the house of Abraham Beim, who was a {{em:maskil}}, a businessman, and the {{em:ḥazzan}} of the Odessa Karaite community. Gottlober was much impressed by the atmosphere and furnishings in his house and by the garments of the householder—all of which were in Oriental style, reminding him of a Jew of Jerusalem dressed in similar garments whom he had once met in Moldavia. Gottlober recalls:

I became in my eyes as if I had entered one of the palaces of which I had read in the book {{em:One Thousand and One Nights}}. Yet more was added to this dream when the sage R. A. Beim extended his right hand and said, “Peace be upon you!” [“Shalom ʿaleikhem”] in the accent of the Sephardim and the people of the East, and he began speaking with me in Hebrew, and I too answered him in that accent… and I became in my eyes as if I had turned into a different man.{{fn:280}}
content.comments: [280] Gottlober. {{em:Zikhronot u-masaʿot,}} vol. 1, pp. 261–262.

content.english: Like many other {{em:maskilim}}, Gottlober had a somewhat romantic view of the Karaites as a mysterious group with a unique character and history within which might lie the key to returning Judaism to its pre-exilic youth: a life based on the scriptural ideals of the Land of Israel.

Gottlober soon became a friend of the Beim family. Abraham Beim respected him and even consulted with him on some issues, and Gottlober became friends with Beim’s sons, David and Solomon. When writing his aforementioned book on Karaite history, Gottlober made use of Beim’s large Karaite library. Gottlober recalls that one day, as he was sitting in their house, a letter was delivered to Beim from the Karaite community of Istanbul. This letter asked for a proper decision on a certain issue according to the Karaite {{em:halakhah}}. Beim, unsure of how to answer, showed its contents to Gottlober, asking for his advice. Written in Hebrew, the letter told the story of a Rabbanite Jew in Istanbul who had converted to Karaism and married a Karaite woman; then, one day, he decided to return to the Rabbanite faith and divorce his wife. The community leaders in Istanbul were not sure whether the divorce required a Karaite {{em:get}} or a Rabbanite one. Gottlober expressed his opinion that because this person had married the woman according to Karaite law, he could not give her a Rabbanite {{em:get}}, and the divorce had to be performed according to Karaite practice. Beim accepted Gottlober’s view on this case and outlined it in his answer to the Istanbul Karaite community.

David Beim once suggested that Gottlober convert to Karaism to escape the legal restrictions on Rabbanite Jews and, more importantly, to marry David’s sister. However, Gottlober was not prepared for such a conversion. In any case, the maskilic perception of Karaism created fertile ground for friendship and cooperation be-tween {{em:maskilim}} and Karaites. This situation lasted about five decades until the Russian Karaite communities put themselves on the path of de-Judaization.

Gottlober was also on friendly terms with David’s brother (and Abraham Beim’s other son), Solomon (1817?–1867), even dedicating a poem in Hebrew to him.{{fn:281}} Gottlober describes his visit to the Karaite synagogue with Solomon on a Friday afternoon in 1830. According to Gottlober, it was a new, beautiful building that had been erected to replace the old one. The building was divided into two parts—the {{em:ʿazarah}} and the {{em:heikhal}}. The entrance to the {{em:heikhal}} was limited to only those who had purified themselves. Gott­lober, who had never previously visited a Karaite synagogue, was surprised that the congregation members took off their shoes before entering and knelt while praying.{{fn:282}} He reports that their pronunciation was very close to the Sephardic, though they pronounced the {{em:ṣade}} as “ch” and that the Shabbat prayer took place before nightfall to avoid having candles emitting light during Shabbat.
content.comments: [281] Abraham ber Gottlober. {{em:Bikoret le-toldot ha-Kara}}ʾ{{em:im}}. Vilna, 1865 (repr. Jerusalem: Qedem, 1972), p. 207 (in Hebrew). | [282] According to Pigit, who grew up in Chufut-Kale, the Polish Karaites also knelt while praying but did so in a different way. He reports that he saw Firkovich praying while “sitting on his knees as Catholics do, and not as we [the Crimean Karaites] do.” See Pigit. {{em:Epistle}}, p. 15.

content.english: 125On another day, Gottlober was invited to attend an examination at the Karaite school that was located near the same synagogue. A Russian official from the local gymnasium was there to test the Karaite pupils on the Russian language and other secular subjects studied in this school. Gottlober mentions that the school also taught, though to a lesser extent, Tanakh, Hebrew grammar, and the book {{em:ʾAdderet Eliyahu}} on issues of {{em:halakhah}}. Gottlober attended another examination, this one conducted by a Karaite {{em:maskil}} from the Crimea named Ilya Kazaz, who was a graduate of Saint Petersburg University. Kazaz was a poet, a pedagogue, and a member of the Karaite community of Evpatoria. He taught at another Karaite school in Odessa, where traditional Karaite studies were emphasized, although its curriculum also included secular subjects. The official Russian supervisors were present during examinations. Gottlober recalls that during the examination on Tanakh conducted by Kazaz, the children translated the text into Tatar. Although Gott­lober did not understand the language, he appreciated the pupils’ demonstrated level of fluency; he also addressed a few questions to them in Hebrew and Russian, and they answered him in these languages. One of this school’s examinations was also attended by Simḥah Pinsker (1801–1864), a prominent maskilic figure, scholar of Karaism, author of {{em:Liqqutei Qadmoniyot}},{{fn:283}} and friend of Fir­kovich.
content.comments: [283] See note 247.

content.english: Solomon ben Abraham Beim played an important role in the modernization of Karaite education. Beim was a public figure, a disciple of the Karaite scholar Mordecai Sultanski, an independent self-educated scholar, and an author of several articles and books on the Karaites in Russian. A leader of a new generation, he had also received a secular education and was fluent in Russian, French, and German. Beim was appointed {{em:ḥazzan}} of the Chufut-Kale community in 1843. After the death of Simḥah Babovich in 1855, he was appointed chief {{em:ḥakham}} of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory and served in this role for two years. After the death of his father, who was {{em:ḥazzan}} of the Odessa Karaite community, he returned to Odessa to occupy his father’s position from 1861 to 1867.

In 1839, he accompanied Abraham Firkovich in his travels around the Crimea and the Caucasus to help him search for anti­quities. In the mid-1840s, he conducted independent archaeological expeditions. He was a member of the Imperial Archaeological Society and in 1852 submitted a plan to the society for the study of Karaite antiquities in the Crimea. At some point, Beim quarreled with Firkovich, accusing him of stealing from and desecrating the Karaite cemetery of Chufut-Kale after he cut inscription stones from nine tombs and brought them to Saint Petersburg. In an extensive correspondence with Beim and officials, Firkovich tried to justify himself, saying that he took these tombstones by order of the government officials in Saint Petersburg and with the permission of the local authorities, including the police, and the Karaite community. Finally, the local authorities demanded the return of these tombstones to the Chufut-Kale cemetery.{{fn:284}} Interestingly, eight of these tombs’ inscriptions displayed sensationally early dates—anterior to the eighth century CE—and were apparently Firkovich’s forgeries. Following this event, Firkovich’s relations with Beim remained poor. Beim was his competitor in research on Karaite history as well as his challenger for various community positions, including for the leadership of the Spiritual Consistory.

However, despite this rift, Solomon Beim played an important role in popularizing Firkovich’s ideas. Like Firkovich, he was a self-educated historian. Beim’s books, which were written in Russian, {{em:Chufut-Kale and the Karaites}} (1861) and {{em:Memory of Chufut-Kale}} (1862), and his articles, offered a survey of the history of the Crimean Karaites based almost exclusively on the dubious theories advanced by Firkovich. These books had a considerable impact on their Russian readers, who accepted these “sensational discoveries,” allegedly made by Firkovich and beautifully described by Beim, as the last word in science. Although they were written as travel guides with additional (often erroneous), haphazardly compiled ethnographic and historical contents, Beim’s books were in great demand.

Some impressions of Solomon Beim were left by Russian and European travelers who visited Chufut-Kale and found him a polite, hospitable, and learned person with European manners.{{fn:285}} Even the czar, Alexander II, was impressed by Beim’s personality during his visit to Chufut-Kale in 1861. Indeed, two years later, the czar invited Beim and his family to his summer house in Livadia in the Crimea.
content.comments: [285] Mikhail Kizilov. {{em:Karaites through the Travelers’ Eyes: Ethnic History, Traditional Culture, and Everyday Life of the Crimean Karaites According to the Descriptions of the Travelers}}. San Francisco: Al-Qirqisani Center for the Promotion of Karaite Studies, 2003, pp. 79–88.

content.english: In late 1852, Beim founded a Karaite school in Chufut-Kale along the lines of the {{em:Haskalah}}. In addition to the Tanakh and Hebrew, he taught Russian and other secular subjects. During this period, about forty Karaites lived in Chufut-Kale, mostly poor people who could not afford to move to Evpatoria or other cities, and their children attended this school. The number of Beim’s pupils increased during the Crimean War, as Karaite refugees arrived from Evpatoria and Sevastopol. This school existed until 1857, when it was closed due to lack of financial support. In addition, Beim was instrumental in the opening of a Russian school in Chufut-Kale, although the details of this last institution and Beim’s involvement are scant.

The documents reveal the existence of a thoroughly unexpected plan submitted by Beim to the authorities for the restoration, rebuilding, and development of Chufut-Kale; the aim was to enable the Karaite population of the Crimea to gather there. This plan included the establishment of a large study hall and the relocation of the publishing house in Evpatoria—and even of the office of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory. However, the heads of the consistory feared that this plan would destroy communal life in Evpatoria and categorically rejected it, even seeking to convince the authorities that the project was unnecessary and unrealistic.{{fn:286}} As noted above, Firkovich suggested a very similar project to the authorities, and this may have been an additional aspect of the competition between the two men.
content.comments: [286] See Bely. “New Materials,” pp. 661–663.

content.english: We can learn about the tensions between Beim and the older generation of Karaite community leaders and educators from the abovementioned book by Samuel Pigit, who admired Solomon Beim.{{fn:287}} At the age of six, Pigit started attending the study hall of his grandfather, Moses Koylü, who taught him Tanakh with Tatar translation, but Moses Koylü had no command of Hebrew grammar. Pigit recalls that his family came to his grandfather every Shabbat “to kiss his hand” and to receive his blessing—{{em:birkat kohanim}} (the priestly benediction). After the meals, Moses Koylü would teach the Torah to his grandchildren, who were sitting on the floor. Pigit adds that in their study hall, they also sat on the floor. It is unclear whether this study hall had its own building, was part of the synagogue complex, or was simply a gathering of a group of children in the private home of the teacher. Moses Koylü did not allow his grandson to be sent to the school of Solomon Beim, where the children were seated in their classes behind “black tables” and studied Torah, Hebrew, Russian, and some secular subjects.{{fn:288}} Despite the Karaites’ general openness toward secular sciences, Pigit emphasizes that Moses Koylü staunchly objected to teaching children secular matters, especially the Russian language under a Christian teacher, which he regarded as a desecration of the name of God ({{em:ḥillul ha-Shem}}). His grandfather’s discontent turned into personal hostility toward Beim, whom he blamed for infringing on the {{em:miṣvot}}. For instance, once on Yom Kippur, as Beim was leading the synagogue service, a Cossack messenger from the authorities arrived on horseback, entered the synagogue, and handed Beim a sealed letter. Beim stopped the prayer, removed the seal before the eyes of the congregation, and read the missive. He apologized to the public, explaining that this was an imperial order directing him to leave urgently. Beim then asked one of the community members to take his place as prayer leader ({{em:sheliaḥ ṣibbur}}), mounted a horse, and went away with the messenger.{{fn:289}}
content.comments: [287] Pigit. {{em:Epistle}}, pp. 1–18. | [288] Unfortunately, there is no detailed documentation of Beim’s school. | [289] Pigit. Ibid., pp. 2–3.

content.english: In addition to deviations from the commandments, Beim at- tempted to ease the severe Karaite laws but encountered strong opposition among the local community. Some of his legal decisions were unacceptable to the community leaders of the older generation. Pigit testifies that Beim allowed the carrying of necessary objects during Shabbat within the boundaries of Chufut-Kale, justifying it by claiming that there was no public domain ({{em:reshut ha-rabim}}) in this town because there was no longer a non-Jewish population living there. Moses Koylü attacked Beim, asserting that none of the great sages, such as Isaac Kalfa, Isaac ben Solomon (the author of ʾ{{em:Or ha-Levanah}}), or Beim’s teacher Mordecai Sultanski, had ever permitted such a practice.{{fn:290}}
content.comments: [290] Pigit. Ibid., p. 3.

content.english: The conflict had its roots in different approaches to the Karaite laws but also in the fact that the older community leaders deeply resented the figure of Beim, not even forty years old and wearing European dress, who saw himself as a legal decisor despite taking a lax attitude toward the {{em:miṣvot}}, even violating them on Yom Kippur. There was also a further aspect of this conflict. The old leaders had lived in a society in which their authority was based on their status within the community rather than on the extent of their know­ledge. They were not always required to explain the legal basis of their decisions: the claim that previous sages had allowed or forbidden a certain practice was sufficient. However, this way of ruling the community was no longer adequate. A new generation of leaders had emerged whose authority stemmed from their level of general knowledge and degree of integration into the wider society. In this period, the old elites were gradually losing ground to the new ones, and the old guard had no answer to the new challenges of the modern world and could offer no profound traditional know­ledge that would furnish new answers based on Torah studies to the realities of modern life.

Pigit further reports that the elders of the community would gather and talk on a long bench in front of a store. While they sat there, children were not allowed to pass near them: “Any young man who would walk in front of them would be considered an impudent, immoral and impolite individual, let alone the women…[who] walked the long way around… with their faces covered by a scarf…”{{fn:291}} Modernization in this society was still a difficult and painful process.

Pigit mentions that his family sent him to Evpatoria, where he studied Hebrew for two years under the {{em:ḥazzan}} R. Judah Uzun, making use of various books of Hebrew grammar, including {{em:Kelalei Diqduq}} (Rules of Grammar) by the eighteenth-century Venetian R. Simḥah Qalimani. There, he also studied the philosophy of the {{em:Ruaḥ Ḥen}} as well as Maimonides’s treatise on logic, {{em:Milot ha-Higa­yon}}, and, after that, {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}. However, he was compelled to return to Chufut-Kale. From there, he would walk every day to the study hall of the {{em:ḥazzan}} Moses Tipsi in Bakhchesaray. Some twenty other students, mostly from wealthy families, attended this study hall, and Pigit did not have to pay a fee to the teacher. There, in addition to classical Karaite and Rabbanite books on philosophy and grammar, he studied two books by maskilic authors. One was {{em:ʾAggadat Arbaʿ Kosot}} (Legend of Four Glasses){{fn:292}} by the German moderate {{em:maskil}} Solomon Pappenheim—a sample of modern Hebrew literature written in poetic prose that preached reason and morality. The other was {{em:Meliṣat Yeshurun}}—the biblical poetry of Solomon Loewisohn,{{fn:293}} a Hungarian scholar and poet.
content.comments: [292] Published in Berlin, 1790, and often reprinted. | [293] Published in Vienna, 1816.

content.english:
In this period (the 1830s to the 1870s), Crimean communities were trying to maintain their traditional education. In the best study halls, this included Karaite books, Hebrew grammar, and medieval Jewish philosophy. Under the impact of the {{em:Haskalah}}, however, another concept of education developed, which was manifested in two parallel phenomena. One was the emergence of new schools, supported by the authorities, that taught “useful” secular subjects, such as the one established by Beim in Chufut-Kale—the first Karaite maskilic school in the Crimea. The other phenomenon mentioned in Pigit’s book was the spread of maskilic literature in the traditional Karaite study halls. Some teachers who participated in this new trend to one degree or another and read the maskilic literature and journals thought it important to expose their students to the new ideas and presented them with these texts. Unlike Firkovich, Sultanski, or Yashar Lutski, Beim represented a new generation of educators who were much more concerned with integrating their students into general society regarding language and professional activity—a goal impossible to fulfill before the 1860s. Beim’s gener-
ation was in conflict with the older Karaite elites because the younger generation began distancing itself from the traditional and religious way of life. Beim died during a visit to Saint Petersburg, where he had come to deliver models of typical Karaite garments to the Russian Museum of Ethnography, and he was buried in the capital.

97The memoirs of Jacob Duvan from Evpatoria (1842–1902),{{fn:294}} the grandson of Eben Yashar Lutski (see Section 2.8.2), provide a similar picture of the Karaite educational system’s gradual modernization. Duvan began his studies at the study hall of his grandfather, who taught the children of wealthy individuals but also accepted gifted poor children without charging tuition. Eben Yashar’s teaching included Hebrew grammar at a high level and, for advanced students, medieval Jewish works on philosophy. The leaders of the Evpatoria community were concerned that none of the young people would be worthy to succeed this prominent, already aged scholar. Hence, they asked Eben Yashar to stop teaching the children of wealthy families, which was his only source of income, and to focus on potential scholars and teachers, including those from poor families, for whose teaching the community pledged to pay him. He gave his appropriate students the title of “rabbi” and prepared them for the function of ritual slaughterer ({{em:shoḥet}}).
content.comments: [294] Duvan’s autobiography, written in Hebrew, was preserved in the early twentieth century by his descendants, and only short fragments were published in Russian translation. See “Moi detskie i yunosheskie gody. Iz avtobiografii J. Duvana” [My Childhood and Youth, from the Autobiography of J. Duvan]. {{em:KZh}} 7 (1911): 64–71 (in Russian).

content.english: During his first three years of study, Duvan attended the study hall from morning until noon and from two o’clock in the afternoon until evening, as was practiced in most of these institutions. He was taught the common Karaite curriculum, reading and translating the books of the Tanakh under the tutoring of advanced students who assisted his grandfather. He records that during these years, they translated the entire Tanakh in class, one page or one chapter a day, with one of the children reading a verse and the others translating it in turn. Duvan emphasizes that they translated the texts without any knowledge of Hebrew grammar, frequently without understanding their meaning because these texts had not been explained to them.{{fn:295}} In the evening, he repeated each lesson orally in front of Eben Yashar. Later, his grandfather began to teach him grammar, which Duvan initially found very difficult to understand.
content.comments: [295] J. Duvan. “Moi Detskie”: 64.

content.english: In 1853, amid the Crimean War, the inhabitants of Evpatoria had to flee the city. Duvan, who was then eleven years old, relocated with his mother and grandfather to Ekaterinoslav (Dnepropetrovsk, Dnipro) in Novorossia, where there was a newly established Karaite community. Eben Yashar opened a study hall in this city, which was attended by numerous students, including Duvan, but his grandfather died of cholera two years later. Duvan was unable to find another good teacher to succeed his grandfather, even after returning to the ruined city of Evpatoria after the war. Instead, he entered a Russian school and became enthusiastic about the Russian language and arithmetic, later also learning German.

Duvan once visited the study hall of Isaac Sultanski (the son of Mordecai Sultanski), where one of Duvan’s friends attended, and sat down in the back row of the classroom. The teacher asked, “If A = B, and B = D, what can you conclude?” The class remained silent. Duvan stood up and answered, “That A = D.” Sultanski was surprised; he asked Duvan if he could read the Tanakh, and Duvan told him about his studies under his grandfather. Duvan remained in Sultanski’s study hall for a year but then left because Sultanski could not help him deepen his knowledge of Hebrew grammar any further. Duvan’s uncle then suggested that he study with a former student of Eben Yashar, Judah ben Isaac Savuskan, who had relocated, at Duvan’s uncle’s invitation, from Herson to Evpatoria, where he found numerous students. Although Duvan does not provide details about the study hall of R. Judah Savuskan, he praises his knowledge. Savuskan (1832–1900) was a Karaite {{em:maskil}} who published poems of his own and other texts (including a prayer for an uneventful sea journey by Nahmanides) in Hebrew journals, such as {{em:Hameliṣ}}, {{em:Hakarmel}}, and {{em:Hamaggid}}. He also had a good command of Arabic and could read early Karaite treatises in that language. He was on friendly terms with many Rabbanite {{em:maskilim}} and wrote the following in the foreword of the book {{em:Gan ʿEden}}, which he printed in 1866:

Blessed be the God of Israel… who ordered in our days… to remove and take off the envious emblem of jealousy, planted among two houses of Israel—Rabbanites and Karaites… and roused the heart of some scholars of the generation among our Rabbanite brethren to investigate and research the history of the Karaites… And their intention is desirable… And we should not be pinning the blame on them because of their words about us and our religion, which sometimes are not appropriate… [referring to] the Talmud and their sages, and this is nothing but their jealousy of the truth.{{fn:296}}
content.comments: [296] Quoted by Samuel Abraham Poznanski. “Savuskan, Judah ben Isaac.” {{em:Encyclopedia of Bnei Mikraʾ}}.

content.english: Judah Savuskan was a proponent of a rapprochement between Karaites and Rabbanites and lived during a period when this process, although restricted to certain circles in both communities, led to collaboration in research, literary creation, and publishing, along with personal contacts. Savuskan spent the last eight years of his life in Odessa, where he served as a {{em:ḥazzan}} and {{em:melamed}} of the local Karaite community.

By then, Odessa was one of the most important centers of the {{em:Haskalah}}. In 1863, Jacob Duvan also relocated to this city, where he found a position as Hebrew teacher at a school of the Karaite community and developed contacts with maskilic figures. Six years later, he went to live in the capital, Saint Petersburg, where he spent the rest of his life; there, he eventually published a textbook in Russian in 1890 called {{em:The Basics of Karaite Law}}. Such textbooks came to be in demand toward the end of the nineteenth century, when there was a growing number of Karaites who had a very weak background in traditional studies and whose mother tongue was Russian. According to Poznanski, Duvan converted to Christianity following his clash with the Odessa community, members of which accused him of eating non-kosher foods and fired him from his highly paid position. In this period, conversion became a frequent phenomenon among the Karaites, especially the educated Russian-speaking individuals who settled in the main cities of the Russian Empire. However, because no additional details about this unexpected event or Duvan’s motivations have been uncovered, this matter requires further investigation.

Among the Karaite {{em:maskilim,}} the most notable figure was the aforementioned Ilya (Elijah) Kazaz (1832–1912) from the Crimea.{{fn:297}} Kazaz was an example of exceptionally successful Karaite integration into Russian society. He began his education in the study hall of his hometown, Armyansk, where, according to him, there were 60 to 70 pupils attending different classes in a single room who simultaneously read different texts and tried to shout each other down. Kazaz was sent by his parents to Evpatoria, where he studied with Judah Savuskan and others under Eben Yashar Lutski. In addition to his Karaite education, he went on to study secular subjects in Kherson under a Christian priest. Kazaz began writing Hebrew poetry at a young age under the influence of the Rabbanite {{em:maskil}} Yekuthiel Berman,{{fn:298}} who introduced him to contemporary Hebrew literature. Kazaz studied history at the University of Moscow but moved to Saint Petersburg, attending its university and finally completing a degree in the Department of Oriental Studies.
content.comments: [297] Dmitrii Prokhorov. {{em:I. I. Kazaz: The Enlightener of Karaites and Crimean Tatars}}. Simferopol: The Crimean Branch of the Institute of Oriental Studies of Ukraine, 2009 (in Russian). | [298] Yekuthiel Berman was born in Kherson in 1871. He was a pedagogue who disseminated maskilic literature in that city, and he published a number of articles on conscription, blood libels, and other subjects.

content.caption: Ilya Kazaz (middle row on the left) with his family,

content.english: Evpatoria, 1890s

During the 1860s, Kazaz taught Latin and general history at the Russian gymnasium for boys in Simferopol and convinced some Karaite families to enroll their children there. He also taught at the girls’ gymnasium in the same city and made great contributions to the creation of an educational system for the Crimean Tatars, including the establishment of the Tatar pedagogical college. He was a judicial officer, a member of a local archives committee, an inspector of the state educational system, and a member of the municipality of Simferopol. Kazaz was invited on two occasions to official receptions for a visit of the czar to the Crimea and even attended the coronation of Alexander III in Moscow with the chief {{em:ḥakham}} of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory, Samuel Panpulov.

In addition, Kazaz published two collections of Hebrew poetry,{{fn:299}} as well as poems and articles that appeared in the pages of the Hebrew periodicals {{em:Hameliṣ}} and {{em:Reshumot}}{{fn:300}} and in the journal {{em:Karaite Life}} (in Russian).{{fn:301}} He was fluent in Russian, English, German, French, and Turkish and published several books that he translated from European languages. Some of Kazaz’s poems express a longing for Jerusalem and an anticipation of a Jewish national rebirth.{{fn:302}} He established two Karaite journals, {{em:Davul}} and {{em:Tavrida}}, and contributed to a Crimean Tatar periodical, {{em:Terjiman}}, promoting the ideas of the Enlightenment.
content.comments: [299] Ilya Kazaz. {{em:Shirim aḥadim}}. Leipzig, 1857, and {{em:Yeled shaʿashuʿim}}. Odessa, 1910; repr. Ashdod, 2002 (in Hebrew). | [300] Kazaz’s letters were posthumously published in {{em:Reshumot}}; many of his poems remain unpublished. | [301] See, e.g., his Russian article: I. Kazaz. “Obshchie zametki o Kara- imakh” [General Notes on Karaites]. {{em:KZh}} 3–4 (1911): 37–71 (in Russian). In this article, which primarily discusses the religion and leadership of the Karaites, Kazaz advocates for a permissive approach to Karaite ritual observance. | [302] See, e.g., his poem “Kinnor David” (David’s Harp) in Ilya Kazaz. {{em:Yeled shaʿashuʿim}}, pp. 27–28.

content.english: In 1859, Kazaz founded a modern Karaite school in Odessa at his own expense. There, children aged eight and nine were taught arithmetic, geography, the Russian language, history, and writing—all in Russian. They also acquired basic traditional Karaite know­ledge. Kazaz was the first Karaite educator to write modern textbooks for children. His Hebrew language textbook {{em:Le-Regel ha-Yeladim}}{{fn:303}} included a vocabulary of Hebrew words with a Tatar translation and a reading anthology of Hebrew texts. The Tatar translation was replaced in later editions by a Russian one because Russian had gradually become the Karaites’ mother tongue. This textbook became a pedagogical bestseller, remaining in use for more than twenty years.
content.comments: [303] Ilya Kazaz. {{em:Le-regel ha-yeladim}} [For Children]{{em:.}} Evpatoria, 1896. He wrote the textbook in Hebrew and Tatar, and it was later translated into Russian. Kazaz also translated the Karaite prayer book, {{em:Qetoret Tamid}}, into Russian in 1905.

content.english: Intensive efforts by Kazaz and other Karaite community leaders led to the opening of the Alexander III Spiritual College in Evpatoria in 1895 with the official sanction of Czar Alexander III. For years, Kazaz had developed the general concept and curriculum of this institution, discussing these matters with the leadership of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory and with Russian educational authorities. The aim of the college was to produce a new generation of teachers and {{em:ḥazzanim}} with a modern education who could easily integrate into Russian society. This institution was modeled to a large extent after the Russian gymnasiums. Kazaz headed the college and remained in this post until 1908. Its foundation marked a turning point in the life of the Russian Karaites and had a significant impact on the future of new generations.

It should be noted that although the official policy of the Russian Empire toward minorities was to provide them with basic education according to the principles of the European Enlightenment, its strategic goal was “their Russification and merging with Russian people.”{{fn:304}} To achieve that goal, a network of schools designated for national minorities was established under the surveillance of the minister of national enlightenment (from 1866 to 1880, Dmitri Tolstoi); the network’s curriculum included the study of the Russian language and, as a rule, Russian history and literature. Minorities were also encouraged to send their children to these Russian schools. To implement this policy, the authorities used the leaders of minority groups as intermediaries between their people (or communities) and the officials, urging community leaders to promote this policy in exchange for personal benefits and official positions of their own. The Karaite community was no exception to this rule. The opening and operation of the Alexander III Spiritual College was enthusiastically supported by the Karaite Spiritual Consistory and by generous donations of rich community members, including merchants and manufacturers from the Crimea, Vilna, Warsaw, Odessa, Riga, Moscow, Saint Petersburg, and many other places.
content.comments: [304] Dmitri Tolstoy. “Rules on Measures for the Education of Foreigners Living in Russia.” {{em:Astrakhanskii listok}} 113 (30.05.1903) (in Russian). The first general census of 1897 showed that non-Russian peoples constituted more than half of the inhabitants of the empire.

content.english: The seven-year curriculum of the Alexander III Spiritual College included Russian, which was also the language of instruction, a basic course on Russian literature and history, German,{{fn:305}} geography (Russian and general), arithmetic, physics, and practical geometry. These subjects were taught mostly by teachers of Russian origin, using the same textbooks as the Russian state schools and gymnasiums. The traditional subjects included Hebrew grammar, using Kazaz’s textbook {{em:Le-Regel ha-Yeladim}}; Tanakh, including translation; and the Karaite books {{em:Sefer ha-Mivḥar}}, ʾ{{em:Adderet Eliyahu}}, and {{em:Pinnat Yiqrat}} by Isaac ben Solomon of Chufut-Kale.{{fn:306}}
content.comments: [305] There was a discussion about which foreign language should be taught in this study hall. The members of the Spiritual Consistory suggested French, but Kazaz insisted on German, which he apparently saw as the language of {{em:Haskalah}}, in which major research was written on Jewish studies (including Karaite studies). | [306] Prokhorov. {{em:I. I. Kazaz}}, pp. 141, 146–147.

content.english: In Kazaz’s eyes, familiarizing the children with European thought and science was no less important than teaching them the Karaite books. Therefore, he translated certain works on ethics and philosophy into Hebrew for inclusion in the curriculum. Among these was the book {{em:Éléments de Morale}} by Paul Janet (Paris, 1870).{{fn:307}} A professor of philosophy at the Sorbonne, Janet deals with such issues as an individual’s obligation’s to God, family, and society. Kazaz also translated the work of another French philosopher, {{em:La Religion naturelle}} (1856) by Jules François Simon, adapting it for children and giving it the title {{em:The Secrets of the World: On the Existence of God, Providence, and the Immortality of the Soul}}.{{fn:308}} He also translated excerpts of a book{{fn:309}} by the French Catholic scholar of the Bible, Fulcran Grégoire Vigouroux, who at the time was one of the major Catholic defenders of the historicity of the Bible based on archaeological discoveries. In addition, Kazaz wrote a biography of Cicero in Hebrew (published in Odessa, 1908) and dedicated it to the students of the Alexander III Spiritual College.
content.comments: [307] Ilya Kazaz. {{em:Torat ha-ʾadam}} [Ethics]. Warsaw, 1889 (in Hebrew). | [308] Ilya Kazaz. {{em:Kivshono shel ʿolam}} [The Secrets of the World]. Evpatoria, 1899 (in Hebrew). | [309] Fulcran Grégoire Vigouroux. {{em:La Bible et les découvertes modernes en Palestine, en Égypte, et en Assyrie.}} Paris: Berche et Tralin, 1879. See Ilya Kazaz. “ʾEmet me eretṣ: kiṣur sippur ha-ḥakham ha-Ṣorfati Viguru.” {{em:Sifrei ha-Qodesh ve-ha-meṣiʾot ha-ḥadashot asher nimṣeʾu be-ʾEreṣ Yisraʾel, be-ʾereṣ Miṣraim u-be-ʾereṣ Ashshur}}, vol. 1. Odessa, 1909 (in Hebrew).

content.english: Children began their studies at this college from the age of ten, and about twenty pupils from poor families were subsidized by the community. This institution, which existed until the Bolshevik Revolution (closing in 1918), was an important factor in creating a Russian-speaking Karaite educated class that was fully integrated into Russian society. This intellectual stratum had an important impact on the Karaite community, even though no more than sixty alumni were involved.

If we compare the parallel process that took place in the Rabbanite community, where some children attended the state study halls opened by the Russian authorities, we see a number of notable distinctions, especially in the results of this project. The state study halls, opened in Vilna and Zhitomir in 1837 with the aim of fostering a new generation of Jewish leaders, including rabbis and teachers, were similar in their basic principles to the Karaite Alexander III Spiritual College. The aim was to provide a secular education to students who were intended to become mediators between the Jewish community and the authorities, helping the latter implement their policy toward the Jews. The Russian authorities exclusively appointed graduates of these institutions to such positions in the communities.{{fn:310}} Unlike the Karaites, the leaders and the masses of Ashkenazi Jews (especially those belonging to the Hasidic streams) did not voluntarily cooperate with this project. Most families were unwilling to send their children to these institutions because of their extremely limited Torah studies. A handful of poor families opted to do so because it exempted their sons from military service and they received food, clothes, and a small stipend in return. Communities that were compelled to hire the graduates of these institutions did not use their services. In practice, this situation created a double leadership—the official one and the real one. In addition, unlike in the Karaite communities, a network of {{em:yeshiva}} s existed (especially in Lithuania) that offered a high level of Gemara studies and to which all would be accepted. Hence, the state’s effort to supervise Jewish education ultimately failed, with the main reason being that graduates could not develop a career due to legal restrictions preventing Jews from being recruited into governmental services. Although Jews were accepted in Russian schools, most families were unenthusiastic about sending their children to those schools.
content.comments: [310] Verena Dohrn. “The Rabbinical Schools as Institutions of Socialization in Tsarist Russia, 1847–1873.” {{em:Polin}} 14 (2001): 83–104; Yehudah Slutski. “Bet ha-midrash la-rabanim be-Vilnah.” {{em:He-ʿAvar}} 7 (1960): 29–48 (in Hebrew).

content.english: The maskilic system of education, which combined traditional and secular subjects, was more successful from the mid-nineteenth century.{{fn:311}} During the liberal reforms of Alexander II (who reigned from 1855–1881), Jews were also allowed to study in gymnasiums and at universities; however, there was an established numerical limitation on their admittance, and the quota was lower than Jewish demand for such an education.
content.comments: [311] Regarding maskilic Jewish schools, see Mordechai Zalkin. {{em:Modernizing Jewish Education in Nineteenth Century Eastern Europe: The School as the Shrine of the Jewish Enlightenment.}} Leiden–Boston: Brill, 2016.

content.english: {{h4:3.1.3.1 Karaite Women’s Access to Knowledge}}

This period saw drastic transformations in the educational status of Karaite women, who, in the mid-nineteenth century, were still covering their faces with scarves and often did not leave their homes (according to Pigit). The fact that Karaite women began to gain access to formal education, even attending Russian gymnasiums, sparked a revolution with far-reaching consequences for Karaite society.

Russian girls’ gymnasiums first appeared in the 1860s. In Simferopol, where Ilya Kazaz was teaching, his daughters were among the first Karaite pupils of such institutions. One of them, Anna Kazaz, became a teacher herself after graduation and applied to the authorities in 1891 for a permit to open a school for Karaite girls in Simferopol. This school, which opened in 1892, was free of charge, had a three-year curriculum for pupils aged seven to eleven, and was supported by Karaite donations and the city council. Because the school operated under the supervision of the Ministry of National Enlightenment, its curriculum included secular subjects (similar to the Alexander III Spiritual College), such as the Russian language and literature, arithmetic, gymnastics, singing lessons, and needlework (sewing, knitting, and embroidery), to comply with official requirements. Traditional Karaite studies included the basics of the Karaite faith, Tanakh, Karaite holidays, and a short history of the emergence of Karaism—the teaching of ʿAnan ben David and the biographies and ideas of certain Karaite scholars and thinkers.{{fn:312}}
content.comments: [312] For further details on this school, see Prokhorov. {{em:I. I. Kazaz,}} pp. 138–139.

content.english: Owing to the activity of Ilya Kazaz, of the Spiritual Consistory, and of philanthropists of the community, similar Karaite schools for girls were subsequently opened in Evpatoria, Feodosia, and other cities. The school in Evpatoria also accepted girls of non-Karaite origin. In the school of Feodosia, a class was opened for adult Karaite women. In the Crimea, about 200 Karaite girls attended such schools in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a relatively small number given the total Karaite population of about 13,000 in the Russian Empire at that time. Some graduates of these schools became teachers who taught traditional Karaite subjects and secular disciplines. In addition, an unknown number of Karaite girls attended Russian schools.

The education of girls in Karaite schools (and in Rabbanite maskilic ones), as in the general Russian educational system, was conducted in accordance with Enlightenment concepts. The aim, in keeping with the spirit of the time, was to provide basic know­ledge that would enable a woman to hold meaningful conversations with her educated husband and pass on knowledge to her children, thereby encouraging their children to seek a formal education.{{fn:313}} Higher-level studies were still out of reach, and the only profession available to an educated woman was teaching in either a school or in a wealthy family as a private tutor or governess. Nevertheless, the emergence of women’s education in Karaite society was a dramatic innovation that significantly altered women’s social status and the model of relationships in the Karaite family.
content.comments: [313] Shmuel Feiner. “The Modern Jewish Woman: A Test Case in the Relationship between Tradition and the Haskalah.” {{em:Zion}} 58.4 (1993): 453–499 (in Hebrew).

content.english: A new phenomenon in the Karaite population in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was the large number of unmarried men and women.{{fn:314}} This issue was actively discussed in the pages of {{em:Karaite Life}} after the publication of an anonymous article called “The Painful Question,”{{fn:315}} which was signed under the penname “Tatly Jan.” The article points out that the Karaite population was dying out because young Karaite men left the Crimea with no intention of returning, formed relationships, and even begot “illegitimate” children outside the community. Some of these men even converted to Christianity and married Russian women. Another aspect of the problem was how difficult it was for Karaite women to find a suitable match because upper-class women were often forced to consent to marriage arrangements with any available eligible bachelors, be they poor, elderly, or even disreputable individuals attracted by the size of the bride’s dowry. The author claims in his article:
content.comments: [314] Unfortunately, we have no data on this subject. | [315] Tatly Jan. “Bolʹnoi vopros” [A Painful Question]. {{em:Kzh}} 5–6 (1911): 105–107 (in Russian).

content.english: I loudly declare that a Karaite girl is not a sister of mercy, who has to take care of an old and often sick husband during the best period of her heyday! First of all—she is a person, who has a right to her happiness, and second—she buys him at a high, and even at a very high, price! I don’t justify any Karaite who converts to another religion for any reason, but I see myself as an ardent defender of Karaite girls who marry non-Karaites. Possibly you will tell me that I am ultra-feminist. Maybe, but, being weak and almost completely deprived of her basic rights, she [the Karaite woman] needs protection.{{fn:316}}

The next issue of {{em:Karaite Life}} published the reactions of two readers. The first—an anonymous reaction signed A. M.—defines this situation as “a matrimony strike” and asserts that the Karaites have no means to combat this reality. He calls upon them to come to terms with the phenomenon of mixed marriages and argues that it is time to get rid of obsolete Karaite nationalism, which he sees as a manifestation of backwardness.{{fn:317}}
content.comments: [317] A. M. “Chto delalatʹ?” [What Is to Be Done?]. {{em:Kzh}} 7 (1911): 82–86 (in Russian).

content.english: Another reader, who used the pen name “Janyk Jan,” emphasizes an additional factor that prevents educated Karaite men from finding a match in their community.{{fn:318}} Because marriages were still being arranged by the families, especially among the wealthy, young Karaites had no opportunities to meet each other and make the decision to wed by themselves. Parents preferred to marry their daughters to distant relatives, disregarding education, age, or personal traits in the potential groom, as long as the wealth would remain within the family. They did not regard young Karaites who had acquired a university education and become physicians, engineers, or lawyers as suitable matches. Therefore, many of these educated young men, who also preferred more educated women, tended to form relationships outside the community, taking the path of conversion. Of note, all the authors were resigned to the growing prevalence of mixed marriages and even conversion to Christianity.
content.comments: [318] Janyk Jan. “Na bolʹnuyu temu” [On the Painful Question]. {{em:Kzh}} 7 (1911): 86–90 (in Russian).

content.english: {{h2:3.2 Modern Karaite Literature}}
