These dramatic changes in Karaite life, which were fostered by the spread of the Enlightenment movement and the processes of modernization, also found their expression in the emergence of a new kind of literature written in Hebrew and Karaite-Tatar and later in Russian and (in Lithuania and Poland) Polish. A short period of about sixty years—from the late 1850s to the first decades of the twentieth century—saw the publication of numerous newspapers, journals, and literary works, including fiction, poetry, autobiographies, plays, translations from European languages, and historical essays. As previously mentioned, this process was already evident among certain Karaite intellectuals of the transitional period. Firkovich and Judah Savuskan—and later Samuel Pigit—were among the first Karaite authors to publish articles and poems in maskilic Hebrew periodicals. Eben Yashar translated the {{em:Mishlei Musar}} and fables by Ivan Krylov into Tatar. He also translated into Tatar from the Hebrew original a drama by the {{em:maskil}} Joseph ha-Efrati, {{em:Melukhat Shaul}} (The Reign of Saul, published in Vienna in 1794), which is based on the biblical story of the struggle between David and Saul. In addition, Eben Yashar wrote a collection of poems titled {{em:Shoshanim}}.

Ilya Kazaz, while living in Odessa in the early 1860s, was among the founders of a Karaite literary circle. Its participants were young Karaite intellectuals, including the previously mentioned Jacob Duvan; Joseph Erak, a Karaite poet, translator, and author of a tragic play called {{em:Dinah}}; Abraham Michri, who was exceptionally erudite, knew numerous European and Oriental languages, owned a vast library, and was a friend of Pinsker; and a certain Isaac Shamash. Together, they constituted the voice of the Karaite national revival. They referred to themselves as “the black-bearded,” that is, the young, juxtaposing themselves against the old, “white-bearded” traditionalists and emphasizing their opposition to the Karaites’ traditional way of life and to some of their values. They were strongly influenced by the ideas of the {{em:Haskalah}} and by modernization, and they linked the Karaite revival to the notions of enlightenment, broad education, and integration into general society. This mindset was reflected in their periodical, a free, weekly, handwritten journal titled {{em:Davul}} (“drum” in Tatar), written in the Karaite ethnolect of the Crimean Tatar language with Hebrew letters,{{fn:319}} which first appeared in March 1860. These writers published poems, essays, and articles, many of which offered a fierce critique and satire of the backwardness of Karaite society and of the fanaticism and rigidity of the “white-bearded.”
content.comments: [319] Prokhorov. {{em:I. I. Kazaz}}, pp. 173–174.

content.english: Their critique did not go unnoticed by the Karaite religious establishment, and some community leaders, including officials of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory, expressed their indignation at the insolence of these young voices. Some even demanded putting an end to the journal’s publication. Kazaz, who had established a modern Karaite school in Odessa, left that city for Simferopol, possibly because of this confrontation with the establishment. His school was closed and publication of the journal was halted, but it was later revived by other intellectuals in a more moderate form between 1864 and 1872.

Such intergenerational conflict was also typical of Rabbanite society during the {{em:Haskalah}} and frequently manifested itself in even more extreme ways, such as young members of traditional Jewish society (especially in Hasidic communities) being excommunicated for reading maskilic books. One of the most vivid examples of excommunication can be found in the autobiography of the aforementioned {{em:maskil}}, Abraham Gottlober, who grew up and lived in a Hasidic environment. When his passion for maskilic literature became known to his father-in-law, the latter went for advice to his rebbe, who demanded that Gottlober be excommunicated and divorce his wife.{{fn:320}}
content.comments: [320] Gottlober. {{em:Zikhronot u-masaʿot,}} vol. 1, pp. 243–248.

content.english: The confrontation between the young Karaite generation and the older establishment also found expression in new literature, such as the play {{em:Who Is Right?}} written in 1912 by Aaron Katyk.{{fn:321}} This author (1883–1942) was the first {{em:ḥazzan}} to graduate from Alexander III Spiritual College, where he was a student of Kazaz, subsequently becoming a Karaite writer and poet in Karaite-Tatar and Russian, a public figure, and pedagogue who received a degree in philosophy from the University of Odessa. {{em:Who Is Right?}}—published in Russian and translated into the Karaite-Tatar language—presents conflict between generations as unresolvable. The protagonist, a young Crimean Karaite named Shalom, lives with his parents and two sisters. Seeking to become a student at the university, he makes the appropriate preparations for admission there with the support of a friendly student. Shalom fiercely criticizes the existing Karaite establishment, including specific individuals among the community leaders who employ his father as a {{em:ḥazzan}}. He maintains that the Karaites are in a state of ignorance and spiritual and moral decline, and he dreams of their national revival. In addition, Shalom gathers around him a group of young people to whom he sets forth his views. He suggests implementing reforms in the traditional study halls that would enable educating a new generation of preachers, {{em:ḥazzan}} s, and teachers, along with knowledgeable laymen. He also writes literary works that criticize contemporary Karaite society.
content.comments: [321] Aaron Katyk. {{em:Kto prav? Drama iz karaimskoi zhizni v III deistviyakh}} [Who Is Right? A Drama from Karaite Life in Three Acts]. Feodosia, 1913.

content.english: 95Shalom claims that the Karaite national revival must also include a change in the status of women and their education. The women in the play are presented as miserable and even tragic. The main goal in the life of Shalom’s illiterate mother is to cook well so as to placate her husband, and her world is restricted to addressing the material needs of her family. In a conversation with his older sister Leah (Liolya), who is barely able to read and write, Shalom tries to convince her of the need to struggle for change because the present state of women, in his eyes, is an “abuse of living souls:”

Remember our sister, the late Sarah. Our parents married her, without her consent, to a scoundrel, whom she had never seen before. And then what? This tuberculous drunkard ruined our beautiful sister… and know, Liolya, that this will also happen to you. In less than a year, the matchmaker will come to us with a bridegroom who will bargain for your soul and body, as for buying a horse. He will marry you and will torment your body with his trembling hands of a vulgar drunkard. But if you only even give a hint of divorcing, the parents will answer you…“Be patient, daughter, be patient!”{{fn:322}}
content.comments: [322] Katyk. {{em:Who Is Right?}} p. 36.

content.english: Shalom’s father, Azariah, the respectable {{em:ḥazzan}}, wants his son to become a rabbi. He is certain that Shalom should not study at the university and seeks ways to make Shalom abandon that idea. He asks Siyaka (Isaac), a {{em:shamash}}, to spy on his son. Siyaka finds Shalom’s composition in his room, which is a comedy that satirizes and ridicules traditional Karaite society. Azariah decides to throw these pages into the fire; although his wife begs him not to burn the pages on which their son has worked for so long, her words mean nothing to Azariah. This deed intensifies the conflict between son and father, which reaches its peak when guests—members and leaders of the community—come to Azariah’s home. This evening gathering ends with Shalom castigating the guests (who have gotten drunk and want Shalom to sing for them) and denouncing the plagues of their generation in prophetic style. As a result, his father is fired from his post as {{em:ḥazzan}}, and the family is reduced to poverty and must sell most of their furniture. Shalom, the maximalist, sees no other solution than suicide and shoots himself.

The plot and dialogues of this play are neither sophisticated nor distinguished by depth of thought. However, the composition is full of details of everyday Karaite life. It depicts contemporary Karaite society with its real crises and conflicts, and the characters are typical of that society. In addition to the figure of Shalom, the idealist and maximalist, there are figures representative of the older generation, such as his father and other community members who try to maintain tradition in its superficial form: they observe the {{em:miṣvot}} but misunderstand the true principles of their faith.

The synagogue {{em:shamash}}, Siyaka, also belongs to the older generation but represents another type of traditional Karaite; he is merely a pawn in this traditional system that depersonalizes him, depriving him of moral constraints in his struggle to survive. Siyaka says to Shalom,

Don’t think that I am not satisfied with the community… Actually, what is a {{em:shamash}}? I will tell you: a {{em:shamash}} is—with your pardon for the expression—a person to whom God gave ears but not to hear, eyes but not to see, and a tongue to keep on hold. A {{em:shamash}} is… a slave of the society. The most miserable person on earth.{{fn:323}}

After Azariah loses his position as {{em:ḥazzan}}, Siyaka mocks him, reminding him of all the abuses, insults, and humiliations he has undergone, trying to wound his pride and hurt his feelings as much as possible.

Another character in this play—Simḥah, one of Azariah’s guests who comes without an invitation—is a person devoid of any values, an utmost cynic and hedonist. Only two characters accept Shalom’s criticism and his views: his sister, Leah, and their uncle, Samuel. However, both are unable to take action. Leah is not prepared to stand up to her father, believing in compromise, whereas uncle Samuel thinks it is not the time for struggle and that Shalom’s criticisms are not helpful, only endangering him and his family. Shalom, however, sees this struggle as the only solution. His father embodies all the principles to which he is staunchly opposed, and Shalom finds value in the very nature of the struggle as a tool for progress and social change. This play was strongly influenced by Hebrew maskilic literature{{fn:324}} and nineteenth-century Russian literature, including works by Alexander Griboedov, Mikhail Lermontov, and Ivan Turgenev.
content.comments: [324] See, for instance, Reuben Asher Braudes. {{em:Ha-dat ve-ha-ḥayyim}} [Religion and Life]. Jerusalem: Mosad Bialik, 1974 (in Hebrew).

content.english: {{h2:3.3 The Transformation of Identity among the Russian Karaites}}

By the beginning of the twentieth century, notable transformations had occurred in Karaite self-identification in Eastern Europe and the Crimea, as they now sought to detach themselves from Judaism. These changes found expression in various spheres, including the use of languages and terms, way of life, education, and attitudes toward tradition. The Karaites used the Hebrew language less and less, preferring to write in Karaite-Tatar or Russian—a phenomenon that also affected Karaite periodicals. During the early decades of the twentieth century, Karaites published journals that promoted integration into general society and discussed current events in the lives of the Karaites of Lithuania, Poland, and the Crimea. The most important of these were {{em:Karaite Life}} ({{em:Karaimskaya zhiznʹ}}), a Russian-language periodical published in Moscow in 1911 and 1912; {{em:Karaite Word}} ({{em:Karaimskoye slovo}}), also published in Russian in Vilna in 1913 and 1914; {{em:News of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory}} ({{em:Izvesiya karaimskogo dukhovnogo pravleniya}}), published in Russian from 1917 to 1919; and {{em:Karaite Thought}} ({{em:Myśl karaimska}}), published in Polish from 1924 to 1939.{{fn:325}} The Hebrew language was dismissed in the late nineteenth and the twentieth centuries as “the language of the Old Testament” or “the biblical language.” A significant proportion of the works published in Hebrew during this time consisted of adapted Karaite folktales and poetry in liturgical style written in honor of the czars. Original texts were no longer written in Hebrew; the use of this language was now confined to prayer.
content.comments: [325] A new series was published in 1945–1949.

content.english: These changes were also demonstrated by the terminology introduced in communal and religious life. The Karaite leaders submitted a request to the authorities to make their official appellation “The Russian Karaites of the Old Testament Faith.” Another request, submitted in 1911 by the {{em:ḥakham}} of the Karaite Spiritual Consistory, Samuel Panpulov, to the minister of internal affairs was that official documents should use the Karaite word {{em:kenassa}} (also from a Semitic root) instead of “synagogue” to distinguish the Karaites from the Jews.{{fn:326}}
content.comments: [326] Mikhail Kizilov. {{em:The Sons of Scripture: The Karaites in Poland and Lithuania in the Twentieth Century.}} Berlin: De Gruyter, 2015, pp. 96–100.

content.english: In the early twentieth century, a profound identity crisis among the young generation of Russian Karaites resulted in mass abandonment of religious observance. This identity crisis was explicated by David Kukizów, one of the descendants of the scholar Mordecai ben Nisan (author of {{em:Dod Mordecai}}), in an article titled “National Consciousness.” Kukizów suggests several possible solutions, although he obviously had only a superficial understanding of the problem and of the basic concepts of Judaism. For instance, he argues that the Jewish people had never developed a notion of national identity due to the rigidity of their age-old religious system, having produced instead the distorted idea of being a “chosen people.” According to Kukizów, this notion, which reflected a disdain for other nations, resulted in the Jews’ backwardness and lack of scientific and artistic development. This claim was very similar to the Christian view commonly expressed in polemics against Judaism, although the traditional concept of a “chosen people” in Karaite and Rabbanite Judaism differed completely. Kukizów further states that this concept, combined with a lack of basic education among the Jewish people, had prevented the Karaites’ intellectual development, which is critical in promoting a national consciousness. He asserts that a key instrument for constructing national consciousness was integration into broader society through education in secular subjects and the Russian language, which ought to be common to all Karaites in the empire, along with the training of professional teachers and an improvement of the education provided in Karaite schools, including Hebrew instruction. Kukizów adds that debates and symposia concerning national consciousness, with participants from all the Karaite communities in the world, were also essential to the Karaites’ national revival. However, most of his suggestions did not diverge from existing practices, while a lack of motivation prevented any change in the study of the Hebrew language and Karaite tradition, which had been reduced to a minimum in this period.

This position, which was shared by Kukizów, Kazaz, and many others, was essentially a late maskilic notion (in its more radical form) of a synthesis between general culture and values and certain elements of the Karaite national heritage, freed from its religious confines. However, in Kukizów’s view, Karaite schools, including the official Alexander III Spiritual College, which practiced this approach, were failing to fulfill their national mission. The number of students in Karaite educational institutions decreased from one year to the next. Parents saw no need for their children to study religious subjects and preferred to register them in Russian schools.

The stance of the Karaite communal leaders was far from consistent, advocating for the development of a Karaite national idea yet failing to provide a univocal definition of this concept. As these leaders urged Karaite society to discard the Jewish content of its heritage, the concept of national consciousness gradually ceased to have any meaning. For this reason, the actions of the Karaite {{em:maskilim}}, while opposing their coreligionists’ assimilation into Russian society, in practice accelerated this process. Even if, outwardly, the path of Karaite assimilation ran parallel to that of Rabbanite Jews (albeit on a much larger scale), there were also fundamental differences. Assimilation put the very existence of Karaite communities in significant danger for a number of reasons. Among these were the integration of the communities into Russian society following their emancipation, the small size of Karaite communities, and the fact that they strove to distance themselves from Judaism without having any cultural or religious alternative.

In the 1870s, two articles by anonymous Karaite authors were published in the Russian press. These articles openly advocated the Karaites’ abandonment of the observance of certain religious commandments strongly identified with “Rabbanism.” One of these articles, which appeared in the newspaper {{em:Novorossiyskie Vedomosti}} (The Novorossia Bulletin),{{fn:327}} called on Karaites to cancel the celebration of the Purim festival because it had significance only for Jews. Another article in the same periodical, in addition to providing arguments for the Karaites’ descent from the Khazars, called on them to cease observing the Sabbath, Jewish festivals, dietary restrictions or those related to ritual purity, as well as other practices seen as purely “Rabbanite.” This article urged Karaites to renounce not only the Hebrew language but also the “antiquated Tatar dialect” in favor of the exclusive use of Russian.{{fn:328}} This assimilative agenda accorded with the prescriptions of the radical Rabbanite {{em:maskilim}}. In the Karaite version of the late {{em:Haskalah}}, this agenda included disengagement from Judaism, which was deemed a religion having nothing to do with the Karaites. In the early twentieth century, the attitude of the Karaite majority was characterized by a dichotomy whereby anything identified with the Jewish tradition was viewed as specifically Rabbanite, whereas Karaism became an amorphous ethnocultural concept that combined elements from the Khazars, the Turkic peoples, and the lost tribes.
content.comments: [327] S. I. “Neskolʹ slov o karaimakh” [A Few Words about Karaites]. {{em:Novorossiiskie vedomosti}} 37 (1870) (in Russian). Quoted in Mikhail Kizilov. “Social Adaptation and Manipulation of Self-Identity: Karaites in Eastern Europe in Modern Times.” In Dan Shapira and Daniel Lasker (eds.). {{em:Eastern European Karaites in the Last Generations}}. Jerusalem: Ben Zvi Institute, 2011, p. 143. | [328] S. I. “Koe-cho o karaimakh” [Something about Karaites]. {{em:Novorossiiskie vedomosti}} 65–66 (1870) (in Russian).

content.english: The narrative that the Karaites originated in the Kazars{{fn:329}} became, and remains, popular among Crimean and Eastern European Karaites. As already noted, Mordecai Sultanski was the first to try to link Karaites and Khazars. Abraham Firkovich developed this idea and buttressed it using bogus manuscripts and burial inscriptions. Moreover, he hinted at anthropological distinctions between Karaites and Rabbanites:
content.comments: [329] See note 1, above.

content.english: There are distinct physical features in the shape of [the Karaites’] faces as well as special moral traits which are dissimilar from those of their brethren the Rabbanites, to such an extent that the scholar and writer Grigoriev in his book on religious sects has therefore opined that they are not of Israelite origin, or that they had intermingled for a long time with other peoples, although he did not know or see that they do not even resemble their Karaite brethren from Istanbul, Jerusalem, and Egypt.{{fn:330}}
content.comments: [330] Firkovich.{{em:ʾAvnei Zikkaron}}. “Introduction,” p. 7.

content.english: Solomon Beim succeeded in popularizing the idea of an intermingling between Karaites and Khazars, among both Karaite and Russian readers. Beim developed Firkovich’s ideas, such as in his book, {{em:Memory of Chufut-Kale}}, which gave a prominent place to the Khazar hypothesis:

Here [i.e., in the Crimea] the Khazars established a synagogue with the assistance of the Jews living in the area… and they took upon themselves the yoke of the pure faith under the leadership of the sage Isaac Sangari… From the close and lengthy association between these Jews, the Karaites, and the Khazars, the Karaites acquired their language and many of the names of the women among them. Furthermore, they preserved many of the customs of the peoples that ruled the Crimea.{{fn:331}}
content.comments: [331] Solomon Beim. {{em:Pamiat$’$ o Chufut-Qaleh}} [Memory of Chufut-Kale]. Saint Petersburg, 1862, p. 26 (in Russian).

content.english: This claim about the connections between Khazars and Karaites, accompanied by “sensational discoveries” of manuscripts, was intensively propagated by Karaite leaders, especially Firkovich, and found its way into Russian (and later Polish) historical research. For instance, the Russian Orientalist Vasily Grigoriev, who had previously described the alleged negative character traits of the Jews, began contrasting the Karaites with the Rabbanites in terms of faith, character, and lifestyle and also wrote about the origins of the Karaites. According to him, “they were not Jews, but descendants of the Turkic Khazars who were known to have behaved according to the Mosaic Law and ruled the Crimea in the eighth to eleventh centuries CE.”{{fn:332}} As they had done previously, Firkovich quoted Grigoriev, and Grigoriev, in turn, quoted Firkovich.
content.comments: [332] Vasilii Grigoriev. {{em:Rossia i Azia}} [Russia and Asia]. Saint Petersburg, 1876, p. 435 (in Russian).

content.english: Another Russian scholar, Vasily Smirnov (1846–1922), a historian and Turkologist, propounded his views about the non-Jewish origins of the Karaites. He asserts that they bore only a superficial resemblance to the Jews and were distinguished from them by speaking a Turkic dialect. It is difficult to believe that Smirnov, an expert in the history of the Crimea, was unaware of the existence of Rabbanite Jews (Krymchaks) who spoke this same dialect. Interestingly, he argues that the Karaites’ adoption of the local Turkic languages or, in other lands, of the language of the ruling people—Greek, Turkish, or Arabic—was a reflection of their placid character and their ability to live in peace with their neighbors.{{fn:333}} He does not make any reference to the existence of a similar phenomenon among Rabbanite Jews. Concerning the connection between the Karaites and the Khazars, Smirnov writes:
content.comments: [333] Vasilii Smirnov. Introduction. In Zarah Firkovich. {{em:Sbornik starinnykh gramot i uzakonenii kasatelʹno prav i uzakonenii russko-poddannykh karaimov}} [Collection of Ancient Charters and Laws Regarding the Rights and Conditions of Russian-Citizen Karaites]. Saint Petersburg, 1890, pp. x–xi (in Russian).

content.english: It may be assumed that the Karaites of today are simply the remnant of the farraginous people that would have been produced by the intermixing of the biblical Karaites with the Khazars. When they taught the Khazars the precepts of their religion, the Karaites had in turn adopted the Turkish language, and in the wake of such religious and linguistic consolidation they had also assimilated ethnographically among those who adopted their religion and who exceeded them in number and in political power.{{fn:334}}
content.comments: [334] Ibid., p. xii.

content.english: We find in this passage Sultanski’s and Firkovich’s claim about the conversion of Khazars by Karaites. In turn, Smirnov’s work was later used by the Karaites as an authoritative source corroborating their contentions.

The interest taken by Firkovich and other Karaite authors in the Khazars in the context of Karaite history resulted from the rise of the Khazars as a subject of Russian scholarship. This inspired Karaite leaders to develop the notion of a connection between the two groups, fostering the aforementioned story about Sangari as a Karaite hero who played a key role in the conversion of the Khazars. The Khazar hypothesis found a new cohort of proponents among Karaites in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Although Karaite society increasingly abandoned its Jewish prac- tices and spurned its Jewish roots, Ilya Kazaz, who had a university degree in Oriental studies, initially rejected this novel ahistorical narrative about the antiquity of the Karaites and their Turkic origins. Kazaz expresses some reservations about this theory in his article published in {{em:Karaite Life}}. He writes that there was an alternative theory to the one identifying the Khazars as the forebears of the Karaites and asserts that although the theory of kinship between the Karaites and the Khazars was intended to prove that the Karaites had emerged not from a Semitic origin but from a Turkish one, this view had not been scientifically validated. Kazaz adds that the presence of priests ({{em:kohanim}}) and Levites among the Karaites, in addition to the lack of any Karaite traditional narrative claiming descent from the Khazars, was in fact indicative of their Semitic origin. Still, although Kazaz himself casts doubt on the scientific validity of this theory, in this same article, he offers a theory of his own:

There is a more plausible explanation… The Karaites were in perpetual contact with these Judaizing Khazars and formed marital alliances with them that could not but have affected their physical characteristics… On the basis of the foregoing, it may be concluded only that the Karaites are not pure Semites, but their identification with the Khazars is quite a bold conjecture.{{fn:335}}
content.comments: [335] Ilya Kazaz. “General Notes on Karaites.” {{em:KZh}} 3–4 (1911): 48 (in Russian).

content.english: Kazaz was clearly in search of a way to bridge the gap between historical facts and the new concept foisted by their leaders on the Karaite community in the Russian Empire. Being a steadfast {{em:maskil}}, he looked for the most logical and least ahistorical explanation. He ultimately came to terms with and accepted, at least in part, following the trend of other Karaite leaders who promoted “the scientific nature” of this theory.{{fn:336}} Eventually, Kazaz decided to adopt this theory, even becoming one of its outspoken advocates. The example of Kazaz demonstrates how difficult it was in Karaite society to oppose an outlook whose goal was separation from Judaism. The doubters who expressed their uneasiness with this hypothesis were apparently a minority. In the late nineteenth century, Karaite authors produced a number of books and articles in which the Khazar theory appeared in its various stages of development.
content.comments: [336] See Maxim Zaveriayev. “Hashpaʿat ha-modernizaṣyah ʿal todaʿtam ha-etnit shel Qaraʾei Mizraḥ Eropah.” In Yosef Algamil (ed). {{em:Ha-Yehudim ha-Qaraʾim be-Mizraḥ Eropah be-}}ʿ{{em:avar uve-hoveh}}, pp. 53–73. Ramle: Mekhon Tifʾeret Yosef le-Ḥeqer ha-Yahadut ha-Qaraʾit, 2001, p. 64 (in Hebrew).

content.english: In 1896, Judah Kukizów (1840–1917), the son of the aforementioned David Kukizów, a Karaite expert in calendrical issues, wrote {{em:The Karaites: A Short Historical Survey}},{{fn:337}} an essay published in Russian. Judah Kukizów approved of Firkovich’s ideas and tried to buttress his arguments about the ancient Crimean origins of the Karaites. Kukizów relied on tombstone inscriptions and colophons forged by Firkovich and provides a lengthy discussion of Khazar history, quoting, among other things, a colophon produced by Firko- vich{{fn:338}} that contained the words “and the Khazar community further bestowed [on the Karaites] a large pot for cooking food.” Like Firkovich, Kukizów stresses that the historical origins of the Russian Karaites differed from those of other Karaite communities.{{fn:339}} In his chapter on Karaite literature, Kukizów includes a list of the Karaite sages (twenty-four names), which was reminiscent of the chain of tradition in premodern Karaite works; the last name was that of Abraham Firkovich.{{fn:340}}
content.comments: [337] Judah Kukizów. {{em:Karaimy: kratkii istoricheskii ocherk}} [The Karaites: A Short Historical Survey]. Saint Petersburg, 1900 (in Russian). | [338] Ibid., p. 14. | [339] Ibid., p. 28. | [340] Ibid., pp. 29–33. He also published an apologia for Firkovich’s work: Judah Kukizów. “V zashchitu pamiati A. Firkovicha [In Defense of A. Firkovich’s Memory].” {{em:KZh}} 7 (1911): 52–62 (in Russian).

content.english: Other Karaite works of this period are written in a similar style and, in some cases, copy passages from each other. Far removed from scientific scholarship, they are based on studies by the Russian historians discussed above and on Firkovich’s arguments. Ananiasz Zajączkowski (1903–1970), a Polish Karaite scholar of Turkic languages, asserts that the Karaites had indeed converted the Khazars and were their cultural successors{{fn:341}} but did not argue explicitly that the Karaites were descendants of the Khazars and Turkic tribes.
content.comments: [341] Ananiasz Zajączkowski. {{em:Karaims in Poland: History, Language, Folklore, Science.}} Warsaw: Panstwowe Wydawnictwo Naukowe, 1961, pp. 20–23.

content.english: The image of the Khazar kingdom as a mighty, just, and mysterious power, which was enticing to the imagination, was a source of excitement among nineteenth-century Russian scholars. At the same time, it offered the Karaites an opportunity to renounce their Jewish-Semitic roots in favor of Turkic-Khazar ones, while providing an explanation for their biblical faith and fostering a distinction between their religious identity and their ethnicity. The Karaite leaders also sought to prove that their community had deep historical roots in the region, being an indigenous people of the present Russian Empire. In addition, the notion that a large and powerful kingdom had converted to the Karaite faith bolstered the truthfulness of Karaism.

One of the most passionate advocates of the Khazar theory was the Crimean Karaite Seraya Szapszał/Shapshal (1873–1961), a diplomat, Orientalist, and graduate of Saint Petersburg University who turned this theory into the “official” Karaite line.{{fn:342}} Szapszał was the personal tutor of the Iranian crown prince, Muḥammad Ali Shah, having been sent to Persia by the Russian government as a spy. Following the prince’s coronation, he was elevated to the position of vizier, earning the nickname “Bloody Szapszał” for his violent crushing of the Persian Constitutional Revolution. He was later expelled from the country on suspicion of espionage, and in 1915, following his return to Russia, he was chosen as {{em:ḥakham}} of the Crimean Karaites, despite his meager traditional education and the widespread opposition of the community. In 1928, he became the {{em:ḥakham}} of the Karaites of Poland.
content.comments: [342] Kizilov. {{em:The Sons of Scripture}}, pp. 216–293; Dan Shapira. “A Jewish Pan-Turkist: Seraya Szapszał (Şapşaloğlu) and His Book Qırım Qaray Türkleri (1928).” {{em:Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae}} 58.4 (2005): 349–380.

content.english: In 1896, Szapszał published {{em:The Karaites and Chufut-Kale in the Crimea}},{{fn:343}} a Russian-language book based largely on the works of Grigoriev, Smirnov, and Firkovich. His principal thesis was that the lineage of the Karaites of the Crimea and Eastern Europe was Turkic, primarily Khazar. Szapszał developed the thesis of the Karaites’ Turkic and thoroughly non-Judaic identity, making alterations in the terms and practices related to the Karaite tradition and communal life. He used symbols, concepts, and customs of his own invention to highlight the Karaites’ affinity with the Turkic peoples. For instance, he substituted the word {{em:gaḥan}}, with its similarity to {{em:khan}}, for {{em:ḥakham}}, and contrived a coronation ritual for the {{em:gaḥan}} in the form of a Khazar ceremony. Szapszał replaced the Star of David on the gate of the Troki synagogue with a Tatar {{em:tamgas}}.{{fn:344}} He also gave Turkic names to the Karaite holidays, reflecting his contention that Karaism was a distinct religion that, like Christianity and Islam, had also emerged from Judaism.
content.comments: [343] Seraya Szapszał. {{em:Karaimy i Chufut-Qaleh v Krymu}} [Karaites and Chufut-Kale in the Crimea]. Saint Petersburg, 1896; repr. Simferopol, 1993, 1995 (in Russian). | [344] {{em:Tamga}}—a type of tribal emblem common among Turkic peoples that was transmitted from one generation to the next and served, {{em:inter alia}}, for marking tribal property, such as livestock, weapons, and rugs.

content.english: In Szapszał’s eyes, Karaism was the offshoot of the early Christianity practiced by Jesus in the time of his clashes with the Pharisees. He claims that the Karaites had accepted Jesus and Muḥammad as prophets, but their own religion was a thousand years old and distinct from all others.{{fn:345}} To support this argument, Szapszał draws on the words of the contemporary Russian Orthodox clergy, such as those of the Metropolitan Seraphim: “The Karaite faith, in the estimation of the Russian Orthodox Church, is indeed an independent religion.”{{fn:346}} Szapszał continues, “The will to view the Karaites of the Crimea as Jews,{{fn:347}} simply because their faith evolved among the Children of Israel, is bewildering. It follows from this analogy that the Christians also ought to be viewed as Jews, and all Muslims ought to be viewed as Arabs.”{{fn:348}}
content.comments: [345] Szapszał. {{em:Karaites and Chufut-Kale}}, pp. 30–31. | [346] Ibid., p. 31. | [347] From the beginning of the twentieth century, the word “Jew” was used in Russian-language Karaite literature as a contrast to “Karaite.” | [348] Szapszał. {{em:Karaites and Chufut-Kale}}, p. 32.

content.english: According to Szapszał, the survival of pagan beliefs and practices among the Karaites was proof of their affinity with the Turkic peoples and their lack of connection to Rabbanite Jewry. He argues that the Karaites had preserved the memory of an ancient mythology that demonstrated their belief in two gods: the good god, Ulug Ata, believed to bring peace, rain, and produce; and the evil god, Kargal Ata, deemed responsible for disease, famine, and various disasters. Szapszał also mentions the “sacred” oaks (which he calls {{em:Balta Tiimez}}, literally, “the ax shall not touch”) in the Karaite cemetery of Chufut-Kale. According to Szapszał, during the period when there was an active Karaite community in this city, when famine struck, the faithful would come to these oaks with the Tanakh in hand to pray for rain.{{fn:349}} There is no known evidence of this practice, though it was ardently accepted by the generations of Karaite theorists that succeeded Szapszał. He stresses these customs as proof of the Karaites’ historical link with the Khazars and Chuvashes.{{fn:350}} He also offers racial arguments for the Karaites’ ostensible Turkic origins, contending that there was no visual resemblance between Rabbanite Jews and Karaites.{{fn:351}}
content.comments: [349] Ibid., p. 33. | [350] The Chuvashes, a Turkic people in the Volga Upland, speak a unique Turkic language similar to ancient Bulgarian-Turkish, possibly one that is the language of the Khazars. | [351] Ibid., p. 10.

content.english: Szapszał almost totally “Turkified” the Eastern European Karaites in the span of the twentieth century. The model of Karaite nationalism that he conceived was apparently inspired by the pan-Turkism of Kemal Atatürk (ruled 1923–1938). While in Istanbul from 1919 to 1928, Szapszał witnessed the accelerated reforms underway in Turkey, aimed at creating a secular model of nationalism to mold a new Turkish identity based on the history of the various Turkic peoples but without the Islamic religion or the Arabic language while including European practices and values. Atatürk led reforms in the area of language, abolishing the Arabic alphabet as well as Arabic and Persian words, and decreed that the prayers and the Qurʾan be recited in Turkish. This model appears to have been Szapszał’s primary, or even exclusive, source of inspiration.{{fn:352}} He labored to turn the Karaites into part of the great pan-Turkic nation, emphasizing the heritage of the Khazars and devising Karaite practices, ostensibly of Khazar origin, and an allegedly ancient Karaite ethos.{{fn:353}}
content.comments: [352] Shapira. “A Jewish Pan-Turkist.” | [353] Kizilov. {{em:The Sons of Scripture,}} pp. 245–250.

content.english: It is worth stressing that the evidence offered for these Turkic origins and the emphasis on alleged racial differences between Karaites and Rabbanites (e.g., skull size, width of face, shape of eyes, and character) were entirely in line with prevailing thought during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Physical anthropology was a popular pursuit throughout Europe and Russia. For the Karaites, anthropology offered “scientific evidence” of their difference from the Jews. {{em:Karaite Life}} and other periodicals published many articles with anthropological “information” on the differences between the two groups. For instance, in 1911, {{em:Karaite Life}} ran an editorial endorsing the origins of the Crimean Karaites as proposed by Firkovich, which was based on the assumption that they were descended from the captives taken from Samaria by Shalmaneser in 722 BCE, while asserting that they were the last of the Khazars. As proof of this ahistorical claim, the authors provided evidence from the field of physical anthropology.{{fn:354}} Each scholar developed the idea in his own way, with the addition of various conflicting perspectives and narratives.
content.comments: [354] Editors. “Antropologia Karaimov” [The Karaite Anthropology]. {{em:KZh}} 1 (1911): 2–29 (in Russian).

content.english: The Khazar narrative persisted in the Soviet period. In its entry on the Karaites, the {{em:Great Soviet Encyclopedia}} explains that they were “descendants of ancient Turkic peoples that resided within the borders of the Khazar kingdom from the eighth to the tenth century.”{{fn:355}} This theory of the Karaites’ Khazar origins became the accepted one in official Soviet science; it fit the general policy of selecting theories that detached and alienated the peoples of the Soviet Union from their historical roots and cultural heritage. These words were frequently quoted as an authoritative source by the Karaites, the modern “scholars” of Karaism in the Soviet and, especially, post-Soviet periods.
content.comments: [355] “Karaimy.” {{em:The Great Soviet Encyclopedia.}} Moscow: Nauka, 1973, vol. 11, p. 110 (in Russian).

content.english: The generation of Karaites that came of age after World War II in the Soviet Union had no memory of the community’s Jewish roots. Many modern proponents of Karaism who emerged with the fall of the Soviet Union espoused the theories advocated by Szapszał, whereas many activists of Karaite origin sought to distance themselves from the very concept of Karaism. For example, Alexander Polkanov, an ideologue of the Crimean Karaites, writes in his book {{em:Karaites}}:{{fn:356}}
content.comments: [356] Alexander Polkanov. {{em:Krymskie Karaimy}} [The Crimean Karaites]. Paris, 1995 (in Russian). The book was published in 1995 but written more than fifty years earlier. Polkanov was a Russian married to a Karaite woman.

content.english: Today, it can be established on the basis of translations of Mongol and Persian authors of the thirteenth through sixteenth centuries that the Karaites of the Crimea, whose true name is {{em:Kara}} in the singular, and {{em:Kerait}} in the plural, are descendants of the Turkic tribe of the same name, and thus they called themselves in Asia, thus they were called in the Golden Horde, thus they call themselves in the Crimea, Poland, and Lithuania.{{fn:357}}

He continues, “There is information from Chinese sources that during the sixth century they separated from the Kyrgyz tribe and settled in Altai.”{{fn:358}} The Kerait mentioned by Polkanov were a Christian-Nestorian Mongol tribe completely unrelated to the Karaites. The above work and a host of others published in recent decades{{fn:359}} demonstrate that during the twentieth century, the Karaites of Eastern Europe and the Crimea became a different nation unconnected not only to Judaism but also to the Karaism propounded by Szapszał. They deny the existence of any historical link with Karaite communities outside the Crimea and Eastern Europe.

content.english: One of the proponents of this change was Michael Sarach (1909–2000), a Crimean Karaite, businessman, and lawyer who emigrated from the Soviet Union in 1920 and lived most of his life in Paris, where he converted to Christianity and even studied in a Jesuit school. According to Sarach, the Crimean Karaites had neither developed religious teachings nor followed the commandments of the Old Testament but had only practiced shamanism and magic, as was the case with Turkic tribes. Sarach maintained that they had adopted the teachings of ʿAnan from the Khazars (and not {{em:vice versa}}) but only in a superficial form. The teachings of ʿAnan, he argued, were universal and, hence, acceptable to Christians and Muslims. In Sarach’s opinion, it was possible to be Karaite-Christian or Karaite-Muslim.

Sarach financially supported the publication in the former Soviet Union of the {{em:Popular Karaite Encyclopedia}} and of the newspaper {{em:Karaim Haberler}} (Karaite News), both of which were written in Russian. These publications, in addition to news about contemporary Karaite life in the former Soviet Union, had the proclaimed goal of educating the Karaite population. However, the “Karaite legacy” presented in these publications by Sarach and members of the newly built community that was established in the Crimea in the 1990s was quite unconventional. For example, the May 1994 issue of {{em:Karaim Haberler}} includes an article on “famous figures” of world history who were related to Karaism, among them Jesus, being the Prophet of Karaism, and Genghis Khan. In 1998, the newspaper’s editors concluded that its name did not sufficiently reflect the Tur-kic origins of the Crimean Karaites, so they changed it from {{em:Karaite}} {{em:Haberler}} to {{em:Karay Haberler}}, according to the abovementioned root {{em:Kara}} (black) used by Polkanov.
) today

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Karaites, along with other peoples living in the territories of the former USSR, began to return to their roots, establish new communities, and start a process of communal property restitution. However, for most Karaites, the revival of the Karaite heritage is not identified with a return to Judaism. For that matter, they cannot define what Karaism is, and their publications are full of contradictions and unscientific claims. A similar situation exists in contemporary Karaite communities in Lithuania and Poland. A small number of Karaites in the Crimea are returning to Judaism. The possibility of a return is unacceptable to the other Karaites, who identify as a Turkic people.

According to the most recent census in 2014, there are about 570 people in the Crimea who call themselves Karaites. In addition to identifying as a Turkic people, most were born from mixed marriages, and we have no reliable information on how many identify themselves as Jews and with Judaism.
{{header:Conclusion}}
The Karaite communities of the Crimean Peninsula passed through several phases from their settlement there in the thirteenth century until modern times.

During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, under the Tatar Khanate, these communities flourished both economically and culturally. They also supported their coreligionists in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, Jerusalem, Cairo, Damascus, and Istanbul. They developed their own social and educational institutions while collaborating with the Rabbanites across multiple educational disciplines, including information sharing, particularly via book exchanges. They produced a considerable number of treatises in different genres: exegesis, calendrical and halakhic issues, historical chronicles, liturgical poems, and philosophical and polemical works in Hebrew and the Karaite-Tatar ethnolect. The biographies of the authors of these works are mainly unknown or little known. Most of these texts still exist only in manuscripts, having been preserved in Firkovich’s collections. A smaller number of them have found their way into European and American libraries and are still awaiting research and publication.

Following the Russian annexation, Karaite communities entered a new era. The 1830s saw the beginning of a blossoming of economic and cultural life that came to an end in the 1880s. During this period, the changes inherent in the process of modernization, accompanied by the spreading influence of the {{em:Haskalah}} throughout the Russian Empire, led to several results. The successful struggle for equal rights by Karaite leaders, which took several decades to achieve, enabled the Karaites to integrate into Russian society and establish new communities outside the Pale of Settlement.

90This period also saw the emergence of a new Karaite secular literature and numerous periodicals in Karaite-Tatar and Russian. However, this cultural flourishing was replaced by the disintegration of traditional education and institutions and a decline in religious practice. Many of the new communities dissolved as the young men relocated elsewhere for studies or careers, with some converting to Christianity, making it difficult for Karaite women to find matches within the community. This period was characterized by an unprecedented decline in the number of marriages between Karaites. The Hebrew language was gradually forgotten, and synagogues were closed. The Karaite identity underwent a profound and irreversible change, not only as a result of the temptations offered by Russian society, the granting of equal rights, and the consequent assimilation, but also due to the concomitant internal process of disconnection from Judaism. The Karaite leaders, in their struggle for emancipation, promoted severing the links to Judaism, finally presenting it as a specifically Rabbanite phenomenon.

95The Crimean and Eastern European Karaite leaders of the modern era not only established new patterns of relations with the ruling authorities but also completely redefined the Karaite historical, ethnic, and religious identity. The most prominent of these leaders was Abraham Firkovich, a learned Karaite who was deeply rooted in the Karaite tradition and played a central role in altering Karaite life in dramatic ways, far beyond his own expectations. He viewed himself as a leader ushering the members of his flock into a better historical era. While making a decisive contribution to the Karaite community by transforming it into a separate nation, he unintentionally laid the foundations for its de-Judaization. The far-reaching consequence of his activity was the metamorphosis of the Karaite Jewish community into a new ethnocultural group.

After Firkovich’s death, Karaite nationalism adopted a thoroughly anti-Judaic separatist stance, which he had not foreseen. The leaders who succeeded him went further, espousing new theories of an alleged Turkic and Khazar origin of the Karaites. The endeavors of Seraya Szapszał, who deliberately sought to reshape the Crimean and Eastern European Karaites as a separate Turkic nation by introducing pagan values and traditions that were alien to Karaism, led to further assimilation; his ideas served as a basis for more extreme theories that appeared in the 1990s. They completely nullified all manifestations of the original Karaite religion and traditions, and denied any relation between the Eastern European Karaites and the other Karaite communities.

90Thus, over the course of a few centuries, Eastern European Kara­ites transformed from a traditional Jewish community with a unique history into a marginal group denying its identity in favor of invented pagan-type values. In recent decades, however, a small number of Crimean Karaites have returned to Judaism.
